Communication Skills.
Master's degree holders are able to communicate their design choices to diverse audiences, adapting communication based on different recipients and objectives; maximum sensitivity is required in evaluating and orchestrating graphical and verbal discourse in support of or in opposition to various theses involved; in particular, a secure ability to identify weaknesses and strengths in any design choice corresponds to adequate expertise in identifying the best reasons to justify, defend, and account for one's actions.
In laboratories and courses, the set of described skills is explicitly cultivated; in practical experiences and contexts of intense internationalization, these same abilities are refined in languages other than Italian, so that linguistic barriers can be overcome through translingual permeability of acquired communication skills.
Special attention will be given by instructors and tutors in assessing students' ability to rationally argue in support of (but also, when necessary, against, anticipating possible criticisms) their design choices. In class discussions, the ability to dissociate one's opinion from the willingness to identify arguments supporting other positions will be positively evaluated. Clarity of exposition and conceptual adequacy will be highly valued in completing various exam tasks and in presenting the dissertation.
Learning Ability.
Master's degree holders possess broad and rapid learning abilities, enabling them to autonomously direct themselves toward specific fields of study and research not previously addressed. They have research capabilities that allow them to tackle any issue with intensity and quality, readily applying their design experiences to constant cultural growth.
In addition to the tools indicated in relation to the previous descriptors, the primary tool for assessing learning ability will be the project laboratory, where tutors and instructors will monitor students' ability to interact richly and complexly theoretical knowledge and design skills, with these latter developing a greater research capacity, learning from errors and hesitations, and addressing complexity using the resources of relevance research.

-----

UNIVERSITY: University of Sassari
COURSE: [1235] ARCHITECTURE
TYPE: Master's Degree
CURRICULUM: Interuniversity
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://uniss.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10427?annoOrdinamento=2024

Judgment Autonomy.
Master's graduates use architectural design not merely as a tool for problem-solving, but also as a tool for knowledge and exploration of reality; they know how to apply their critical abilities, and generally the entire cultural depth of their university education, in service of their approach to architectural design. In this way, master's graduates are equipped with mature and open judgment capabilities, and through empirical analysis, knowledge management, and project synthesis, they are able to formulate autonomous evaluations and decisions. This autonomy should be understood both as a responsible ability in recruiting concepts and reasoning in relation to an objective, and as the capacity to structure logically comprehensible paths methodologically anchored to shared practices. These results are achieved through:
- project workshops where the autonomy of choice and judgment, although set within group work and shared responsibility, is encouraged;
- critical discussions where students are invited to individually confront difficult situations typical of professional reality;
- constant didactic invitation to formulate judgments and support them with logical reasoning.
In addition to the tools indicated in the previous descriptors, students' ability to support their preferences and choices with rational argumentation and premises derived from various disciplines will be carefully evaluated in written and oral exams, discussions, and the progression of project activities. Judgment autonomy will also be assessed in the individual ability to create an optimal dialectic between the individual and the work group, where specialization does not yield to the global vision and where the group's inertial tendency is hindered and directed by well-motivated, intentional design. The judgment of tutors and experts who will lead workshops and specific didactic activities will be as important as that of the professors in this regard.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Urban Architectural Design Area The teachings of the Area impart knowledge and the ability to understand as the acquisition of appropriate cognitions to interpret the complex themes related to the design transformation of the built environment. In particular, the teachings of the Area, thanks to the work organized in Laboratories, aim to provide tools and methods of design to interpret the different aspects of the project in the existing, sustainability, and architectural and urban design at various scales.

Structural Analysis and Design of Architecture Area The architecture student must know the most important construction systems of mono- and multi-story buildings, with particular reference to resistance to vertical and horizontal actions. Additionally, they must know the limit state calculation method, and verify simple structures in steel and reinforced concrete. Finally, they must be able to calculate permanent and operational loads, snow and wind, and their effects on structures.

Valuation Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Area Students will appropriate the theory of Valuation of Plans, Programs, and Projects both from a formal perspective of deepening approaches and methods, and from an operational perspective for the application of valuation in the construction of the project.

Urban Design and Territorial Planning Area Regarding the field of planning and urbanism, the master's graduate will acquire knowledge that extends and/or strengthens those typically associated with the first cycle, enabling them to elaborate and/or apply original ideas, often in a research context.

This is primarily achieved through the interdisciplinary experience of project laboratories that address problems and outline perspectives for the transformation of the city, territory, and landscape, respecting the system of constraints that condition every design and planning experience, and developing a deep understanding and critical awareness of the most advanced themes and concepts within the field.

Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration Area Students must possess a deep and analytical knowledge of all disciplines contributing to the structuring of the architectural restoration project, i.e., they must be able to:
- critically define the historical context that generated architecture and highlight styles, materials, techniques, needs, characters, craftsmen, and elements of the construction vocabulary;
- recognize the main structural elements of historical architecture and their traditional materials;
- organize the geometric and dimensional survey of a building and its graphical restitution;
- understand the nature of issues related to the structural functioning of a building;
- view the architectural object as connected to its environment, territory, history, and the complexity of the context;
- extract logical schemes of approach and interaction with problems from styles and design experiences.

Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture Area Fundamental knowledge that allows students to link design choices with energy control techniques and environmental comfort. Understanding of the fundamentals of heat transfer, principles of environmental conditioning, and essential concepts of acoustics and lighting technology applied to construction.

Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Construction Production Area The student is trained through knowledge of the characteristics of construction materials and functional coupling criteria; as well as through knowledge of the different articulations and scales of the design process. The student must also know the environmental constraints acting on the building, which lead to material degradation phenomena; at the same time, they must manage the complex technical control of the design underlying the requirement-oriented-prestational approach.

Representation of Architecture and Environment Area Students must demonstrate understanding and full knowledge, also operational:
- of the tools, methods, and techniques of project representation aimed at communicating with the public, engaging them, raising awareness, and encouraging participation;
- of graphic-visual techniques for presenting and interpreting tangible and intangible cultural heritage;
- of accessibility strategies for physical, cultural, and cognitive access to cultural heritage, intended as a tool for protection;
- of digital communication strategies useful to support the design, communication, and dissemination processes of built works, spaces, territories, and all relevant aspects in the design and transformation process of works and spaces.

Economic, Social, Legal Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Area Students must possess a good knowledge of the role of public institutions, sources of law, mechanisms for controlling construction and planning activities at all levels.

Historical Disciplines for Architecture Area Students, having acquired comprehensive knowledge of the most representative monuments of European architecture from the 14th to the 18th century, must develop an understanding of each architectural monument within its historical-cultural context of the city, applying the methodological basis of iconology.

Related or Integrated Training Activities Area The master's student must acquire fundamental knowledge that enables them to frame the characteristics of a complex design environment in which the territory must be read through its environmental and geological configuration, but also through the cultural signs of its anthropization over time. This will allow the student to specify not so much the answers, but the questions that the Project should address to History and Geology, to clarify whether they can be limited to single objects (monuments/documents) and single places, or must investigate the environmental and historical processes that have affected, over time, territories, cities, landscapes, and even more so their intersections, vertical and horizontal.

They must also demonstrate a deep and analytical knowledge of the main methodological-philosophical problems. In particular, it will be important to have a living and dynamic competence in fundamental questions of epistemology and ethics, and a reached awareness regarding their ability to organize and differentiate concepts, control truth claims, and argue choices and theoretical positions.

Moreover, the student must know the principles of ecology and environmental hygiene and be able to apply them in the field of environmental sustainability of design interventions.

Applying Knowledge and Understanding.
Urban Architectural Design Area Application of knowledge occurs through project laboratories, which become the tool to recombine within the design process the architectural, typological, morphological, structural, and environmental aspects.

Project laboratories may coordinate with other disciplines among the characteristic or related and integrated subjects, thus allowing both the application of acquired knowledge in those subjects and the application of interdisciplinary reasoning.

Structural Analysis and Design of Architecture Area The architecture student must be able to preliminary dimension the load-bearing structure of a mono- and multi-story building. Additionally, they must be able to design and verify a simple steel structure including bracing elements, and a simple reinforced concrete structure (slab, beam, column) subject to prevailing vertical actions.

Valuation Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Area Students will be able to apply in practice approaches, methods, and techniques for the multi-criteria valuation of regional, national, and community-level architectural plans, programs, and projects.

Urban Design and Territorial Planning Area The master's graduate, regarding the field of planning and urbanism, will be able to address complex problems of city, territory, and landscape planning, even when defined incompletely and with conflicting specifications, applying acquired knowledge, methods, techniques, and tools. They will also have the ability to design and conduct experiments and interpret their results within interdisciplinary project laboratories.

Additionally, the master's graduate must be able to identify the most appropriate intervention strategies in relation to the distinct planning and design themes and distinguish the required definition scales for different design occasions.

Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration Area Students must be skilled in applying their knowledge to new and unprecedented situations—knowledge responding to a rigorous design methodology that is the basis of architectural restoration.

They must know how to adapt this method to the surrounding historical built environment, developing a process that connects all their knowledge from the geometric and structural reality of the asset, to its material, conservation status, up to restoration hypotheses.

In this, they must know how to integrate and enrich each application through awareness of the cultural dimensions of the intervention developed regarding analysis, and duly integrated regarding construction and management of complexity arising from new and different uses. They will thus be able to develop their technical-scientific and historical-critical competencies in new or innovative contexts, in situations never before addressed, under conditions of partial or vague knowledge of relevant information.

Finally, they will be able to relate the awareness of the need for protection and conservation of the past with current and historical cultural trends, also in relation to the regulatory and professional framework.

Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture Area Ability to apply acquired knowledge and quantify studied phenomena through practical exercises in energy, climate control, acoustics, and lighting technology. Verification of understanding and acquired competencies, but especially the ability to elaborate and apply them in a design context.

Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Construction Production Area The student, starting from the characteristics of known materials, must be able to analyze catalogued technical elements and then design new ones. They must also be able to, through performance evaluation, verify the environmental impact of adopted construction choices and reconstruct, through the technological design of the building, the synthesis between ideation and realization.

Representation of Architecture and Environment Area Students must be able to apply their knowledge and understanding to demonstrate a professional approach to their work, and must possess adequate competencies for a complete experience in constructing territorial analyses based on cartographic foundations; they must be able to communicate information, ideas, problems, and solutions to specialists and non-specialists in the fields of urban planning and territorial planning.

They must acquire the ability to use drawing as an expressive and visual communication act of the design idea from the formation of the idea to its executive definition. Acquire the ability to choose, use, and combine methods, techniques, and tools of representation and communication within all phases of the design process, while being able to use and apply norms and technical knowledge in representation and projects and the graphic languages in different application fields and possible different expressions.

Economic, Social, Legal Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Area Students must apply their knowledge by framing specific legal issues related to a given operational context, particularly regarding:
- public administration; procedures and administrative acts; agreements; private law activities; public administration liability; judicial protection.
- the regulation of territorial governance and protected interests; territorial planning; different types of plans: contents, procedures, and legal nature.
- control over construction activities; authorization titles; abuses and sanctions.

Historical Disciplines for Architecture Area Application of acquired competencies will allow students to design buildings not only functional but also representative of architecture integrated into the historical-cultural context of the place.

Related or Integrated Training Activities Area Through acquired knowledge, the student must be able to overcome the consolidated opinion that a historical context is a container of particularly evident historical objects, possibly well-preserved physically. This will also apply to the other Project, the historical one par excellence, the only one that elevates cultural memory and its fetishes to absolute protagonists: the Restoration, Recovery, and Valorization Project.

They must also demonstrate the ability to apply disciplinary content in the analysis and cognitive organization of any question. The conceptual tools must be at the service of a non-improvised problematization capacity, based on conceptual distinction, hypothesis formulation, propensity for critical control, imagination of alternatives and logically supervised possibilities, and the centrality of rational argumentation.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN

Competencies Associated with the Function.
Generic Profile - Architect The master's graduate in Architecture will be able to design, through the tools of architecture and civil engineering, construction, transformation, and modification operations of the physical environment, with full knowledge of aesthetic, distributive, functional, structural, technical-constructive, management, economic aspects, with critical attention to environmental sustainability issues and cultural changes and the needs expressed by contemporary society.

Function in the Workplace Context.
Generic Profile - Architect The graduate will be able to design, through the tools of architecture and civil engineering, construction, transformation, and modification operations of the physical environment, with full knowledge of aesthetic, distributive, functional, structural, technical-constructive, management, economic, and environmental aspects, with critical attention to cultural changes and the needs expressed by contemporary society. They may prepare project works and direct their realization, coordinating other specialists and operators in the fields of architecture, civil engineering, urban planning, and architectural restoration.

In particular, the graduate will have the following competencies:
- knowledge of methodological-operational aspects related to the disciplinary fields characterizing the study course and the ability to identify and solve architecture and construction problems using updated methods, techniques, and tools;
- adequate knowledge of aspects related to technical and economic feasibility, cost calculation, and the production and realization process of architectural and construction works, as well as aspects related to their safety;
- ability to use the techniques and tools of architectural and construction works design.

These competencies may enable them to have design autonomy:
- in applied research in the field of architecture and civil engineering;
- in the design of buildings and civil works and the connected ideational and procedural processes;
- in the design of restoration interventions on architectural assets, even of complex nature;
- in processes useful for detecting, representing, designing, overseeing the construction and maintenance of works and installations for use and safety systems;
- in the analysis of prices of architectural processes and the economics of construction works.

Description of Specific Training Objectives.
Students enrolling in the Course may choose to simply obtain the Master's Degree in Architecture or may join one of the international pathways, one of which allows obtaining, in addition to the Architecture Degree, the 'Joint Master's Degree European Master in Integrated Sustainable Design in the Mediterranean World'. This title can be obtained by enrolling in the international pathway and attending at least one semester of the courses provided at partner Universities, as well as participating in the workshops provided in the agreement. Students who do not join the international program, or who decide to abandon it, follow simply the courses offered by the Master's Degree Course and obtain the Master's Degree in Architecture. The Course Council has provided for the possibility of offering some courses and/or semesters in English.

The specific training objective of the Master's Degree Course in Architecture is the formation in the field of architectural and urban design at all scales, understood as an integrated activity based on an interdisciplinary and holistic theoretical background, which materializes with attention to themes of materiality, open space and public space, sustainable construction, and attention to historical urban and territorial contexts.

The Course Council has authorized the modification of the Ordinance necessary for the potential activation of two additional curricula beyond the traditional one in Architecture, one on the theme of Architectural Restoration and Historical Contexts and one on Design; these tracks respond to specific needs of contemporary design related to the increasingly frequent request for skills related to the conservation of ancient built heritage and the rapid changes in markets and production, and therefore design and its communication.

All three curricula share the same main training objectives and maintain the didactic skeleton of the degree course as a recognizable element; they differ only in the courses that contribute to defining for the master's graduate opportunities for deepening in the thematic areas of the specific tracks according to the intervals established by the regulations.

The courses specifying the curricula are, however, delivered not only through frontal lectures but also through laboratories that maintain a strong project component.

The degree course as a whole is organized with an innovative conception based substantially on the following aspects:
- 'learning by doing': not only are all acquired theoretical notions systematically verified against reality, but the confrontation itself with real conditions becomes an additional topic for developing critical reasoning;
- structuring of study plans oriented towards the project, allowing direct application of what is learned in the theoretical sections of the courses; thus, the ability to transform concepts into elaborations is acquired, and students become accustomed to the rhythms and deadlines imposed by professional activity;
- pluralistic training achieved both through the cooperation of different disciplines on each individual project and through the teaching of professors from different schools, Italian and foreign;
- the scheduling of thematic laboratories, generally two in a year, follows the changed learning rhythms;
- language learning during work, also through teaching blocks where instruction is conducted in English, to develop not only language knowledge but also the specific disciplinary vocabulary;
- strong openness to the European dimension given both by the organization of teaching and by the extensive use of Erasmus programs, as well as by inclusion in international agreements for the formation of a European learning space that provide for the attribution of double or joint degrees;
- an optimal teacher-student ratio, allowing students to be continuously followed during lectures and laboratory hours;
- extensive and creative use of new technologies as both a study and work environment, as well as for learning and using new professional tools.

This organization of the degree courses arises from a careful analysis and in-depth evaluation of major international experiences in relation to the evolution of disciplines, learning methods, and professional activities.

Each year is divided into semesters, in which university training credits (CFU) are distributed.

The training activity, according to the norms of the University Teaching Regulation and the Department Regulation, is structured as:
- project and deepening teaching blocks
- single-discipline courses
- student-selected activities and internships
- computer and telecommunication skills
- final exam

The semester teaching blocks are coordinated and didactically linked to each other; they are characterized by a complex project theme, requiring the student to use all possessed disciplinary knowledge and converge them towards the objective of solving problems, conducting analyses, and justifying choices.

In each block and for each discipline, frontal lectures, exercises, and integrated project laboratories with teachers and tutors are carried out. Throughout the academic year, courses with extended development and single-discipline courses are also held.

The widespread use of new technologies characterizes the study plan programs, creating a creative study and work environment and allowing the learning and use of new professional tools.

The exam calendar is structured in three sessions: February, July, and September (for project laboratories, the exam is scheduled at the end of the block).

The first year for all available tracks is structured in two semester blocks focused on architectural design and enriched with courses of disciplines converging on the themes raised by project reflection, while the second year presents a first semester part coinciding with the final project block and a second part dedicated to acquiring free credits, further computer and telecommunication knowledge.

Foreign degree Fees and contributions Regulation Career - Fees Roles President ENRICO CICALÒ Program, texts and objectives Professional title conferred by the degree.
Generic profile - Architect The Master's graduate in Architecture can obtain authorization to practice the following regulated professions: Architect, Agricultural Engineer and Forestry Engineer, Civil and Environmental Engineer, Landscape Architect, Territorial Planner.
After passing the professional examination, the graduate naturally finds employment in technical offices of public bodies and private companies, in architecture and engineering firms operating in the field of architectural design or production of building processes and products.
In detail, the graduate may find employment in:
-private design structures organized also as engineering companies;
-public bodies' technical offices integrated in design and management roles of the works tendering process that belong to the contracting authority with primary scientific and disciplinary importance;
-public bodies' technical offices integrated in roles of officials responsible for procedures related to various aspects of territorial control from the perspective of general building activity with primary scientific and disciplinary importance;
-private companies linked to the production and marketing of building products, artifacts and related services.
-professional and educational training structures at various levels, both private and public;
-public bodies of various nature in roles not immediately related to the degree profile but to the level of the academic qualification as an access requirement.
Final exam characteristics.
The final exam consists of submitting a portfolio of activities carried out during the degree program and discussing a final thesis in a public session, prepared under the guidance of a supervising professor, in the form of a graphic design and/or monographic essay, which may also be written in English. Video presentations and explanatory models may be used to support the graphic works.
The CFU allocated for the final exam are 9.
The total points awarded for the final exam are 9, including
- 6 for the discussion of the final thesis
- 3 for international mobility.
Required knowledge for admission.
Candidates applying for admission to the Master's Degree Program must possess the following requirements:
a) passing the national limited-access admission test;
b) holding a Degree in class L17 or having acquired the minimum credits indicated in class L17 for each disciplinary area.
According to the procedures outlined in the Course's Didactic Regulations, a personal preparation assessment based on the candidate's previous academic curriculum, portfolio, and an interview or test is also required.
This assessment will result in an admission ranking.
The evaluation of academic curricula completed abroad will be based on correspondences between course content and Scientific Disciplinary Sectors. Any curricular integrations in terms of CFU must be acquired before the individual preparation assessment.
Degree awarded.

Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities The Master's student must acquire fundamental knowledge enabling them to frame the characteristics of a complex design environment in which the territory must be read through its environmental and geological configuration, but also through the cultural signs of its anthropization over time. This will allow the student to specify not so much the answers, but the questions that the Project should pose to History and Geology, to clarify whether they can be limited to single objects (monuments/documents) and specific places, or whether they must investigate the environmental and historical processes that have affected, over time, territories, cities, landscapes, and even more so their intersections, vertical and horizontal.

They must also demonstrate a deep and analytical knowledge of the main methodological-philosophical issues. In particular, a living and dynamic competence in fundamental questions of epistemology and ethics will be important, along with a developed awareness regarding their ability to organize and differentiate concepts, control truth claims, and argue choices and theoretical positions.

Additionally, the student must know the principles of ecology and environmental hygiene and be able to apply them in the field of environmental sustainability of design interventions.

Application of Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Urban Architectural Design Application of knowledge occurs through project workshops, which become the tool to recombine within the design process the architectural, typological, morphological, structural, and environmental aspects.

Project workshops may coordinate with other disciplines among the core or related and integrative subjects, thus enabling both the application of acquired knowledge in those subjects and the application of interdisciplinary reasoning.

Area of Structural Analysis and Design of Architecture The architectural student must be able to preliminary dimension the load-bearing framework of a single- and multi-story building. Additionally, they must be able to design and verify a simple steel structure, including bracing elements, and a simple reinforced concrete structure (slab, beam, column) subject to predominantly vertical actions.

Area of Valuation Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Students will be able to apply in practice approaches, methods, and techniques for multi-criteria valuation of regional, national, and community-level architectural plans, programs, and projects.

Area of Urban Planning and Territorial Planning The Master's graduate, regarding the field of planning and urbanism, will be able to address complex planning problems of cities, territories, and landscapes, even when defined incompletely and with conflicting specifications, applying acquired knowledge, methods, techniques, and tools. They will also have the ability to design and conduct experiments and interpret their results within interdisciplinary project workshops.

Furthermore, the Master's graduate must be able to identify the most appropriate intervention strategies in relation to distinct planning and design themes and distinguish the required definition scales for different design opportunities.

Area of Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration Students must be skilled in applying their knowledge to new and unprecedented situations—knowledge responding to a rigorous design methodology that forms the basis of architectural restoration.

They must know how to adapt this method to the surrounding historical built environment, developing a process that connects all their knowledge from the geometric and structural reality of the asset, to its material, state of conservation, up to restoration hypotheses.

In this, they must integrate and enrich every application through awareness of the cultural dimensions of the intervention developed in terms of analysis, and duly integrated in terms of construction and management of complexity arising from new and different uses. They will thus be able to develop their technical-scientific and historical-critical competencies in new or innovative contexts, in situations never before addressed, under conditions of partial or vague knowledge of relevant information.

Finally, they will be able to relate the awareness of the need for preservation and conservation of the past with current and historical cultural trends, also considering the regulatory and professional framework.

Area of Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture Ability to apply acquired knowledge and quantify studied phenomena through practical exercises in energy, climate control, acoustics, and lighting technology. Verification of understanding and competencies acquired, but especially the ability to elaborate and apply them in a design context.

Area of Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Building Production Starting from the characteristics of known materials, the student must be able to analyze cataloged technical elements and then design new ones. They must also be able to, through performance evaluation, verify the environmental impact of adopted construction choices and reconstruct, through the technological design of the building, the synthesis between ideation and realization.

Area of Architecture and Environment Representation Students must be capable of applying their knowledge and understanding to demonstrate a professional approach to their work, possessing adequate competencies for a comprehensive experience in constructing territorial analyses based on cartographic foundations; they must be able to communicate information, ideas, problems, and solutions to specialists and non-specialists in urban planning and territorial planning.

They must acquire the ability to use drawing as an expressive and visual communication act of the design idea, from the formation of the idea to its executive definition. Acquire the ability to choose, use, and combine methods, techniques, and tools of representation and communication within all phases of the design process, while being capable of using and applying norms and technical knowledge in representation and projects and the graphic languages in different application fields and possible different expressions.

Area of Economic, Social, and Legal Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Students must apply their knowledge by framing specific legal issues related to a given operational context, particularly regarding:
- public administration; procedures and administrative acts; agreements; private law activities; public administration liability; judicial protection.
- territorial governance regulations and protected interests; territorial planning; different types of plans: content, procedures, and legal nature.
- control over construction activities; authorization titles; abuses and sanctions.

Area of Historical Disciplines for Architecture Application of acquired competencies will enable students to design buildings not only functional but also representative of architecture integrated into the historical-cultural context of the location.

Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities Through acquired knowledge, the student must be able to overcome the entrenched opinion that a historical context is a container of particularly evident historical objects, possibly well-preserved physically. This will also apply to the other Project, the historical one par excellence, the only one that elevates cultural memory and its fetishes to absolute protagonists: the Restoration, Recovery, and Valorization Project.

They must also demonstrate the ability to apply disciplinary content in the analysis and cognitive organization of any issue. The conceptual tools must serve a non-improvised problematization capacity, based on conceptual distinction, hypothesis formulation, critical control propensity, imagination of alternative and logically supervised possibilities, and the centrality of rational argumentation.

Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIAN Associated competencies for the role.
Generic Profile - Architect The Master's graduate in Architecture will be able to design, through the tools of architecture and civil engineering, construction, transformation, and modification operations of the physical environment, with full knowledge of aesthetic, distributive, functional, structural, technical-constructive, managerial, economic aspects, with critical attention to environmental sustainability issues and cultural changes and the needs expressed by contemporary society.

Role in the workplace.
Generic Profile - Architect The graduate will be able to design, through the tools of architecture and civil engineering, construction, transformation, and modification operations of the physical environment, with full knowledge of aesthetic, distributive, functional, structural, technical-constructive, managerial, economic, and environmental aspects, with critical attention to cultural changes and the needs expressed by contemporary society. They may prepare project works and direct their implementation, coordinating other specialists and operators in the fields of architecture, civil engineering, urban planning, and architectural restoration.

In particular, the graduate will possess the following competencies:
- knowledge of methodological-operational aspects related to the disciplinary fields characterizing the study program and the ability to identify and solve architectural and construction problems using updated methods, techniques, and tools;
- adequate knowledge of aspects concerning technical and economic feasibility, cost calculation, and the production and realization process of architectural and construction works, as well as aspects related to their safety;
- ability to use the techniques and tools of architectural and construction works design.

These competencies may enable them to exercise autonomous design:
- in applied research in the fields of architecture and civil engineering;
- in the design of buildings and civil works and the connected ideational and procedural processes;
- in the design of restoration interventions on architectural assets, even of complex nature;
- in processes useful for surveying, representing, designing, overseeing construction, and maintaining architectural and engineering works and systems related to safety;
- in the analysis of prices of architectural processes and economic aspects of construction works.

Specific training objectives description.
Students enrolling in the Course may choose to simply obtain the Master's Degree in Architecture or may join one of the international pathways, one of which allows obtaining, in addition to the Architecture degree, the 'Joint Master's Degree European Master in Integrated Sustainable Design in the Mediterranean World'. This title can be obtained by enrolling in the international pathway and attending at least one semester of the courses provided at partner universities, as well as participating in the workshops provided in the agreement. Students who do not join the international program, or who decide to leave it, follow only the courses offered by the Master's Degree Course and obtain the Master's Degree in Architecture. The Course Council has provided for the possibility of delivering some courses and/or semesters in English.

The specific training objective of the Master's Degree Course in Architecture is the formation in the field of architectural and urban design at all scales, understood as an integrated activity based on an interdisciplinary and holistic theoretical background, materializing through attention to themes of materiality, open space, public space, sustainable construction, and attention to historical urban and territorial contexts.

The Course Council has authorized the modification of the Ordinamento necessary for the potential activation of two curricula beyond the traditional one in Architecture, one on the theme of Architectural Restoration and Historical Contexts and one on Design; these specializations respond to specific needs of contemporary design related to the recurring demand for skills related to the conservation of ancient built heritage and the rapid changes in markets and production, and thus design and its communication.

All three curricula share the same main training objectives and maintain the didactic structure of the degree course as a recognizable element; they differ only in the courses contributing to defining for the Master's graduate opportunities for deepening in the thematic areas of the specific curricula according to the intervals established by the regulations.

The courses specifying the curricula are, however, delivered not only through lectures but also through workshops maintaining a strong design component.

The degree course as a whole is organized with an innovative conception based substantially on the following aspects:
- 'learning by doing': not only are all acquired theoretical notions systematically verified against reality, but the confrontation itself with real conditions becomes an additional topic for developing critical reasoning;
- structuring of study plans oriented toward design, allowing direct application of what is learned in the theoretical sections of courses; thus, the ability to transform concepts into elaborations is acquired, and students become accustomed to the rhythms and deadlines imposed by professional activity;
- pluralistic training achieved both through the cooperation of different disciplines on each individual project and through the teaching of professors from different schools, Italian and foreign;
- the scheduling of thematic workshops, generally two per academic year, follows the changed learning rhythms;
- language learning during work, also through didactic blocks where teaching is conducted in English, to develop not only language knowledge but also the specific disciplinary lexicon;
- strong openness to the European dimension, given both by the organization of teaching and by the extensive use of Erasmus programs, as well as inclusion in international agreements for the formation of a European learning space that provide for the attribution of double or joint degrees;
- an optimal ratio between the number of professors and the number of students, allowing students to be continuously followed during lectures and workshops;
- extensive and creative use of new technologies as both a study and work environment, as well as for learning and using new professional tools.

This course organization arises from a careful analysis and in-depth evaluation of major international experiences in relation to the evolution of disciplines, learning methods, and professional activities.

Each year is divided into semesters, during which the university training credits (CFU) are distributed.

The training activity, according to the norms of the University Didactic Regulation and the Department of Architecture, Design, and Urban Planning Regulation, is structured as:
- project and in-depth didactic blocks
- single-discipline courses
- student-selected activities and internships
- computer and telecommunication skills
- final exam

The semester-long didactic blocks are coordinated and didactically linked to each other; they are characterized by a complex design theme requiring students to use all their disciplinary knowledge and converge it toward the objective of solving problems, conducting analyses, and justifying choices.

In each block and for each discipline, frontal lessons, exercises, and integrated project workshops with professors and tutors are carried out. Throughout the academic year, prolonged development courses and single-discipline courses are also held.

The widespread use of new technologies characterizes the study plan programs, creating a creative study and work environment and enabling the learning and use of new professional tools.

The exam calendar is structured into three sessions: February, July, and September (for design workshops, the exam is scheduled at the end of the block).

The first year for all available curricula is structured into two semester blocks focused on architectural design and enriched with courses of disciplines converging on the themes raised by design reflection, while the second year presents a first semester coinciding with the final design block and a second part dedicated to acquiring free credits, further computer and telecommunication knowledge.

Program, Texts, and Objectives Professional status conferred by the degree.
Specialist Social Worker (after passing the State Exam and registration with the appropriate Register); expert in social policies and social services planning; expert in community development policies and well-being planning; expert in organizing resources and structures for managing third-sector and social private organizations. The main work areas where the graduate can primarily exercise their profession are those connected to public bodies (e.g., Municipalities, Provinces, Regions, Territorial Offices of the Ministries of Justice and Health, etc.), to social private entities (e.g., Social Cooperatives, Social Enterprises, Consortia of Cooperatives, etc.), as well as independent professional practice.
The main professional opportunities for which the course provides solid specific preparation are those of Specialist Social Worker (after passing the State Exam and registration with the Professional Register of Social Workers), the expert in social policies and social services planning, and the expert in community development policies and processes.
Final Exam Characteristics. The Master's thesis consists of an original treatment conducted by the student under the guidance of a supervisor and a co-supervisor, whose outcome takes the form of a written document (approximately 150 pages) on a topic consistent with the specialist path followed by the student (LM-87); the thesis may refer to theoretical elaborations, empirical research paths, field observations, or in-depth re-evaluation of internship experiences.
The final document, whether entirely theoretical, empirical and research-based, or practical design, must be built around a broad and solid theoretical framework based on an adequate and in-depth exploration of the classical and contemporary literature.
Students may be directed towards the preparation of a service thesis. A service thesis is a particular form of research with the explicit purpose of providing knowledge services to organizations (public bodies, associations, third-sector organizations, etc.) and private citizens who request it from the Course of Study regarding issues of collective interest.
In such cases, the student's work is particularly aimed at meeting the quantitative and qualitative requirements of a standard thesis. Additionally, under the scientific supervision of the supervisor and co-supervisor, the student will be required to provide the requesting organization or body with a knowledge product, in the forms to be agreed upon each time, based on a specific research agreement between the interested student, the scientific supervisor, and the requesting organization.
This method of conducting the final exam is particularly aimed at satisfying the European descriptors of the degree title (so-called Dublin Descriptors) related to the application and management of skills and knowledge in new and broad contexts, communication abilities with specialist and non-specialist interlocutors, and autonomy in study and judgment.
Service theses fall within the framework of the now forty-year experience of Science Shops, active especially in Europe but also present outside the European context (http://www.livingknowledge.org/science-shops/about-science-shops/).
Required Knowledge for Admission. To access the Master's Degree Course, one must possess one of the following titles:
a) four-year degree in Social Service Sciences
b) three-year degree in Social Service (L-39 or Class 6)
c) D.U.S.S. diploma and schools directed for special purposes for social assistants + Registration with the Social Assistants Register
d) university validation of the Social Assistant diploma (validation as per Article 5 of D.P.R. 14/1987. Diplomas of Social Assistant validated under Article 4 of D.P.R. 14/1987 are not valid) + Registration with the Social Assistants Register + Exercise of the profession for at least five years
If one does not possess one of the above titles, at least a first-level degree is required, and at least 60 ECTS credits, as follows:
- IUS/01 and/or IUS/09: at least 12 ECTS
- SPS/07: at least 9 ECTS
- SPS/08 and/or SPS/09 and/or SPS/10 and/or SPS/11 and/or SPS/12: at least 6 ECTS
- M-PSI/01 and/or M-PSI/04 and/or M-PSI/05: at least 15 ECTS
- M-DEA/01: at least 6 ECTS
- INF/01: at least 6 ECTS or equivalent university training activity or internationally recognized certification
- All SSD related to EU foreign languages: at least 6 ECTS or equivalent university training activity or internationally recognized certification
Additionally, personal preparation must be verified.
The criteria for enrollment in the Master's Degree Course in Social Service and Social Policies (LM87), as well as the required knowledge and admission criteria, are established by the Didactic Regulations. They are published on the website of the Department of Humanities and Social Sciences (www.dumas.uniss.it) well in advance of the enrollment opening.

Communication Skills.
It is expected from LM 87 to train a professional capable of clear communication – of the acquired knowledge – with the various actors of social policies: with institutional and non-institutional interlocutors, with specialists and non-specialists (with particular reference to third-sector operators but also to informal caregivers and citizens); the communication ability must also take into account specific professional languages, relevant to coordination and collaborative work with other social professions that, in different capacities, participate in the realization of cohesion and social integration projects. Intercultural competencies will be encouraged to foster the ability to dialogue with various actors in order to promote and manage participatory processes.
The teaching tools through which these learning outcomes can be achieved are on-site internships, group work, research methodology workshops, thematic research seminars, and the production of scientific documentation (specific to their field of study). Within some courses, laboratory and group activities specifically dedicated to writing are provided. In addition to passing exams, formative evaluation methods are provided through interviews, practical tests, and self-assessment meetings. A specific teaching tool for the development of communication skills is constituted by the so-called 'service thesis' (see further: A5.b)
Learning Ability.
The graduate in LM 87 must be able to identify research issues that allow for autonomous continuation of studies and research, as well as to identify appropriate training paths for necessary professional updating and continuous education; they must recognize those institutional organizational opportunities useful for social leadership that responds to changing needs, a situation requiring constant adaptation of interpretative competencies. The teaching tools through which these learning outcomes can be achieved are on-site internships, group work, research methodology workshops where further knowledge questions are developed (with specific reference to their field of study). In addition to passing exams, formative evaluation methods are provided through interviews, practical tests, and self-assessment meetings.

Critical Judgment.
The graduate in LM 87 must demonstrate discernment and direction in the task of collecting and interpreting data related to the study and organization of factors of collective well-being; must be able to express reflective professionalism, aware of the reasons for their actions and ready to account for their social and ethical responsibilities; in light of the professional ethics of the social assistant and the principles of responsible research and innovation, must ensure to the community the fundamental skills and knowledge for the design of social services. The teaching methods and tools through which the expected learning outcomes can be achieved include on-site internships, theme-based research seminars, training stages, research methodology workshops focused on social design, group work on case studies, and field research experiences. In addition to passing exams, formative assessment is provided through interviews, practical tests, and self-assessment meetings. A specific teaching tool for developing critical judgment is the so-called "service thesis."
Knowledge and Understanding.
Sociological and Social Service Disciplines. Students must acquire in-depth knowledge of sociological and social service theories in relation to various intervention and research methods, as well as the design and evaluation of interventions in social contexts within complex settings. The course structure aims to stimulate students to develop a critical perspective on the main fields of application of different social work methods in the current context of public policies in general and social policies in particular. Special attention is given to the complexities of contexts characterized by high multiculturalism and social fragility. Particular attention is dedicated to the specificity of the person and their resources, especially in family and community contexts. Students must acquire adequate understanding of participatory processes in the dynamics of social promotion and community development. They must also develop in-depth knowledge of the cultures and values of social professions alongside current and future challenges facing the profession.
Legal Disciplines. Students will be required to develop adequate knowledge of the legal aspects characterizing the operational fields of services for individuals, in order to interact with public, private, and third sector institutions operating in territories with communities and individuals. Students must know the legal and administrative principles related to social services, have an adequate overview of the reform of social services and public administration, know the legal subjects operating in the third sector, and understand the tools for implementing the integrated social services system, the regulatory framework of social services, administrative responsibilities, and the limits of professional action. They must also know elements of law related to the European Union and the protection of human rights to place the legal discussion within a broader context and an international horizon.
Political, Economic, and Statistical Disciplines. Students must acquire knowledge useful for understanding decision-making and management processes applied to the field of social policies. They must know the orientations linked to social entrepreneurship, approaches to business strategies and policies, and the impact assessment of technologies on the territory. They must also develop adequate skills in manipulating and analyzing standardized data to support programming and the formulation of social policies.
Psychopedagogical, Anthropological, and Philosophical Disciplines. Students will be required to develop concepts and tools for understanding the dynamics of space usage in relation to social and cultural change processes through the main contributions of social sciences, also in a comparative perspective. Students must know analytical models based on exemplary ethnographic cases and anthropological models for analyzing the use of urban and rural space.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Sociological and Social Service Disciplines. Students must be able to collect and organize the information and knowledge necessary to understand and coordinate the work of professionals in social and educational services in contexts characterized by multiculturalism and social fragility. They must be able to develop project ideas in complex contexts and place them within the broader framework of social policies. They must be able to organize and coordinate network services and interventions and evaluate the impacts of professional work with reference to scientific evidence. They must be able to initiate genuinely promotional participatory designs in the field of services for individuals. They must be able to critically read territorial dynamics in relation to their needs, resources, and main social and cultural characteristics. The teaching methods and tools through which the expected results are verified include written and/or oral exams, exercises, and assignments that require students to demonstrate competent acquisition of tools, methodologies, and autonomous critical ability.
Legal Disciplines. The applied competencies developed in the legal field will enable graduates to perform leadership tasks in complex welfare structures and services, with a view to the responsibility of processes and outcomes. Graduates must be able to retrieve, understand, and use the regulations governing administrations and the social private sector in relation to the organization, management, and programming of services for individuals. They must be able to identify and use the main legal tools for constructing an integrated services system. The teaching methods and tools through which the expected results are verified include written and/or oral exams, exercises, and assignments that require students to demonstrate competent acquisition of tools, methodologies, and autonomous critical ability.
Political, Economic, and Statistical Disciplines. Students must have acquired the ability to participate in the construction of social policies and the production of data related to social issues, and to guide the construction and coordination of social programs or enterprises. The teaching methods and tools through which the expected results are verified include written and/or oral exams, exercises, and assignments that require students to demonstrate competent acquisition of tools, methodologies, and autonomous critical ability.
Psychopedagogical, Anthropological, and Philosophical Disciplines. Students must be able to understand and guide policies for the use and transformation of urban spaces and landscapes in relation to social and cultural change processes, social inequality phenomena, globalization, mobility, and gentrification. The teaching methods and tools through which the expected results are verified include written and/or oral exams, exercises, and assignments that require students to demonstrate competent acquisition of tools, methodologies, and autonomous critical ability.

Competencies Associated with the Role.
Specialist Social Assistant (following the passing of the State Exam and registration with the appropriate Register); expert programmer of social policies and social services; expert programmer of development policies and community well-being; expert in the organization of resources and structures for managing third sector and social private organizations. Graduates of this program must:
- Possess competencies for decoding complex needs of individuals, families, groups, and territories, for formulating social diagnoses, for psychosocial counseling, for mediation interventions in family, juvenile, social, and penal contexts, for managing and organizing resources in both public and social private sectors;
- Possess in-depth social research methodologies related to data collection and processing and understanding the functioning of complex societies, particularly in specific application areas;
- Possess theoretical and practical competencies related to Community-Based Research and community empowerment through participation;
- Possess competencies for designing integrated systems of territorial and community well-being and initiating and managing, at local, national, and international levels, programs for information, awareness, responsibility, consensus, and social protection for individuals, groups, and communities, to safeguard their social rights;
- Possess managerial design, planning, organization, and management skills in the fields of social policies, social services, and socio-health services, public and social private; analysis and evaluation of service quality and performance;
- Possess adequate competencies for communication with diverse publics and interlocutors and correct information management;
- Be able to use at least one European Union language in addition to Italian, including disciplinary terminology.
Role in the Workplace Context.
Specialist Social Assistant (following the passing of the State Exam and registration with the appropriate Register); expert programmer of social policies and social services; expert programmer of development policies and community well-being; expert in the organization of resources and structures for managing third sector and social private organizations. Graduates of this program can perform organizational, management, and consulting roles for individuals, organizations, and institutions; these roles may concern relational dynamics, human resource management, organization of resources and structures, economic management of entities, services, and organizations, as well as programming and designing social policies for territorial and community development. Graduates can also perform coordination, programming, and design roles for services and activities, promotion, prevention, and recovery of complex need situations related to individual, group, and community work. Graduates can engage in professional activities, including independently, in preventive-promotional, managerial, educational-training, and research areas, as well as in supporting processes of social inclusion and cohesion, recognition of social rights, promotion of community development and well-being, and fostering participatory processes and active citizenship. Graduates can perform the above roles in collaboration with other professional figures operating in the field of social policies and services for individuals, families, and communities, such as professional educators, psychologists, political science specialists, etc.
Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
Educational Objectives:
The course aims to train professionals capable of occupying roles in public administration or social private organizations related to the programming of territorial social policies, organization and coordination of services, promotion and management of processes through which social policies are designed and implemented, and promotion of well-being and community development. At the end of the educational path, graduates must:
- Possess adequate knowledge of the organization of welfare services and the administrative structures and rules that organize and govern them;
- Be able to understand the overall framework of public and social policies and contextualize governance projects within such settings;
- Possess adequate knowledge of the organization of welfare services and the relationships linking programming, governance, and service delivery of public utility with the involvement of the social private sector;
- Be able to carry out activities of elaboration, planning, and direction of programs in the field of social policies and services;
- Be able to carry out activities of directing services in the field of social policies and services and coordinating interventions;
- Be able to design and implement monitoring and evaluation processes for implemented interventions;
- Be able to promote and govern participation processes;
- Possess tools for effective analysis of processes concerning major social issues, such as social exclusion and deviance, youth distress, intergenerational relationships, poverty, social conflicts, migrations, etc.;
- Be able to conduct social research to support public decision-making (Research-Based Policies);
- Be able to combine social research with intervention aimed at promoting change (Community-Based Research);
- Possess adequate tools for analyzing inter-ethnic integration processes and community cohesion.
Educational Path:
Consistent with the above objectives, the educational path is structured around a substantial offering of sociological, social policy, and social service subjects. These courses address the evaluation of services for individuals, as well as programming, public policies, and the challenges social services face in the current welfare structure. Related courses also explore themes concerning participation dynamics, community cohesion, and activation of collective resources for development and well-being (courses in discipline sector SPS/07). Special emphasis is placed on training the link between research, programming, and intervention (SPS/07). Specific focus is given to phenomena of human mobility, inter-ethnic relations, and family (SPS/08). Legal discipline modules pay particular attention to the institutional and administrative dimension of public and social policy systems and the public-private nexus in programming and management (IUS/09 and IUS/10). The international dimension is emphasized, particularly regarding existing European regulations (IUS/14) and international humanitarian law and human rights protection (IUS/13). The educational offering in political, economic, statistical, and anthropological disciplines is dedicated to acquiring knowledge related to the political, social, cultural, and economic dimensions of territories where collective service delivery systems operate. Special attention is given to using data for territorial analysis to support public decision-making (SECS-S/05), managing social private enterprises (SECS-P/07), and in-depth knowledge of cultural systems in communities (M-DEA/01). Learning occurs through traditional classroom activities, as well as through systematic engagement with practice via field experiences, visits, and testimonies from international experts. Group and laboratory activities are emphasized. Special attention is given to theoretical-practical training through 300 hours of internship (12 CFU), supervised by qualified specialist social assistants and/or experts in service programming. Placements occur in both public entities and social private organizations, in line with the student's individual study path. Internship access is organized according to principles established in a specific regulation.

Program, texts and objectives Access to further studies.
Master's Degree or Specialist Degree for access to doctoral schools, second-level master's.
Professional status conferred by the title.
Scientific Researcher Historical Sciences Researcher Philosophical Sciences Researcher Cultural Manager and Operator Archivist Librarian Public and Private Enterprise Consultant Communication and Information Field Consultant Editors, Publicists, and Journalists (after registration with the order, if necessary) Text Reviewers
Final exam characteristics.
The final exam consists of the presentation and discussion of a written dissertation (thesis), characterized by the originality of the research, consistent with the training path, and agreed upon with the supervising professor.
The dissertation text, articulated and in-depth, will be supported by an appropriate critical apparatus and, if necessary, supplemented with sources and multimedia supports.
The thesis will be discussed before the Commission and in the presence of at least one co-supervisor who will verify: the competencies acquired by the graduate in their field of study; the ability to develop original research paths; possession of solid critical skills in formulating the topics treated; awareness of research tools.
Required knowledge for access.
For admission to the Course, one must hold a degree, obtained under D.M. 270/2004, in Cultural Heritage Sciences - L1, Philosophy - L5, Letters - L10, Linguistic Mediation - L12, Education and Training Sciences - L19, Communication Sciences - L20, History - L42, or a degree obtained according to the corresponding classes of D.M. 509/1999 or previous regulations, or another foreign degree recognized as suitable for admission to the Course.
Additionally, graduates in the aforementioned classes must have earned at least 40 CFU in some of the following SSD: M-FIL/01 - Theoretical Philosophy M-FIL/02 Logic and Philosophy of Science M-FIL/03 Moral Philosophy M-FIL/04 Aesthetics M-FIL/05 Philosophy and Linguistic Theories M-FIL/06 History of Philosophy M-FIL/07 History of Ancient Philosophy L-ANT/02 Greek History L-ANT/03 Roman History M-STO/01 Medieval History M-STO/02 Modern History M-STO/04 Contemporary History M-DEA/01 Ethnoanthropological Disciplines M-GGR/01, M-GGR/02 Geography
Additionally, a level of competence in one of the European Union languages to be taught in the Course at B1 level is required.
Curricular requirements and initial knowledge necessary for access to the course will be verified through the assessment methods to be established in the didactic regulation.
Expected employment and professional opportunities for graduates.
Scientific Researcher Historical Sciences Researcher Philosophical Sciences Researcher Cultural Manager and Operator Archivist Librarian Public and Private Enterprise Consultant Communication and Information Field Consultant Editors, Publicists, and Journalists (after registration with the order, if necessary) Text Reviewers
Communication skills.
Master's graduates in the interclass course will be able to argue at a high level the topics of their research.
Awareness of the differences between various historical periods and contexts will be translated into the ability to use oral, written, and multimedia registers with mastery.
They must be able to develop and organize, both in oral and written presentation, a style appropriate for communicating their ideas, using standard text types of their scientific field, such as reviews, critical essays, reports within defined timeframes, and the preparation of papers.
They must be able to differentiate their knowledge transmission technique according to the chosen communication circuit, also through the use of the most modern and appropriate educational technologies.
Such skills will be acquired through participation in various teaching activities (lectures, seminars), participation in cultural events (conferences, debates, workshops), and consultation of texts of different critical orientations.
The acquisition of such skills will be assessed through the following methods: passing exams and written assessment tests, exercises during teaching activities, evaluation of the final thesis.

CURRICULUM: Judgment Autonomy
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://uniss.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10758

Judgment Autonomy.
Attention to research implies a strong and constant encouragement for students to develop their own ability to formulate independent, reasoned, and articulated judgments. This encouragement is based on motivating students to know the most up-to-date developments in disciplinary research in each of the specialization and orientation areas of the study program, as well as to be able to enrich that knowledge by developing original contributions. In this regard, two characteristic features of the study program assume particular importance: the constant comparison with sources and the plurality of approaches and interpretations. Judgment autonomy will be acquired through participation in various teaching activities (lectures, seminars), participation in cultural events (conferences, debates, workshops), and consultation of texts of different critical orientations.
The acquisition of this ability will be assessed through the following methods: passing exams and written assessment tests, exercises during teaching activities, evaluation of the final thesis.
Learning Ability.
Master's graduates must have developed flexibility in understanding and arguing, as well as the ability to independently organize their study and research paths, also in view of further progression (Doctorates, additional Master's Degrees, Active Training Internships, or Masters). They must also have developed the ability to navigate the high-specialization training offer through full awareness of the different research orientations in the field of human sciences and the communication of knowledge. Such learning abilities will be acquired through participation in various teaching activities (lectures, seminars), participation in cultural events (conferences, debates, workshops), and consultation of texts of different critical orientations. The acquisition of these abilities will be assessed through the following methods: passing exams and written assessment tests, exercises during teaching activities, evaluation of the final thesis.
Knowledge and Understanding.
Philosophical disciplines Independent knowledge of the themes, historical moments, and problematic aspects addressed by philosophical thought from antiquity to the contemporary age.
Historical-institutional disciplines Advanced knowledge of the developments of civilization history from antiquity to the present, of institutions, sources for historical knowledge and reconstruction, and heuristic and historiographical tools.
Social and territorial disciplines Knowledge of anthropological research practices; knowledge and understanding of issues related to identity and multiculturalism in historical and contemporary contexts. Knowledge of conceptual tools for analysis and interpretation for reading the landscape in an evolutionary sense.
Philological disciplines Knowledge of the Latin language, ancient, medieval, and humanistic philologies and literatures expressed in Latin or in Romance vernaculars.
Linguistic disciplines Valid knowledge (both written and oral) of a foreign language.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Philosophical disciplines Ability to independently analyze internal issues within the philosophical tradition, skills in navigating new trends in contemporary philosophical debate, critical elaboration of ideas and concepts, ability to deepen and transmit the cultural content and values of philosophical inquiry.
Historical-institutional disciplines Advanced skills in understanding the historical dynamics underlying phenomena, processes, and structures of the contemporary world; mastery of critical tools for source exegesis; critical knowledge of historiographical orientations; understanding and knowledge of historical-institutional events and ability to critically evaluate past and current interpretations.
Social and territorial disciplines Ability to apply theoretical-practical knowledge in social or cultural research, particularly in relation to fundamental social issues of identity and multiculturalism. Advanced skills in understanding the complex relationships between the physical environment and human group activities.
Philological disciplines Ability to approach original texts and use acquired knowledge in research for direct engagement with sources.
Linguistic disciplines Use of a language for effective communication on content related to the disciplines covered by the course.
Official Language(s) of Teaching and Assessment.
ITALIAN Associated Competencies.
Scientific Researcher Ability to set up, conduct, and coordinate specialized research in the fields of historical or philosophical disciplines.
Manager and Cultural Operator Ability to promote and coordinate cultural initiatives that relate not only to the humanistic field but also to interdisciplinary competencies.
Ability to provide consultancy support to public bodies and private companies operating in the field of cultural production and scientifically qualified communication.
Ability in managing and coordinating human resources.
Consultant in Communication and Information Ability to provide consultancy support to public bodies and private companies operating in the field of cultural production and scientifically qualified communication.
Ability to coordinate editorial activities at various levels.
Work Context Role.
Scientific Researcher Researcher and consultant for universities, research centers, and public and private institutions.
Manager and Cultural Operator High-responsibility operator in the field of cultural services and production, responsible functions in human resource management.
Consultant in Communication and Information Consultant and coordinator in the field of communication and information with specific reference to historical-philosophical competencies.
Description of Specific Training Objectives.
The interdepartmental Master's Degree in Historical and Philosophical Sciences aims to achieve an interdisciplinary training that effectively and cohesively integrates the knowledge derived from a solid historical education with the analytical rigor and habit of abstract reasoning characteristic of philosophical disciplines. Through an extensive and in-depth study of the disciplinary content of the two reference areas, the graduate in Historical and Philosophical Sciences must have developed a deep awareness of the historical nature of every philosophical problematization exercise and will be able to accompany this awareness with adequate knowledge of the methodological and epistemological debate on the status of historical and philosophical sciences. On this basis, one of the main specific objectives the Master's program aims to achieve is to train the figure of a cultural operator capable of reading and interpreting historical sources and texts of the philosophical tradition with competence, appropriate knowledge, and critical abilities. The Master's program seeks to achieve this objective by providing students with appropriate tools for both contextualization and content and formal analysis of the documents in question. This is not only in terms of knowledge of the specific disciplinary knowledge of the historical and philosophical area, but also in the development of aptitude for critical and dialogic thinking.
