UNIVERSITY: University of Sassari
COURSE: [1212] SCIENCES OF ARCHITECTURE AND DESIGN
SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://uniss.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10402

Autonomy of Judgment.
Graduates are able to formulate pertinent and insightful judgments on various disciplinary and transdisciplinary issues, doing so by correctly and rationally applying the acquired knowledge, demonstrating the ability to skillfully manipulate concepts and theories, and to draw upon knowledge in the service of the moment's cognitive and operational objectives. Their judgment capacity is guided and open to the multiplicity of possible approaches, structured by awareness of the complexity of issues and distant from a merely solution-oriented conception of architectural or urbanistic projects. Typically formulated judgments by graduates contain notable elements of originality, but are always anchored to the fundamental ability to explore and understand the world, so that even the formulation of a judgment becomes, always, an additional heuristic and a hypothesis to be tested. Moreover, graduates subject every judgment to their own ability to discuss and doubt, supporting it with reasoned argumentation. It is particularly important to highlight, in every occasion, the cultural, social, philosophical, historical, and technical-scientific aspects that deepen and give substance to any design issue. These outcomes are pursued through:
- integrated teaching blocks where the same dialogue between professors forces students to continuously translate and compare personal and disciplinary viewpoints;
- project workshops inspired by complexity and interdisciplinarity;
- constant didactic reference to the adoption of new theoretical perspectives and the necessity to provide reasoned justifications for actual and possible choices;
- interpersonal discussion, achieved through group work and critical classroom discussions;
- cultivation of autonomy of judgment.
Evaluation tools, in addition to those indicated in previous descriptors, consist of constant verification by professors and tutors of students' ability to work in groups with a critical spirit and autonomous judgment capacity. It is important, both during the examination and thesis verification, to require and reward autonomy of judgment; and, in collective teaching activities, to evaluate that dynamics between individual and group (both in discussions and in project collaborations) serve both synergy and the valorization of innovative and reasoned personal contributions.
Learning Ability.
Graduates are able to synthesize acquired knowledge to form a valid basis for further deepening, and are able to formulate autonomous judgments on various issues—though guided by main theoretical orientations. They have derived from the study course a learning methodology that enables them to approach further studies by optimally utilizing acquired skills within a framework of increasing autonomy and progressively greater conceptual and theoretical complexity. Every opportunity for professional growth naturally becomes a moment for knowledge and theoretical deepening. They possess critical awareness to identify, among their experiences, those with relevance to motivate theoretical research representing the continuation of university training during subsequent professional engagement.
The project laboratory—with its multiple interim evaluation moments—is the primary tool for evaluating students' ability to select the most important teaching experiences for new tasks they gradually face. Professors and tutors can observe the growth over time of learning abilities through constant contact during project activities, continuous interaction, and progressive requests for feedback.
Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematical Disciplines for Architecture Knowledge and understanding of the languages, concepts, and theorems of the basic disciplines of linear algebra, mathematical analysis, and information processing systems.
Area of Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture Fundamental knowledge enabling students to link design choices with energy control techniques and environmental comfort. Understanding of the fundamentals of heat transmission, principles of environmental conditioning, and essential concepts of acoustics and lighting technology applied to construction.
Area of Historical Disciplines for Architecture Students must:
- critically define the historical context that generated architecture and highlight in it styles, needs, characters, craftsmanship, and elements of the construction vocabulary;
- recognize the main construction elements of architecture;
- understand the nature of issues related to the functioning of a building;
- view the architectural object as connected to the environment, its territory, history, and the complexity of the context;
- extract from styles and design experiences the logical and non-rigid schemes for addressing and interacting with problems.
Area of Architecture and Environment Representation Students must acquire:
- Knowledge and understanding of graphic languages useful for developing design ideas and drawing the project.
- Knowledge and understanding of techniques and tools for representing space, 3D modeling software, and project communication tools.
- Knowledge and understanding of drawing as an expressive act and visual communication of the design idea.
- Knowledge and understanding of the theories, methods, techniques, and tools of project representation and communication at different operational scales.
- Knowledge and understanding of technical standards in representation and project matters.
Area of Urban Architectural Design Understanding the meaning of architectural design and the necessary knowledge to approach it, through design exercises starting from the elementary cell of housing and its various aggregations and articulations. The project must be understood and comprehended by the student as a drawn prefiguration of construction.
Area of Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration Students must possess good knowledge of all disciplines contributing to the structuring of a restoration project, particularly urban and historical contexts, meaning they must be able to:
- define the historical context that generated architecture and highlight in it styles, needs, characters, craftsmanship, and elements of the construction vocabulary;
- recognize the main construction elements of historical architecture and their traditional materials, with particular regard to the system of street fronts of historical urban facades;
- organize the geometric dimensional survey of an architectural complex and its graphical restitution;
- understand the nature of issues related to the structural functioning of a building;
- view the architectural object as connected to the environment, its territory, history, and the complexity of the context;
- extract from styles and design experiences the logical and non-rigid schemes for addressing and interacting with problems.
Area of Structural Analysis and Design for Architecture Graduates must acquire solid knowledge in the fields of structural design and modeling of structural materials, knowledge of main methodologies for calculating displacements and stresses in one-dimensional structures, and mastery in the methods of section and structure verification.
Area of Urban Planning and Territorial Planning Within urban planning and territorial planning, the three-year graduate must know the constituent elements of urban and territorial systems; must develop basic knowledge of urban theory, know basic urban planning techniques and tools, and acquire the ability for critical analysis of phenomena and evolution dynamics of urban systems. Graduates will thus be able to design public, common, and collective spaces at the urban and territorial scale following design concepts appropriate to the reference context. Experience will be gained within interdisciplinary workshops that will provide a basic understanding of the disciplinary field and stimulate integrated design.
Area of Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Construction Production Students will learn fundamental knowledge in the fields of materials and construction techniques, functional coupling criteria in technical elements. Students will also learn environmental factors conditioning building design and potential degradation actions it undergoes during its lifecycle. They will learn methods and tools for representing the technical project, from broad scale to construction detail. Therefore, at the end of the training path, students will be autonomous in choosing between different technological project solutions and construction materials.
Area of Estimative Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Students will learn the theories, principles, and methods of valuation. They will be able to identify the different economic aspects characterizing a property, the corresponding values, and the valuation criteria for their determination. They will deepen their knowledge of the real estate market and the construction market.
Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities
- Knowledge and understanding of the theme of environmental sustainability and the ecosystem aspects of architecture, settlement, and territory;
- Knowledge and understanding of the theme of protection and conservation of cultural heritage and built heritage at the scale of architecture, city, and territory;
- Knowledge and understanding of the engineering and technological aspects of construction and development of competencies in the field of traditional and innovative materials within architectural design;
- Knowledge and understanding of the philosophical, epistemological, and interdisciplinary aspects of design.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematical Disciplines for Architecture Ability to model problems through the language and tools of mathematics. Ability to calculate, solve, and approximate solutions to basic geometric and analytical problems, with particular reference to disciplines characterizing architecture, design, and urban planning. Ability to formalize and implement automatic solutions to typical processing problems.
Area of Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture Ability to apply acquired knowledge and quantify studied phenomena through practical exercises in energy, climate control, acoustics, and lighting technology. Verification of understanding and acquired competencies, but especially the ability to elaborate and apply them in a design context.
Area of Historical Disciplines for Architecture Students must be able to apply their knowledge to new and unprecedented situations—ability not responding to rigid and predefined rules, nor intuitive or instinctive, but rather responding to a historical study and analysis methodology. They must integrate and enrich every application through awareness of the cultural dimensions of the intervention developed for analysis, and properly integrated for construction and complexity management. They can develop their technical-scientific and historical-critical competencies in new or innovative contexts, in situations never before faced, under conditions of partial or vague knowledge of relevant information. Finally, they can relate the awareness of the need for critical and historical deepening to the needs, trends, and complexity of the architectural project.
Area of Architecture and Environment Representation Students must be able to apply:
- knowledge and understanding of learned graphic languages to concrete experiences of ideation and representation of design solutions to problems at different scales and contexts;
- drawing as an expressive act and visual communication of the design idea to the communication of design ideas related to different themes and application fields;
- ability to choose, use, and combine representation and communication methods, techniques, and tools appropriate within the different phases of the design process and different experiences;
- ability to use and apply technical standards and knowledge in representation and project matters.
Area of Urban Architectural Design The project must also be understood as a moment of synthesis of the various disciplinary contributions present in other courses. Making use of these, the student in the project exercise will be able to clearly express the achieved maturity and the level of acquired knowledge.
Area of Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration Students must be able to apply their knowledge to new and unprecedented situations—capability not responding to rigid and predefined rules, nor intuitive or instinctive, but rather responding to a rigorous design methodology that is the basis of architectural and urban restoration. They must adapt this method to the surrounding historical built reality, developing a process that connects all their knowledge from the geometric reality of the asset, to its material, to its conservation status, up to restoration hypotheses. They must integrate and enrich every application through awareness of the cultural dimensions of the intervention developed for analysis, and properly integrated for construction and complexity management. They can develop their technical-scientific and historical-critical competencies in new or innovative contexts, in situations never before faced, under conditions of partial or vague knowledge of relevant information. Finally, they can relate the awareness of the necessity of protecting and conserving historical center architecture with current and historical cultural trends in relation to the regulatory and professional framework.
Area of Structural Analysis and Design for Architecture Graduates must have acquired the ability to apply classic methods and tools of structural design to the study of civil buildings.
Area of Urban Planning and Territorial Planning Graduates, regarding urban planning and territorial planning, will be able to address the complexity of territorial and urban systems by applying acquired methods, techniques, and tools. They will be able to critically and consciously identify interventions following principles and strategies appropriate to different scales.
Area of Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Construction Production Students, starting from the characteristics of known materials, must be able to analyze cataloged technical elements and then design new ones, limited to the complexities that the acquired knowledge allows them to address. Moreover, what is learned, viewed through an eco-compatibility lens, will enable students to adopt construction and technological design choices to reduce the environmental impact of construction on the surrounding territory.
Area of Estimative Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Students will be able to apply in their practical activity the estimation of Market Value, Cost Value, Transformation Value, Complementary Value, and Surrogate Value.
Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities
- Ability to apply to the project the knowledge acquired in the field of environmental sustainability and the ecosystem aspects of architecture, settlement, and territory;
- Ability to apply to the project the knowledge acquired in the field of protection and conservation of cultural heritage and built heritage at the scale of architecture, city, and territory;
- Ability to apply to the project the knowledge acquired in the field of engineering and technological aspects of construction and development of competencies in the field of traditional and innovative materials within architectural design;
- Ability to apply to the project the knowledge acquired in the field of philosophical, epistemological, and interdisciplinary aspects of design.
Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN
Competencies Associated with the Function.
Junior Architect The three-year architecture graduate will be able to perform autonomous professional activity after registering with the Architects' Order Section B.
The graduate will also be able to carry out design, direction, and management of works, measurement, supervision, accounting, and settlement of simple civil constructions realized with standardized methodologies. These also include instrumental and direct surveys on current and historical construction.
Function in the Work Context.
Junior Architect After passing the relevant state exam, the graduate will be able to register with the Register of Architects, Planners, Landscape Architects, and Conservators as a Junior Architect and perform professional activities, contributing and collaborating in programming, design, and implementation activities of interventions for organizing and transforming the built environment at various scales.
In particular, the graduate will have the following competencies:
- knowledge of methodological-operational aspects related to the disciplinary fields characterizing the study course and the ability to identify and solve architecture and construction problems using updated methods, techniques, and tools;
- adequate knowledge of aspects regarding technical and economic feasibility, cost calculation, and the production and realization process of architectural and construction artifacts, as well as aspects related to their safety;
- ability to use the techniques and tools of architectural and construction artifact design.
These competencies may allow for design autonomy or collaboration capability:
- in applied research in the field of architecture and civil engineering;
- in the design of buildings and civil artifacts and in the connected ideational and procedural processes;
- in processes useful for surveying, representing, designing, overseeing construction and maintenance of artifacts and equipment, and safety-related systems;
- in the analysis of the prices of architectural processes and the economics of construction works.
Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The bachelor's degree in Sciences of Architecture and Design pursues the following educational objectives:
- know the methods and have the ability to use techniques for the analysis and definition of architecture, space, and objects within it, territory, and landscape;
- be able to set up conservation and transformation design programs from the object to the territory, both in reference to various disciplines and to the organizational and competency methodologies of design groups;
- master the contents of legal frameworks regulating the protection and transformation of architecture, cities, and landscape in relation to design levels and expected results;
- ability to interact with complex clients (both public and private) and with interdisciplinary work groups.
The study course will be oriented towards the formation of professional figures capable of recognizing and understanding architectural works, both in their logical-formal, compositional, typological-distributive, structural, constructive, technological aspects, and in their relationships with the historical, physical, institutional, and environmental context. Specific competencies of the graduate relate to activities connected with architectural and urban design in different fields and at various application scales. The study course, structured in credit intervals, is prepared for an articulation into distinct curricula, should the needs of the local market require it, as well as with the aim of harmonizing and making the first-cycle training path as congruent as possible with a potential future differentiation of the educational offer at the second-cycle level.
The study course's teaching regulation provides, in relation to specific objectives, the possibility of external activities, such as training internships at companies, enterprises, and public bodies, and internships at other Italian and foreign universities, also within the framework of international agreements.
Definition of the Offer and Teaching Methods.
The bachelor's course is organized with an innovative conception that is substantially based on the following aspects:
- learning by doing: not only are all acquired theoretical notions systematically verified against reality, but the comparison itself with real conditions becomes an additional topic for developing critical reasoning;
- this leads to a study plan structure oriented towards the project from the first year, allowing direct application of learned theoretical concepts; thus, the ability to transform acquired concepts into projects is gained, and one becomes accustomed to the rhythms and deadlines imposed by professional activity;
- a pluralistic training achieved both through the cooperation of different disciplines on each individual project, and through teaching by professors from different schools, Italian and foreign;
- language learning during work, also through blocks where teaching is conducted in English, to develop not only language knowledge but also specific disciplinary vocabulary;
- the possibility of carrying out an intermediate and final professional internship abroad, supported by the activation of specific Erasmus projects;
- an optimal ratio between the number of professors and students, allowing students to be continuously followed during lecture and laboratory hours;
- a wide and creative use of new technologies both as a study and work environment, and as learning and using new professional tools.
This organization of bachelor's courses (innovative for Italy, but already successfully adopted by some foreign schools) arises from a careful analysis and in-depth evaluation of major international experiences in relation to the evolution of disciplines, learning methods, and professional activities. Each year is divided into two semesters, during which the university training credits (CFU) are distributed.
The training activity, according to the rules of the University Teaching Regulation and the Department of Architecture, Design, and Urbanism Regulation, is structured into:
- project and in-depth teaching blocks
- single-discipline courses
- student-choice activities and internships
- foreign language (English)
- final exam.
Teaching blocks are characterized by a project theme developed through various disciplines, chosen among those most important for the theoretical and practical development of the project. In each block and for each discipline, frontal lessons, exercises, and integrated project workshops with professors and tutors are carried out. A widespread use of new technologies characterizes the study plan programs, creating a creative study and work environment and allowing the learning and use of new professional tools. The exam schedule is divided into three sessions: February, July, and September. The third year, in its first part, follows the usual block structure, while the second part contains an area for free credits, a block for final exam preparation activities, and the final exam, also in view of completing the training path in the Master's Degree in Architecture of the same Department. The CFU for final exam preparation activities can be dedicated to the internship, allowing sufficient duration for activating an Erasmus Placement, or to acquiring other knowledge useful for drafting a project or other work to be discussed in the final exam, which will be better defined in the Regulation. This organization is represented in the curriculum grid as a credit interval that can be assigned to either "Training and Orientation Internships" or "Other useful knowledge for entering the workforce." The activation of one or both credit intervals will occur during the definition of the Study Manifesto, together with the definition of "other useful knowledge," to ensure the necessary flexibility for a study course that must offer both the possibility of entering the workforce and training oriented towards continuing in the Master's Degree.

UNIVERSITY: University of Sassari

High school diploma Fees and contributions Regulations - Fees Roles President NICOLÒ GIACOMO BERNARDO CECCARELLI Program, texts and objectives Professional title conferred by the degree.
Designer The three-year graduate is able to interpret different contexts with versatility, looking beyond immediate perspectives to anticipate behaviors and future responses. They can therefore engage with companies, organizations, and productive realities at regional, national, and international levels, bringing strategic visions, creativity, and innovative approaches.
Their employment prospects are diverse: from the freelance professional offering design proposals, direct solutions, and consultancy services moving freely in the creative design market, to the operator capable of guiding team work and actively integrating into companies' internal offices as a design technician, but also as an analyst and process facilitator.
Characteristics of the final project.
The final project plays an important role in our training program: as a stimulus and assumption of responsibility by students, before being an assessment of the maturity acquired by the student along their training path.
The final project may take place along two main directions: one path involves a detailed and comprehensive presentation of activities carried out during the internship; alternatively, students may agree with a faculty supervisor on a topic to explore, which may be design-oriented or research-based, also within a path combining the internship and activities in the Final Synthesis Laboratories. Particular attention will be given to the candidates' ability to approach the chosen topic problematically. Students are required to demonstrate analytical and synthesis skills, according to a model inspired by a multidimensional approach (thus checking both the overall scale in terms of process, and the detail, i.e., proposing specific and precise solutions).
Students must also demonstrate full familiarity with the topic addressed, proving, through the choice of appropriate modes and languages for its transmission, to have acquired adequate communication skills.
The achievement of autonomous methodological control, the overall quality of final outcomes, their coherence, and the full awareness of the work carried out represent additional evaluation criteria.
Required knowledge for admission.
To be admitted to the course of study, one must hold a secondary school diploma of the second level or another equivalent foreign degree recognized as suitable. The required initial knowledge and preparation concern analytical, expressive, and communication skills; synthesis and systemic vision; reading and processing of visual and textual content, as well as general cultural level, verified through a specific admission test that will result in a score.
For students admitted to the course of study with a score below the predetermined threshold, specific additional training obligations will be indicated in the teaching regulations to be fulfilled within the first year of the course.
Expected employment and professional opportunities for graduates.
Designer The three-year graduate is able to interpret different contexts with versatility, looking beyond immediate perspectives to anticipate behaviors and future responses. They can therefore engage with companies, organizations, and productive realities at regional, national, and international levels, bringing strategic visions, creativity, and innovative approaches.
Their employment prospects are diverse: from the freelance professional offering design proposals, direct solutions, and consultancy services moving freely in the creative design market, to the operator capable of guiding team work and actively integrating into companies' internal offices as a design technician, but also as an analyst and process facilitator.

SECTION: Communication Skills

Communication Skills.
The practice of communication skills plays a key role in the educational project. This is to enable graduates to acquire tools and strategies with which, during the design process, the future designer can interface with their interlocutors, whether clients, experts and collaborators, stakeholders, individual users or groups. In this direction, the main lines of work encompass the two fundamental communication dimensions for the designer:
· those related to the operational level (in a multiplicity of interpretations and expressions) and thus aimed at both the design process in the strict sense – through conceptual models and schematizations of reality – and at the production, technical and execution aspects;
· those linked to the strategic level and the promotion of the project, through appropriate languages and formulas to convey its core ideas and reference scenarios, using conceptual representations, visualizations, narratives, and illustrations of imaginaries.
All this while navigating agility within the current communication and media landscape.
The educational project places particular emphasis on acquiring these skills, structuring their learning throughout the entire three-year period, in a series of incremental teaching moments. The entire educational program also bases itself on a plurality of moments for practicing and verifying the ability to argue design choices: in reviews and intermediate presentations, in internships, in final project plenary presentations, as well as in opportunities for discussion and interaction, even outside our school community, with a plurality of external stakeholders (stakeholders, experts, visiting professors and researchers).
Learning Ability.
Bachelor's degree students must have developed the ability to apply both "indirect" knowledge – of a speculative nature – acquired during the educational path, and "direct" knowledge – based on design-based discussion, experience through trial and error, analysis of case studies and experiences conducted by others – to filter future experiences and problems, deriving new knowledge from them. This within the framework of personal acquisition of a non-abstract methodological processing and analysis model, alongside the maturation of one's own value system to interpret a multiplicity of demands, identifying synthesis through an overall vision of the process and the ability to harmoniously balance the variables at play. A key component of responsible design is the designer's ability to assume responsibility: meaning not only to make choices, but also to position oneself in a conscious manner to give meaning and complete form to the solution of specific problems, within the context of contemporary needs. The educational model underlying this vision of knowledge construction draws inspiration from "basic design" and is structured around a series of intermediate learning opportunities: preparation for practical skills occurs through a sequence of incremental steps, primarily aimed at building a comprehensive design attitude. The positive "interaction" between concentrated small-scale experiences (intensive workshops, interclass workshops with external subjects) and broader design tasks (semester-long design laboratories) also represents an intentional element of problematic growth and maturation. The results achieved by students in design laboratories – particularly in integrated laboratories, where dialogue between different disciplines is intended to introduce, as learning opportunities, different models of knowledge construction and reality interpretation, transversal to the educational program – as well as in final synthesis laboratories and the conduct of the final assessment, represent the verification moments for this objective.

SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment

Autonomy of Judgment.
The ability of the problem-solver – one of the key qualities traditionally associated with the designer's figure – is accompanied by that of the decision-maker. In fact, the designer guides and coordinates the collection of project data, confronts the problems that inform them and the demands of the various involved actors, but ultimately, they are primarily called upon to make decisions through their design choices, assuming responsibility for their economic, social, ethical, and environmental repercussions. To stimulate students' development of autonomous judgment maturity, the educational project provides for confrontation with a structured set of experiences, aimed at promoting a problematic and complex vision, offering tools to critically interpret reality based on analytical and methodological elements, but also – through the exercise of lateral thinking – according to one's personal perspective. The educational program therefore assigns a key role, from the first year, to the assumption of individual responsibility by those following the course: students are thus encouraged to make informed decisions regarding the opportunities offered by the Study Course in terms of structuring their educational path. Throughout the entire three-year period – in the selection of thematic trajectories of annual interdisciplinary workshops, in identifying internship activities and other elective activities, in defining the theme around which to structure the final project – they are to some extent called upon to outline the 'design' of their personal educational itinerary. The coherence of choices and the overall results achieved – verifiable at multiple levels: from design laboratories to individual courses; from responses to individual project themes to the ability to harmonize the overall design – will serve as testimony of students' acquired autonomous judgment capacity.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Scientific Training Graduates in design are trained in the intuitive and analytical understanding of geometric space, its conceptualization practices, and the modes of its relationships and transformations. They are also able to translate the fields of spatial development and plastic composition into useful and applicable solutions for concrete needs.

Technological Training Graduates in design are familiar with the set of industrial product manufacturing methods in relation to possible options in the selection of resources, materials, and processing, structural characteristics, production contexts, and various economic-production options.

Basic Project Training Consistently with the reference productive, social, and cultural contexts, graduates possess a comprehensive view of design as a system to address and solve design problems within the scope of consumer goods, communication artifacts, and services. They are able to collect and process the elements informing the project in relation to its development and production, usability, and the ability to express values not strictly functional. Design graduates are also capable of exercising control over the management of the various project phases: in relation to clients, interaction with a variety of collaborators, and communication and transmission of design ideas.

Humanistic Training The graduate possesses the foundations to frame the historical progression of design in light of its intersections with culture, technology, and society. They are therefore able to correctly frame the spatiotemporal dimension of artifacts, objects, and environments, recognizing their styles, influences, and references to contexts.

Basic Representation Training Graduates are familiar with the set of representation systems and have acquired the necessary control of the technical-expressive graphic dimension required to develop and communicate design ideas. In particular, they are accustomed to using a variety of drawing and graphic rendering techniques for the expression and communication of design ideas.

Design and Multimedia Communications Graduates in design are able to exercise control over how the design expertise inherent to the designer unfolds across various different application fields. They are able to manage the use of digital tools and techniques for information processing around the project; they control methodologies and procedures for the design, transformation, and production of material goods; they are capable of addressing design themes related to the experience and use of space, also for the translation and presentation of information content to the public; they are familiar with the contemporary "immaterial" declinations of design for digital communication applications, networks, and social media artifacts. Graduates control the theoretical-practical dimension underlying multimedia and audiovisual artifacts populating the current communication landscape, and finally, are able to frame design as strategic activity, for the design of innovative services and as a tool for social innovation.

Technological and Engineering Disciplines Design graduates have a solid preparation on the set of processing technologies with which, at various scales and in different production contexts and in line with environmental concerns, design dialogues for the realization and distribution of new material products and immaterial services. They are also familiar with the set of various graphic expression forms, intended as technical representation elements of the project functional to its design evolution. Of these technical forms, also considering their historical-technological evolution, they know how to use them as distinct languages: design technical, illustrative, artistic.

Economic and Social Sciences Design graduates are able to integrate knowledge from economic and social sciences into their design awareness and sensitivity, deriving additional knowledge elements from interdisciplinary comparison. They are able to profitably grasp the contributions of this disciplinary field, which broadens their cognitive horizons and contributes to the maturation of analytical and critical abilities, through which the designer can position themselves as an interpreter and mediator of diverse demands.

Affine or Integrative Training Activities Design graduates integrate and/or complete their educational path through confrontation with themes useful for dialectically framing their aptitude and approaches more specifically related to design. They are able to place the design of material goods, immaterial artifacts, communication, and services in relation to the needs of environmental balance and within a dimension that encompasses both territorial and residential scales, highlighting the reasons and logics between local and global.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Scientific Training The acquired knowledge translates into the ability to employ the language and tools of geometry, as a basis for articulating an idea of form and translating it, having understood its constructive, procedural, and semantic potentials. The course refers to SSD MAT/03.

Technological Training The direct confrontation offered by the design exercise regarding possible formal solutions, the integration of structural and accessory elements, and the concreteness of production constraints allows the application of knowledge to production processes and understanding of problematic aspects (referable to SSD ICAR/08) through which to make choices in terms of scale economy and sustainability.

Basic Project Training Based on a general framework of methodological knowledge and practical experiences, graduates are able to apply a broad and problematic understanding of the essence of design to a variety of themes and needs. They are also capable of developing appropriate solutions for managing the design and realization process.

Humanistic Training The problematic confrontation with the subject will enable students to transform their historical-critical reading ability into a dynamic tool for interpreting the present reality. Achieving a full awareness of the experiences through which design has been historically articulated constitutes a key element in applying the acquired knowledge and understanding how to structure one's own critical reference framework, even strictly design-related.

Basic Representation Training Graduates are able to apply the disciplinary knowledge framework to their design tasks, through the identification of the most suitable expressive solutions and the personal use of the language of images.

Design and Multimedia Communications A characteristic of the designer is the ability to intertwine the theoretical and practical dimension, constantly applying, in the exercise of the project, the acquired knowledge across a variety of disciplinary fields and occasions. The direct confrontation with multiple and diverse declinations of the design activity is the essential condition for verifying the ability to transfer one's knowledge to the practical plane, developing problematic models of reality understanding and generating new knowledge.

Technological and Engineering Disciplines The confrontation with practical opportunities and concrete issues proposed by the experience of design laboratories, in the face of real cases, allows design graduates to refine their abilities to apply knowledge and understanding of the correspondence between design objectives, costs and production conditions, and possible reference markets. Regarding graphic expression techniques, familiarity – combined with a critical approach and not merely instrumental – with this system of thematic languages, allows design graduates to apply their knowledge and understanding of the methods, in order to convey the most appropriate graphic information for a given communication context.

Economic and Social Sciences A key objective of the entire educational model, graduates' propensity for interdisciplinary integration is also realized in relation to courses pertaining to economic and social sciences, referable to SDD M-DEA 01, SECS-P/08, and SPS/08. The project exercise, aimed at stimulating the aptitude for lateral thinking, indeed offers concrete opportunities to apply the knowledge and understanding acquired from the comparison with these disciplines.

Affine or Integrative Training Activities The comparison of design methodologies with different themes, cases, and intervention scales is an opportunity to apply disciplinary knowledge and verify its understanding, in relation to issues and intervention scales referable to SSD BIO/07, ICAR 14, ICAR 20, and M-FIL/02.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIANO Associated Competencies.
Designer The three-year designer is able to propose innovative solutions in line with the ideational, realization, and distribution processes of service and product design, and with the techniques, languages, and current communication methods, adapting to different work contexts. Inserted into a company, but also proposing themselves as an independent designer/consultant, the three-year graduate is able to control the basic aspects of the strategy, realization, and production of graphic and identity communication projects, the drafting of specifications, and the care in final realization, the development of audiovisual and interactive artifacts, and graphic contributions for web/social platforms. They are also able to intervene in product design, equipping themselves with the appropriate tools to interface with production managers and finalize the engineering and realization aspects of the products they have conceived, providing them with all the necessary execution materials.

Work Context Function.
Designer Upon completion of the Three-Year Degree, the student's preparation encompasses the abilities traditionally associated with the designer profile: innovative charge; analytical and synthetic capacity; autonomous and mature exercise of design thinking. Operating both autonomously, as an external consultant, and as an active participant in internal company teams, the three-year designer is able to conduct research to position new products and services in the market; knows how to indicate guidelines for promotion strategies; finally, is able to provide design contributions across a plurality of fields: graphic and product design, multimedia artifacts, and network communication.

Specific Educational Objectives Description.
The three-year study plan encompasses product and communication design, and at the same time touches upon the various fields in which contemporary designer professionalism is articulated: strategic design, service design, audiovisual and multimedia design, the ideation of events and cultural experiences, info-design, and integrated promotion and communication on new media. On this basis, the central objective of the educational project is to train a designer familiar with the ideational, realization, and distribution processes of service and product design, and with the techniques, languages, and communication methods of the current scenario. A hybrid figure that, based on a preparation combining specific skills, design methodology, and vision capacity, is able to act as an interpreter of a multiplicity of diverse demands, identifying their synthesis and solution in relation with companies, organizations, and social actors at regional, national, and international levels.

The educational organization is structured into thematic semesters, unfolding along the three-year course as a sequence of training experiences, according to a model that starts with a general framework, gradually focusing on specific reference areas. In the first semester of the first year of study, the perspective frames the dimension of emerging global problems (course Design for the Planet), particularly highlighting the urgency of intervention on major environmental issues. Courses Images I (Drawing), History of Design, and courses aimed at providing further basic competencies (Geometry, Philosophy of Art) complete this introductory cycle. In the second semester, with the course Design and Places, attention shifts to the territorial dimension, highlighting the need for constant confrontation between humans and their surroundings. The course of Design Culture, in its structure (which includes a Photography module), is assigned the task of introducing students to the methodological aspects of design and the cultural mediation function that design can perform in society. A course in Cultural Anthropology serves as integration and complement. The first semester of the second year accommodates courses related to communication practices characterizing the current media landscape: Digital Culture Design (Info Design and Digital Design), Theory of Audiovisual Languages, along with the Images II course (dedicated to Graphic Languages). In the second semester, the design teaching shifts to the themes of material culture and product (Material Culture Design), updated to the practices of new craftsmanship and digital fabrication. The courses in Technology of Processing, Models and Technologies of Materials for Design, and Marketing reinforce the path. In the third year, the Exhibit Design lab introduces students to the complex interweaving between communication languages and space organization, while the Design for Society course outlines the scenarios of relationships and interactions between design disciplines and the design of processes and services. The second and final semester is dedicated to synthesis and completion activities of the learning process: professional internships, personal portfolio development, elective courses, English language improvement, and preparation of the final project. The educational project assigns a particularly relevant task for the development of project aptitude to the series of annual interdisciplinary workshops, designed for direct confrontation with problems expressed by territories and the workplace. Workshop activities are based on dialogue with external subjects (organizations, companies, artisans, entrepreneurial initiatives) that bring design practice experiences to confront real-world themes and issues. The predominant workshop themes follow the lines of heritage design, the valorization of territorial products, and the relationship between design and craftsmanship, but may include cross-cutting fields such as fashion, performance, technical, social, and scientific communication. The interdisciplinary workshops are the backbone of an educational project aimed at empowering students in building their personal, cultural, and professional maturation. The three main thematic threads, which configure 'passing' corridors throughout the three years of the course, offer them opportunities for discovery and choice, so that they can trace individual paths autonomously through the basic study plan. These paths may further be enriched by participation in the planned parallel activities (summer schools, free-credit courses), by choosing a targeted internship, by attending a final synthesis lab, and by elaborating the final project. The overall path – in line with the tradition of our Department – will also be characterized by the offer of a structured professional internship program, both within and outside Sardinia, with a strong orientation towards internationalization.

Characteristics of final exam.
The exam consists of preparing a theoretical-critical, experimental or applied paper chosen by the candidate and its critical discussion. Through this exam, the acquisition of learning, maturity, communication skills, as well as the ability for independent processing of acquired knowledge by the student are assessed.
More specifically, the final exam aims to verify the achievement of critical reflection capabilities on acquired knowledge and their potential application in both scientific and practical contexts. Finally, it aims to assess the achievement of the appropriate and necessary level of autonomy to address the complexity of a scientific or applied topic.
Required knowledge for access.
To be admitted to the degree course, one must hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign degree recognized as suitable.
For admission to the degree course, knowledge and skills in Italian and English language, logical-analytical reasoning ability, basic scientific knowledge, and linguistic knowledge are required. In particular, the assessment of such knowledge occurs through the admission test using TOLC-PSI (composed of 50 questions divided into 5 sections: Text comprehension, Basic Mathematics, Verbal Reasoning, Numerical Reasoning, and Biology; plus 30 questions from the module for verifying English language knowledge).
No additional educational obligation (OFA) will be assigned to candidates who, ranked in a suitable position in the merit ranking for admission to the degree course, have correctly answered at least 50% of the questions.
Students who achieve insufficient results will be assigned additional educational obligations, which must be fulfilled by December 31 of the academic year following enrollment. Further details may be specified in the Course Didactic Regulations.

Communication Skills.
The acquisition of communication skills is a fundamental and qualifying element, as the profession of a psychologist is characterized by constant contact with social workers and individuals operating in public and private organizations interested in analyzing opinions, attitudes, and lifestyle surveys. This ability encompasses both non-verbal and verbal communication, including oral and written communication, as well as communication via digital platforms that allow the use of statistical software, enabling the effective graphical presentation of research data. To achieve these skills, practical exercises and learning and application sessions specifically designed and coordinated with various transactional contexts are provided. The ability to process and communicate acquired knowledge will be specifically assessed through ongoing assessments, including oral and/or written assessments, and the final exam.

SECTION: AUTONOMY OF JUDGMENT
URL: https://uniss.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10759

Autonomy of Judgment.
The educational activities as a whole are aimed at developing competencies that foster the necessary professional autonomy to address critical conditions in human and social contexts and in the types of collaboration in research, consulting, and the promotion and development of community interventions. This means that the student must acquire the ability to use scientific, psychometric, educational, and psychological and neuropsychological intervention tools. They must also acquire the ability to read and interpret statistical and experimental data derived from research activities. Finally, they must be able to navigate within the ethical and legal norms governing interactions with clients and, in perspective, the profession of the psychologist.
Autonomy of Judgment is achieved through the exercise of critical ability, both during lectures and practical sessions, and in the applications carried out through laboratory and internship activities. This ability is appropriately assessed and acquired through oral and/or written exams during the assessment process.

Learning Ability.
The graduate must have acquired knowledge and mastery of the fundamental theories and techniques of psychological sciences, both for potential entry into the workforce and in the perspective of continuing studies in master's degrees. Moreover, they must demonstrate the ability to learn from acquired experience and to modify, update, and enrich their professional skills, which do not dispense with the ability to use computer and linguistic tools (libraries, databases, application or analytical software). The assessment of these abilities and their acquisition, in addition to through the performance achieved in individual courses based on oral and/or written exams, occurs specifically through the work underlying the preparation of the final thesis.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Analytical-Experimental Domain. The objective of this domain is to provide the basic knowledge and methodological skills inherent to psychological disciplines and (more generally) scientific disciplines, on a purely experimental plane and oriented towards basic and applied research. To this end, the main tools of experimental methodology, psychometrics, neuropsychology, and neuroscience, experimental research techniques, and psychophysical methods are provided to understand and process quantitative data in all possible areas belonging to the field of psychological science. This objective is complemented by the use of computer procedures for data processing necessary to enable the practical application of acquired knowledge.

Socio-Evolutionary Domain. The objective of this domain is to provide the foundational concepts of psychological and social disciplines, also in light of neuroscience discoveries, enabling students to understand the foundations of the different explanatory potentials of personality, its development, and its manifestations in normal and pathological behaviors.

Clinical-Diagnostic Domain. The objective of this domain is to provide the basic concepts of applying psychological disciplines in clinical and diagnostic contexts, enabling students to understand the different explanatory potentials of personality and its development in pathological behaviors.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Analytical-Experimental Domain. The objective of this domain is to develop capabilities that make concrete interventions effective in various fields, not only in basic research but also in applied research. The logical-experimental domain just described forms the backbone of the following two domains. The verification of the knowledge and skills acquired and their relative application capability by the student involves, for each educational activity, the performance of specific oral and/or written tests, through which the student can demonstrate mastery in using the tools and methodologies learned. For some educational activities that involve the learning, even on-site, of practical skills and their professional application capabilities, verification may be conducted through practical tests with evaluation. Assessments, in addition to at the conclusion of the educational activity, can also be conducted during the activity at the discretion of the designated instructor for the specific educational activity. The teaching regulations and syllabi of each educational activity describe the specific assessment method in detail.

Socio-Evolutionary Domain. The objective of this domain is to develop capabilities for using and applying the acquired knowledge in social dynamics, transformations occurring in the individual, family, and society. This objective is complemented by the development of capabilities for using and applying statistical data for programming, quality assessment of activities, needs analysis, and socio-economic context analysis. The verification of the knowledge and skills acquired and their relative application capability by the student involves, for each educational activity, the performance of specific oral and/or written tests, through which the student can demonstrate mastery in using the tools and methodologies learned. For some educational activities that involve the learning, even on-site, of practical skills and their professional application capabilities, verification may be conducted through practical tests with evaluation. Assessments, in addition to at the conclusion of the educational activity, can also be conducted during the activity at the discretion of the designated instructor for the specific educational activity. The teaching regulations and syllabi of each educational activity describe the specific assessment method in detail.

Clinical-Diagnostic Domain. The objective of this domain is to develop the necessary knowledge to implement effective diagnostic, support, and intervention actions in relation to the specificities of difficulties affecting individuals, families, groups, and the community. The verification of the knowledge and skills acquired and their relative application capability by the student involves, for each educational activity, the performance of specific oral and/or written tests, through which the student can demonstrate mastery in using the tools and methodologies learned. For some educational activities that involve the learning, even on-site, of practical skills and their professional application capabilities, verification may be conducted through practical tests with evaluation. Assessments, in addition to at the conclusion of the educational activity, can also be conducted during the activity at the discretion of the designated instructor for the specific educational activity. The teaching regulations and syllabi of each educational activity describe the specific assessment method in detail.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN

Competencies Associated with the Role.
Bachelor in Psychological Techniques
- ability to access scientific and specialist literature;
- competence in using scientific and disciplinary update tools;
- application of statistical data analysis techniques in various fields of psychology;
- correct use and interpretation of the most significant diagnostic tests;
- knowledge of research and psychometric investigation techniques;
- ability to observe and scientifically analyze human behavior;
- ability to conduct and interpret a psychological interview;
- management of orientation activities in both educational and work contexts;
- ability to implement psychological support throughout the life cycle.

The competencies acquired in the three-year L-24 course prepare for the subsequent master's degree and the formation of an expert who can operate as a supporting figure to a master psychologist registered in Section A of the register.

Professional Role in the Workplace.
Bachelor in Psychological Techniques. The Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of Cognitive Processes, in accordance with the national and European scientific and professional community of psychologists, grants eligibility for independent psychological practice, Section B of the Professional Register of Psychologists, upon completion of the Practical Evaluation Internship (ex DM 654 of July 5, 2022). Graduates of the three-year program, and upon registration with Section B of the Professional Register of Psychologists (passing the State Exam) and under the supervision of a professional psychologist, can effectively operate within services directed at individuals, families, groups, and communities. This role aims at promoting well-being, the effectiveness of educational interventions, and the enhancement of individual and social resources.

Professional Functions in the Workplace: active participation in the programming and evaluation of psychological and psycho-social interventions; implementation of psycho-educational interventions; application of ergonomic knowledge aimed at designing technologies and improving interaction between individuals and specific activity contexts; use of psychological tools (interviews, tests, observation) for evaluating personality, social interactions, opinions, and attitudes; implementation of school and career orientation activities and human resource management; collection and statistical processing of psychological and psychophysical data for research purposes; use of psychological tools to recover cognitive, emotional, relational, and practical skills in disabled individuals; implementation of surveys and investigations using web-assisted questionnaires.

It is essential to emphasize that these functions can only be carried out exclusively within a professional team context and as a supporting figure to a psychologist registered in Section A of the Psychologists' Register.

Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of Cognitive Processes aims primarily to train students by combining psychological research and cognitive neuroscience with human sciences, education, and rehabilitation, through the acquisition of essential technical-scientific tools for professional activity in psychosocial, neuropsychological, ergonomic, psychometric and neuroscientific assessment, human resource management, training, assistance, and health promotion fields, to be carried out in both public and private structures, as well as in businesses and the third sector.

More specifically, knowledge and skills will gradually develop during the three years through the range of activities aimed at the following:
- foundational and characteristic subjects aimed at understanding psychological and neuro-biological disciplines and those related to interdisciplinary training, fundamental for building solid technical and cultural competencies;
- characteristic and related knowledge and skills aimed at using neuro-scientific, neuropsychological, and clinical investigation techniques, methods, and procedures;
- knowledge aimed at mastering the main statistical and applied techniques in various sectors and work contexts;
- knowledge and skills in communication and information management;
- advanced skills in using at least one European Union language, in written and oral form, in addition to Italian.

At the end of their studies, graduates of class L-24 will be able to carry out professional activities in public and private, scientific, applied, and health institutions, educational institutions, businesses, and third-sector organizations. They will be able to carry out activities in services directed at individuals, groups, organizations, and communities, and in services for assistance and health promotion. These activities also relate to contexts concerning psychometric, neuropsychological, psychosocial, and developmental assessment, as well as human resource management throughout the life cycle.

To achieve these objectives, the courses include activities aimed at acquiring theoretical foundations and technical-methodological elements of general and developmental psychology, investigation methodologies, statistical methods, and computer procedures for data processing, the psychophysiological and neural mechanisms underlying behavior, and the dynamics of normal and pathological human relationships. The courses will also be oriented towards achieving an appropriate contextualization of psychological disciplines within the broader context of natural, biological, and neuroscience.

For this purpose, supplementary educational activities are also provided in various disciplinary fields, such as seminars, laboratory activities, and practical experiences in real or simulated situations. These are supplemented by Practical-Evaluation Internship (TPV) and orientation activities, as well as student-selected credits. According to current regulations, the additional professionalizing educational activities, totaling 10 CFU, are carried out during the Bachelor's Degree courses in Psychological Sciences and Techniques - class L-24. The specific structure of these professionalizing educational activities, defined by the university teaching regulations of the L-24 study programs, includes:
a) activities for acquiring basic professional competencies related to empirical methods characteristic of all areas of psychology and techniques for evaluating the functioning processes of the mind and behavior, including their psychobiological correlates, in relation to different age groups and social and life contexts;
b) activities for acquiring basic professional competencies related to psychological assessment and the main forms of intervention on interpersonal, intragroup, and intergroup relationships in various social contexts, at the level of dyads, families, small groups, and organizations;
c) analysis of the main forms of alteration of psychological processes and human behavior, in relation to different age groups and social and life contexts. The training of students carrying out TPV activities and the evaluation of these activities are entrusted to professional tutors registered with the professional order for at least three years, whose training and evaluation activities are conducted in accordance with the tutorial teaching regulations of the study programs.

The course finally includes, in relation to specific objectives, extracurricular activities and study stays at Italian and foreign universities, also within the framework of international agreements.

Judgment autonomy.
Graduates must have acquired the ability to compare the thematic nodes emerging in psycho-pedagogical thought with events, problems, and phenomena originating in other fields of knowledge, their applications, and the multiple situations of life, demonstrating critical mastery and independence of judgment.
After the training path, consisting of theoretical study, exercises, group work, internship activities, and in-depth studies, the graduate must be able to critically, consciously, and creatively face educational and psycho-pedagogical issues, hypothesizing and implementing targeted actions to promote the person and support individuals in difficulty.
The achievement of these expected outcomes will be promoted within specific disciplines and, transversally, through the various teaching and learning activities proposed in the degree course (lectures, laboratories, seminars, conferences, internship, and final thesis). Their evaluation will be carried out both in the intermediate and final exams of individual courses and the curricular internship, as well as overall at the end of the path, through the student's elaboration and discussion of a final thesis.

Work context function.
Professional sociopedagogical educator (3.4.5.2.0)
Design, develop, and manage network interventions in the area of personal and educational services, aiming to promote the development of individual growth potential and social inclusion of people (minors and adults) in a state of discomfort, difficulty, marginality, and/or deviance.
Social reintegration and integration technicians: (3.4.5.2.0)
Work in synergy with the local service network to develop intervention strategies that promote new social and employment opportunities for the reintegration and development of autonomous paths for disadvantaged subjects (young people and adults) with particular personal and socio-family difficulties and/or in a state of discomfort or deviance.
Active elderly care expert (3.4.5.2.0)
Work in synergy with the local service network to develop intervention strategies that promote new social, cultural, and animation opportunities for active elderly people and the reemployment of pensioners to develop autonomous paths within a lifelong learning perspective.
Early childhood educators (3.4.5.2.0)
Analysis of individual and group educational needs of children. Design and programming of educational activities aimed at developing children's evolutionary potential, also through involving the family realities of origin, exercising direct and indirect functions of support for parenting.
Description of specific training objectives.
The specific training objective for graduates of the Course is the acquisition of a solid cultural preparation in the field of education sciences through in-depth study of pedagogical, psychological, philosophical, and socio-anthropological disciplines. Such multidisciplinary skills and knowledge are essential both for entering the workforce and for continuing studies (enrollment in master's degrees). They appear indispensable for the activity of the educator who responds to the diverse needs of the territory regarding educational needs in various fields. Therefore, additional specific training objectives are:
- Acquisition of theoretical and operational skills for understanding and analyzing socio-cultural contexts, achieved through the teachings of anthropological-social, historical, and economic-social geography disciplines, foreign languages, and contemporary multimedia languages;
- Acquisition of skills related to the field of activity of the educator, developed through specialized teachings in education sciences and the mandatory curricular internships at educational and training institutions, companies, and public administration structures, and may also include stays at other Italian and foreign universities, also within the framework of international agreements. The final exam is also related to field work.
The didactic methodology used in the three-year degree will primarily be linked to classroom activities (also with the support of multimedia, interactive, and online tools), which may take the form of frontal communication, in-depth study of problematic nodes (group activities, exercises, and laboratories), reading and comparison with sources, documents, original texts, tables, registers, case studies, etc., also using new multimedia online technologies. Study and thematic in-depth seminars will also be carried out, also with the support of external experts, as well as internship activities, aimed at learning and perfecting professional skills.
Regarding the training path, the acquisition of theoretical skills occurs mainly in the first and second year, while specialized teachings are entrusted to the second and third year. Theoretical reflection activities on professional opportunities take place on various occasions throughout the three years, while field experience occurs through the internship entrusted to the second and/or third year. The thesis concludes the L-19 path, but is preceded by bibliographic research and research techniques treated as integrative aspects of various disciplines and also within the context of the teaching aimed at acquiring the methodology of research in the educational field.

Final exam characteristics.
The final exam represents an important moment to apply theoretical, methodological and practical skills acquired during the course through independent work. The written submission will focus on a historical-geographical-anthropological theme-problem, while simultaneously emphasizing interdisciplinary analytical approaches.
The final work may also consist of an original audiovisual product (in the form of a reportage, documentary, interview, etc.), related to course subjects, always accompanied by a brief written text.
The final exam is worth 6 CFU and is intended as an initial step in conducting research activities.
Required knowledge for access.
To enroll in the Course, a secondary school diploma or another equivalent qualification obtained abroad and recognized as suitable is required.
Students must possess the necessary knowledge for understanding and reading a first-year university text, have developed adequate synthesis capabilities across different disciplinary contents, be familiar with the spatial and temporal dimensions of anthropic and environmental phenomena, and manage the synchronous and diachronic organization of events with sufficient skill. Regarding the chosen first foreign language, entry-level competencies at A2 level will be required. The verification will be conducted in written form. The methods for verifying the possession of required knowledge and any additional mandatory training obligations to be completed within the first year of the course will be defined in the course's didactic regulations.

Communication Skills.
The title of Doctor in Planning, Management and Promotion of Cultural and Environmental Itineraries will be awarded to students who demonstrate they have acquired the necessary knowledge to effectively communicate scientific, methodological and evaluative content, as well as the problems, hypotheses and solutions for an appropriate relationship between territory, environment and health to both sector experts and non-experts, through the appropriate use of linguistically and technologically suitable tools and systems. Verification will occur through examination tests and in-course assessments and the evaluation of the final examination.
Learning Abilities.
The title of Doctor in Planning, Management and Promotion of Cultural and Environmental Itineraries will be awarded to students who demonstrate they have developed the necessary learning abilities to undertake subsequent studies requiring a high degree of applied knowledge, understanding, autonomy and essential communication skills for initiating higher-level analyses.
Verification of the achievement of these abilities will occur through examination tests and in-course assessments and the evaluation of the final examination.
