Autonomy of Judgment.
At the end of their studies, the graduate possesses awareness and autonomy of judgment that enables them to acquire the necessary information and evaluate its implications in a production and market context, to implement interventions aimed at improving the quality and efficiency of agro-zootecnic productions and any other related activity, also in terms of environmental sustainability and eco-compatibility.
Autonomy of judgment will be acquired through courses structured into teaching units that allow the progressive achievement of objectives by the student; in particular, individual tasks will be assigned to students (e.g., technical and scientific reports, activity presentations) capable of stimulating their critical analysis and autonomy of judgment. The verification of the acquisition of autonomy of judgment will occur through the evaluation of the results achieved in the characteristic disciplines as well as in the optional subjects chosen by the student, and through the assessment of the degree of autonomy and ability to work individually and in groups during practical activities and in the execution of the assigned activity in preparation for the final exam.
Knowledge and Understanding.
Macro Area of Basic Disciplines INTRODUCTION The formation process of the graduate in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences requires that basic and characteristic professional knowledge acquired during the course of study be applied throughout the entire agro-zootecnic production chain without separating the understanding of biological and technical phenomena from operational implementation.
Based on this general principle, the bachelor's degree in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences provides knowledge that can be grouped into three macro areas: basic disciplines, disciplines characterizing zootecnic, and economic-project disciplines.
- BASIC DISCIPLINES -
Regarding this macro area, the bachelor's degree in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences provides sufficiently adequate knowledge of mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology.
1. Regarding mathematics, such knowledge must enable the student to fully understand the concept of a function and the basic principles governing differential and integral calculus for real functions of a single real variable, with particular reference to the concepts of limit and continuity.
2. Regarding physics and chemistry, such knowledge must cover the principles of classical physics; the atomic-molecular constitution of material bodies according to weight ratios described by stoichiometry; understanding the role of chemical bonds and structure on the properties of materials; the main chemical and biochemical reactions occurring during the production, transformation, and preservation of foods and agro-zootecnic products.
3. Regarding biology, such knowledge must cover the fundamental aspects of the biology of prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, with particular attention to cytogenetics and animal and plant morphophysiology.
The knowledge of methods, cultural, scientific, and professional content, and the ability to understand will be acquired through courses structured into teaching units that allow the progressive achievement of objectives by the student.
Frontal teaching is complemented for each course with laboratory and field exercises.
The verification of the acquisition of knowledge and understanding abilities will occur through the successful completion of intermediate assessments and final exams of the characteristic and optional subjects chosen by the student.
MACRO AREA OF DISCIPLINES CHARACTERIZING ZOOTECHNIC INTRODUCTION The formation process of the graduate in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences requires that basic and characteristic professional knowledge acquired during the course of study be applied throughout the entire agro-zootecnic production chain without separating the understanding of biological and technical phenomena from operational implementation.
Based on this general principle, the bachelor's degree in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences provides knowledge that can be grouped into three macro areas: basic disciplines, disciplines characterizing zootecnic, and economic-project disciplines.
- MACRO AREA OF DISCIPLINES CHARACTERIZING ZOOTECHNIC -
Regarding the disciplines that characterize the bachelor's degree in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences, the knowledge acquired during the course of study must enable the graduate to:
1. Adequately understand the digestive processes, energy and protein metabolism and their regulation, nutritional requirements in various ages and activities of terrestrial and aquatic animal species of interest in zootecnic;
2. Understand and contextualize the entire production chain of zootecnic feed;
3. Plan, implement, and manage modern breeding and reproduction techniques for terrestrial and aquatic animals used in zootecnic productions;
4. Implement and manage cultivation and production processes of forages and grains in agro-zootecnic enterprises, respecting appropriate and sustainable use of soil and environmental resources;
5. Transform and process zootecnic feed in enterprise or agro-industrial plants (feed mills);
6. Interpret and manage genetic improvement programs, using both quantitative and molecular genetics tools;
7. Understand the basic processes underlying the transformation and preservation of animal products.
The knowledge of methods, cultural, scientific, and professional content, and the ability to understand will be acquired through courses structured into teaching units that allow the progressive achievement of objectives by the student.
Frontal teaching is complemented for each course with laboratory and field exercises.
The verification of the acquisition of knowledge and understanding abilities will occur through the successful completion of intermediate assessments and final exams of the characteristic and optional subjects chosen by the student.
MACRO AREA OF ECONOMIC-PROJECT TYPE INTRODUCTION The formation process of the graduate in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences requires that basic and characteristic professional knowledge acquired during the course of study be applied throughout the entire agro-zootecnic production chain without separating the understanding of biological and technical phenomena from operational implementation.
Based on this general principle, the bachelor's degree in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences provides knowledge that can be grouped into three macro areas: basic disciplines, disciplines characterizing zootecnic, and economic-project disciplines.
- MACRO AREA OF ECONOMIC-PROJECT TYPE -
Regarding the disciplines that characterize this macro area, the knowledge acquired during the course of study in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences must enable the graduate to:
1. Manage the technical-economic operations of zootecnic enterprises, utilizing knowledge of the main economic theories of supply, demand, production, and trade;
2. Understand the fundamental economic characteristics of agro-zootecnic enterprises and the issues of agri-food markets, even at an international level;
3. Possess skills in determining the economic balance sheet of agro-zootecnic and agro-industrial enterprises, economic planning techniques, and the economic valuation of activities and enterprises;
4. Choose, size, and optimize agro-zootecnic facilities;
5. Intervene on the sizing, type, and construction characteristics of structures and buildings for agro-zootecnic use.
The knowledge of methods, cultural, scientific, and professional content, and the ability to understand will be acquired through courses structured into teaching units that allow the progressive achievement of objectives by the student.
Frontal teaching is complemented for each course with laboratory and field exercises.
The verification of the acquisition of knowledge and understanding abilities will occur through the successful completion of intermediate assessments and final exams of the characteristic and optional subjects chosen by the student.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Macro Area of Basic Disciplines The graduate in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences has learned the fundamental principle that applying basic knowledge and techniques acquired during the course of study to practical reality cannot be separated from a careful technical-scientific analysis and understanding of production processes. Therefore, they are able to:
- Conduct technical-economic analyses of individual production processes related to the production and transformation of foods and products, and genetic selection, feeding, and breeding techniques, to identify weaknesses, strengths, and prospects of these processes, evaluate their technical-economic and environmental sustainability, and design their rationalization and optimization;
- Analyze the overall technical-economic management of agro-zootecnic and agro-industrial enterprises to identify weaknesses, strengths, and technical-economic prospects in the short to medium term, aiming to improve the integration of different production processes, identify potential alternative production activities, increase the technical, economic, environmental, and social sustainability of the enterprises, and certify their production processes;
- Analyze the entire agro-zootecnic production chain to identify weaknesses, strengths, and technical-economic prospects in the short to medium term. This will enable the graduate in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences to conduct technical-economic and environmental analyses or planning related to individual production processes or the overall activities of agro-zootecnic and agro-industrial enterprises, from a chain and system perspective, promoting the optimization and rationalization of production activities and facilitating the positive market entry of their products into agri-food markets.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding will be acquired through courses structured into teaching units that allow the progressive achievement of objectives by the student; frontal teaching is complemented for each course with laboratory and field exercises. The learning verification will be carried out through the evaluation of active student participation in practical and laboratory exercises, while theoretical acquisitions will be verified through written (multiple-choice or open-ended) or oral intermediate assessments and final exams.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN Associated Competencies.
Technical for Agro-Zootecnic Productions
- Competencies in technical-economic analysis of individual processes within the agro-zootecnic chain (production and transformation of foods and products; genetic selection, feeding, and breeding techniques) to identify weaknesses, strengths, and prospects, evaluate their technical-economic and environmental sustainability, and design their rationalization and optimization;

Workplace Function.
Technical for Agro-Zootecnic Productions Among the main tasks that a graduate in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences can perform in a workplace context are:
- Consulting activities for the application of technologies to agro-zootecnic productions in quantitative and qualitative aspects;
- Consulting activities for the marketing and analytical and process certification of zootecnic feeds;
- Independent professional activities for the valuation and estimation of land, facilities, technical means, and agro-zootecnic products;
- Consulting activities related to the design and management of agro-zootecnic and aquatic activities, with areas of activity including animal husbandry, cereal-forage productions, construction and facilities for animal husbandry, valuation, and business management;
- Entrepreneurial activities for managing production and service activities for animal husbandry;
- Consulting, assistance, and dissemination activities for agro-zootecnic and zoo-industrial enterprises;
- Consulting activities for quality control and certification of processes and products of zootecnic and zoo-industrial products.
Specific Educational Objectives Description.
The bachelor's degree in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences aims to ensure that students acquire adequate mastery of general scientific methods and content typical of Agricultural Sciences and Technologies, as well as the acquisition of specific professional knowledge necessary to operate in the following areas of agro-zootecnic:
- Agronomic and cultivation techniques;
- Animal production technologies;
- Basic processing and conditioning processes of zootecnic products;
- Basic chemical-physical and microbiological analyses for agro-zootecnic;
- Facilities and technical means for agro-zootecnic;
- Technical-economic management at the enterprise and territorial level of agro-silvo-pastoral and aquatic systems;
- Design, technical-economic management, and environmental protection of zootecnic systems.
To this end, the curriculum of the bachelor's degree is structured into activities aimed at providing basic knowledge in the indicated sectors, as well as adequate preparation on general themes of animal production and management of zootecnic enterprises; it requires, in relation to specific objectives, mandatory laboratory, field, and internship activities. It will enable graduates of the course, in accordance with the qualifying educational objectives of class L-25, to:
- Acquire adequate knowledge of basic scientific and technical disciplines;
- Effectively use, in written and oral form, in addition to Italian, the English language within their specific field of competence and for the exchange of general information;
- Develop appropriate tools for communication and information management, as well as for continuous knowledge updating;
- Acquire the basic elements of scientific research and be able to collaborate in experimental activities and apply knowledge to solve technical problems in the field of animal production and agro-zootecnic chains;
- Possess theoretical, operational, and laboratory knowledge in various sectors of agriculture, with particular reference to quantitative, qualitative, and hygienic-sanitary aspects of animal productions and agro-zootecnic chains, rural territory issues, valuation of land, technical means, facilities, and products of predominant zootecnic interest;
- Perform technical, managerial, and support tasks in production and technical activities, in laboratories, and in public and private service structures;
- Know the business contexts and their related economic, managerial, and organizational aspects in the zootecnic and zoo-industrial sectors;
- Apply estimation methodologies in the zootecnic sector.
The bachelor's degree in Agro-Zootecnic Sciences has a duration of three years, and the required University Credit Units (CFU) for the degree are 180.
The achievement of educational objectives over the three years of the degree is obtained through the development of a sequence of teaching activities related to three macro-areas:
1) Basic Disciplines;
2) Disciplines Characterizing Zootecnic;
3) Economic-Project Type Disciplines.
In particular, during the first year, teaching activities will be carried out to provide graduates with basic knowledge of mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, and anatomy-physiology. During the second year, alongside basic disciplines such as biochemistry and agricultural genetics, the disciplines characterizing zootecnic will be delivered, providing students with knowledge on nutrition and feeding of species of interest in zootecnic, genetic improvement, microbiology of zootecnic products, agronomy, and agricultural economics. In the third year, further knowledge related to disciplines characterizing zootecnic (such as knowledge on breeding technologies for various species of interest in zootecnic, herbaceous crops) will be developed alongside economic-project type disciplines (valuation, facilities, and structures for zootecnic).
The educational path of each student is guided by a tutoring committee operating within the study program.
Training activities will be organized on a semester basis, and for the same, various types (frontal lectures, exercises, practical activities, laboratories, seminars, internship) will be provided depending on the cultural and training characteristics of the individual courses.
The hourly workload reserved for each CFU is regulated by the Department Teaching Regulation.
Teaching courses may be single-discipline and/or integrated, according to the Department Teaching Regulation.
For the assessment of the achievement of expected learning objectives, in addition to the final exam, one or more intermediate assessments may be provided; these may be written, oral, and/or practical.
Knowledge of the foreign language is guaranteed by specific English language courses offered by the Department, followed by a passing exam. The assessment of foreign language knowledge may also occur through recognition of a substitute certification issued by external accredited bodies by the University Language Center. Computer and telecommunication skills, as well as additional language knowledge, are assessed without a grade by a committee appointed by the CCS. The CFU reserved for the internship must be acquired in accordance with the declared educational purposes of the student through a practical-applicative internship period carried out at the University, public bodies, enterprises, and professional offices. The activity carried out constitutes the subject of the final exam.
Students may acquire free-choice CFU by selecting, with the assistance of the tutor, any course offered by the University of Sassari, or choosing other training activities activated by the Department or the University, provided they are recognized as consistent with the educational path by the Teaching Committee appointed by the Bachelor's Degree Course Council.
Pursuant to Article 5, paragraph 7, of DM 270/2004, up to a maximum of 12 CFU may be recognized for certified professional knowledge and skills, as well as other knowledge and skills acquired in post-secondary training activities to which the University has contributed to the design and implementation, provided documented merit assessments were included.
Mandatory attendance for courses is required, distinguishing between full-time students and working students, according to the modalities provided by the Department Teaching Regulation.

Communication skills.
The graduate in Sciences and Agricultural Technologies, through interaction with teachers, students, and managers of organizations and companies where the internship activity is carried out, develops in the study path the ability to express concepts, interpretations and ideas, both orally and in writing, typically adopting deductive logic processes. The graduate also acquires sufficient knowledge of at least one European language - typically English - which enables them to understand and share, even in a project-based group work context, information of a technical, scientific and specialized nature within the disciplinary fields characteristic of the degree.
The graduate in Sciences and Agricultural Technologies is capable of interacting with others, collaborating and adapting to different work environments and topics.
The acquisition of communication skills, both written and oral, will be verified through the evaluation of written assignments related to laboratory activities, ongoing assessments provided for individual disciplines, and the written assignment prepared for the final exam and presented orally to the graduation committee.

UNIVERSITY: University of Sassari
COURSE: [1174] AGRICULTURAL SCIENCES AND TECHNOLOGY
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://uniss.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10313

Judgment Autonomy.
At the end of the training path, the graduate in Agricultural Sciences and Technology possesses sufficient awareness and judgment autonomy to acquire the necessary information and evaluate the related implications, to address specific issues of agricultural production systems and rural planning. The graduate is equipped with methodological and interpretative knowledge that allows them to independently prepare and carry out engineering designs of buildings and agricultural facilities, economic and valuation analyses of budgets and business planning, productive aspects, and the realization and defense of plant and animal productions.
Judgment autonomy will be acquired through courses structured into didactic units that allow the progressive achievement of objectives by the student through, for example, technical and scientific reports, activity presentations, and case study analyses capable of stimulating critical analysis and judgment autonomy.
Overall, the graduate's knowledge is capable of meeting the declaration of competencies attributed to the junior agronomist by the Order of Agronomists and Foresters.
The verification of the acquisition of judgment autonomy will occur through the evaluation of the results achieved in the core disciplines and the optional subjects chosen by the student, as well as the evaluation of the degree of autonomy and ability to work individually and in groups during practical activities and the completion of the practical-applicative internship assigned in preparation for the final exam.

Learning Ability.
During the three-year training path, the student in Agricultural Sciences and Technology confronts, learns, and adopts various forms of learning organization: synthesis in report form, oral and written reports, bibliographic and informative research, research and laboratory techniques, and the use of new communication and information technologies.
The graduate in Agricultural Sciences and Technology possesses the basic tools to carry out continuous post-graduation learning activities in an autonomous professional context, in multidisciplinary work groups, or in a business context.
Graduates will have developed learning abilities that allow them to continue their studies in a master's degree, a first-level master's, or to enter the workforce.
The learning ability of individual students may be assessed based on the time taken to obtain the degree, the grades achieved in the exams, and the time elapsed between attending the course and passing the exam. The final exam constitutes a moment of verification of the self-learning abilities developed during the degree course and in relation to the activities carried out within the practical-applicative internship.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Agricultural Production INTRODUCTION.
The training of the graduate in Agricultural Sciences and Technology is based on a solid preparation acquired through the basic disciplines of mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology.
The training path includes in-depth study of methodological knowledge of investigation and the quantitative and qualitative analysis tools characteristic of agricultural sciences and technology.
Within the context of various courses, the student is encouraged to learn the use of tools useful for continuous knowledge updating, including English language knowledge through two five-credit courses each, aimed at providing the student with the necessary lexical and grammatical knowledge to reach the A2/B1 level.
The multidisciplinary path, elective courses, and practical-applicative internship allow the student to gain practical experience in applying theoretical knowledge and methodologies acquired during the course of study.
The graduate will have the capacity to interpret the dynamics of the main processes of agricultural production systems.
Moreover, the basic and methodological knowledge acquired during the three years will allow the graduate to approach with solid preparation the more specialized training paths of the master's degree.
Overall, the study course can be divided into two main areas: AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTION and AGRARIAN DESIGN.

Agricultural Production.
The specific training path within the Agricultural Production area is particularly oriented to place the student in a position to address issues related to the management of the main biotic and abiotic factors influencing agroecosystems, taking into account site-specific issues, environmental risk, and market dynamics.
In particular, the student will acquire knowledge regarding:
- chemical systems and processes useful for understanding the mechanisms of metabolic pathways underlying the life cycles of plants and animals, as well as soil chemistry;
- cellular organization of prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, gene structure and mechanisms of trait inheritance, specificity of plant organisms and recognition of main agricultural taxa, characterization of microorganisms and their use in food, environmental, and agricultural industries, characterization of fungal organisms, their ecological role, and economic importance;
- morpho-physiological, ecological, and phenological characteristics of herbaceous and woody crops, factors that influence production in terms of sustainability and quality while respecting biodiversity conservation, the environment, and soil fertility;
- morphology, anatomy, and physiology, biological cycles, and population dynamics of insects and pathogens, such as fungi, prokaryotes, and viruses, harmful to agricultural crops, damages, symptoms, possibilities of prevention, and different defense strategies;
- morphological and functional characteristics of the main livestock species and breeds and their productions while respecting the environment;
- principles of microeconomics and their applications to agri-food markets, analysis of business efficiency, and functioning of agricultural markets.

Agrarian Design.
The specific training path within the Agrarian Design area is particularly oriented to provide the student with methodologies and the ability to use basic tools for technical design in the agricultural field and, more generally, for rural territory, while respecting the environment.
In particular, the student will acquire knowledge regarding:
- basic physics and essential mathematical tools for studying all quantitative and economic disciplines;
- planimetric and altimetric survey of the territory, cartographic representations, and the use of geographic information systems (GIS) for managing and processing territorial information within agricultural and forest rural contexts;
- basic knowledge for designing rural structures, with particular reference to buildings for livestock farming, fundamental elements of hydraulics, design techniques for hydraulic systems (pipes and channels), and irrigation systems for managing water resources in an environmentally respectful context, CAD drawing to support design;
- design, construction, operational, functional, and management aspects of machines and equipment for the processes of agricultural and livestock biosystems;
- theoretical foundations and methodologies of rural valuation, appropriate evaluation criteria for correct valuation methodology.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Agricultural Production.
The application of acquired knowledge and methodologies on technical tools and analysis will enable the graduate to competently address the optimization of main production processes and those preparatory to transformation and commercialization phases at the enterprise level and/or in other organizational and managerial contexts characteristic of agricultural supply chains.
The graduate must have developed the ability to interpret the main indicators related to agricultural production systems, also in reference to environmental quality.
The graduate will thus be able to develop synergies with other complementary professional fields, such as legal, naturalist, and engineering sectors, etc.

Agrarian Design.
The acquisition of technical tools and analysis will enable the graduate to competently address the design of works and facilities for the development of agricultural enterprises, technical design in the agro-environmental field within an environmentally respectful context, and rural territory planning, also in collaboration with other professional figures.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN

Competencies Associated with the Function.
Agricultural Production Technician.
The graduate in Agricultural Sciences and Technology will be able to perform their functions with the following competencies:
- Management of production processes in agricultural and agro-environmental fields, with basic competencies in managing crop and livestock systems;
- Basic competencies on agricultural production systems, including mechanization and the biology of pathogens and parasites;
- Specific competencies in rural valuation, agricultural business economics, and accounting;
- Specific competencies in the sizing of rural constructions, and enterprise hydraulic-agricultural infrastructure.

Function in the Workplace Context.
Agricultural Production Technician.
The functions of the graduate in Agricultural Sciences and Technology in a workplace context include:
- application of technologies to agricultural production systems, considering also qualitative aspects;
- management of production activities of goods and services in agriculture;
- consulting, technical assistance, and dissemination to agricultural and agro-industrial enterprises in the sectors of plant and animal production, plant protection, and quality control of agricultural products;
- agronomic technical support in the design and implementation of environmental protection measures, even in parks and natural reserves;
- certification of the quality of processes and products of agricultural and agro-industrial products;
- technical activities in the agricultural field to support rural territory programming and management, including rural construction, design of irrigation and drainage networks, estimation of rural and agricultural assets, business administration, and agronomic technical contribution to environmental impact assessment.

Description of Specific Training Objectives.
The graduate in Agricultural Sciences and Technology must have demonstrated the acquisition of technical-scientific methods and content that form the foundation of professionalism in the agricultural field, with particular reference to the ability to address issues related to quantitative, qualitative, and sustainability aspects of production systems, aspects related to territorial management including cadastral and topographic aspects, estimation of rural assets, correct use of technical means, and simple design and sustainable management of agricultural systems.
They must also be able to provide technical assistance in the agricultural field, know the principles and scope of professional activities, understand business contexts and their economic, managerial, and organizational aspects specific to the agro-zootecnic field in response to territorial needs.
They must be able to effectively use, in written and oral form, in addition to Italian, the English language within their specific field of competence and for the exchange of general information, and must possess adequate competencies and tools for information management and communication, with the ability to work in teams with defined degrees of autonomy.
The Bachelor's degree course in Agricultural Sciences and Technology has been designed to provide a solid foundational preparation for the master's degree in Agricultural Systems, allowing students to choose a three-year professionalizing path.
The basic teaching courses include mathematical, physical, chemical, and biological disciplines that form the essential foundational basis for a professional capable of holistically interpreting the specific issues of agricultural systems.
The core disciplines aim to provide students with methodological tools and professional technical competencies, with particular regard to economic-valuation disciplines and agricultural engineering.
The teaching courses within plant production, protection, and animal sciences aim to provide students primarily with multidisciplinary methodological competence useful for addressing the analysis of agroecosystems with a systemic approach that takes into account territorial reality and thus the interactions present between agricultural and livestock systems.
The activities are also preparatory to the training path of the master's degree in Agricultural Systems.
The course offers students ample opportunity to design a personalized training path, predominantly professionalizing or methodological and preparatory for the master's degree, within the context of the student's elective courses and practical-applicative internship activities, which are aimed at passing the final exam. These training spaces offer the student the opportunity to address concrete issues associated with the specific professionalism of the graduate in Agricultural Sciences and Technology and to gain initial work and professional experience.

Characteristics of final exam.
The final exam takes place at the end of the third year of study and verifies the knowledge and skills developed by the student over three years. The topics developed during the thesis path may be theoretical and design-oriented and concern subjects that deepen knowledge already developed in teaching units or modules. Students are encouraged to propose the thesis topic and develop it in an interdisciplinary manner, especially when it requires in-depth design studies of environmental, territorial and urban nature.
Different modalities are provided depending on the ability to elaborate a topic through an individual dissertation, the ability to synthesize an internship experience, and the possibility to synthesize the experience of a project laboratory on topics characteristic of the Degree Course.
Required knowledge for admission.
To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree Course, one must possess a secondary school diploma of the second level or another equivalent foreign degree recognized as suitable.

The outcome of the initial preparation assessment does not in any case preclude the possibility of enrolling students in the degree course. If the verification is not positive, specific additional training obligations must be indicated to be fulfilled in the first year of the course.

Communication skills.
Graduates have the ability to effectively communicate the premises and purposes of their choices and interventions, knowing how to calibrate and modulate it according to the various objectives to be achieved, contexts, and audiences. The blended teaching approach helps students learn new communication methods and thus digital communication skills, as required by the challenges of the digital era.
They are therefore able to adjust the level of depth—and also the linguistic and lexical register—according to the recipient, situation, objectives, and interfaces.
In particular, students must know how to use argumentative structures with ease, within a framework of communication organization based on the requirements of rational argumentation, taking into account the need for public acts to be understandable even to non-experts and transparent.
These objectives are achieved through constant didactic and pedagogical attention aimed at enhancing the ability to justify each choice with effective argumentative structures, to make implicit or tacit premises explicit or perceptible, to be aware of the strengths and weaknesses of positions, and to be able to adopt new perspectives very different from the starting point.
In this context, the relationship, rich in interactions, with teachers, experts, and tutors, as well as with classmates from their own and other classes, with international students at our campus or in other campuses during Erasmus exchanges, and with graduates (an open learning community), is also extremely important. Equally important is the continuous critical discussion carried out in class and in laboratories. For this reason, project laboratories often include in-process and/or final critical discussions of student work by representatives of institutions, bodies, and stakeholders interested in the project developed in the laboratory, thus simulating a real planning and design context.
The practice of languages other than Italian, familiarity with digital languages, and with different communicative registers used not only in face-to-face interactions but also in virtual ones, completes the construction of graduates' communication skills. They must be able to engage with differing opinions, cultures, ideologies, and cultural approaches, and potentially understand the nature of disagreements to intervene effectively through mediation, negotiation, and conflict resolution.
In addition to the tools indicated in the previous descriptors, a constant activity will be to assess communication skills, both verbal, written, and representational, in exams and in-course assessments; in particular, a portion of the dissertation grade is assigned to communication skills.
Learning abilities.
Graduates know how to synthesize acquired knowledge to form a valid basis for subsequent in-depth study, and are able to formulate independent judgments on various issues, with knowledge or awareness of the main theoretical orientations and project or planning practices.
They have developed a learning methodology throughout their studies that also enables them to tackle further studies by optimally using acquired skills within a framework of increasing autonomy and gradually greater conceptual and theoretical complexity. Every opportunity for professional growth naturally becomes a moment for knowledge and theoretical deepening. They have critical awareness to identify, among their experiences, which have relevance for motivating continued university education, or to understand the needs for updating and training that arise in their professional activities.
In addition to the tools indicated in the previous descriptors and particularly the individual interpretation and analysis exercises of laboratory and course materials, it is the very process of "learning by doing," with numerous assessments and constant interaction with teachers, experts, and tutors, that constitutes the decisive moment for evaluating learning abilities.

SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment

Autonomy of Judgment.
Graduates are able to formulate relevant and insightful judgments on various disciplinary and transdisciplinary issues, using acquired knowledge correctly and rationally, demonstrating the ability to well organize, use, and adapt concepts, techniques, tools, and theories, and to mobilize knowledge in the context of cognitive and operational objectives influenced by the context.
The judgment ability they possess is open to the multiplicity of possible approaches, structured by awareness of the complexity of issues and distant from a merely solution-oriented conception of the project and plan.
The judgments typically formulated by graduates must be flexible and 'original', but must always be anchored to the fundamental ability to explore and know the world, so that even the formulation of a judgment becomes, always, an additional heuristic and a hypothesis to be tested.
Graduates subject every judgment to their own ability to discuss and doubt, supporting it both with argumentative reasoning and with quantitative analyses. It is particularly important to highlight, at every opportunity, the cultural, social, philosophical, historical, and technical-scientific aspects that deepen and give substance to any project-related issue.
These results are pursued through:
- integrated teaching modules where the same comparison between professors forces students to a continuous process of translation and comparison between personal and disciplinary viewpoints;
- project laboratories inspired by complexity and interdisciplinarity;
- constant didactic reference to the adoption of new theoretical viewpoints and the necessity to provide reasoned justifications for actual and possible choices;
- interpersonal comparison, achieved through group work and critical classroom discussions;
- collaborative methods supported by e-learning tools;
- cultivation of judgment autonomy.
In addition to the tools indicated in the previous descriptors, periodic assessments, structured and coordinated also by tutors, will be carried out on theoretical and project-related themes and issues chosen autonomously by students and interpreted by them using the methods and techniques they deem appropriate.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematics, Informatics, and Statistics: The basic languages, concepts, and theorems of linear algebra, mathematical analysis, and geometry provide fundamental knowledge for the use of tools from technical disciplines addressed in subsequent years and for modeling urban phenomena.
Area of Representation: Students acquire knowledge, including practical, of the basic tools for graphical representation of cartography, even digital; they must be able to filter and manage data structure, representation levels, and the graphical coding of a representative dataset's styling; use communication tools and graphical languages to present project solutions and large-scale and/or local planning. In particular, they acquire: knowledge and understanding of drawing as an expressive act and visual communication of the project idea; knowledge of representation and communication tools for plans at various operational scales; graphical languages and tools to build a territorial knowledge base aimed at urban, territorial, and environmental planning; tools for processing digital cartography in a GIS environment.
Area of Architecture and Engineering: The three-year urban planning graduate will have acquired basic knowledge of the evolution of urbanist thought, urban technique, environmental and territorial planning, planning tools, and urban and territorial policies and landscape through continuous comparison between Italian, international experiences, and case studies. Within urbanism and territorial planning, the three-year graduate acquires knowledge of city history, urban theory, experiences related to urban projects and territorial planning, basic requirements for the sustainability of plans and projects, and sustainable mobility. This enables the acquisition of critical analysis capabilities for phenomena and evolution dynamics of urban, territorial, and landscape systems. The three-year graduate will learn knowledge on the principles and methods for addressing planning and the project of space and transportation systems in their role as a structural component of territorial organization. The graduate will acquire particular sensitivity and develop particular attention regarding some cross-cutting knowledge of the architecture and urbanism area:
- the theme of sustainability and urban and environmental risks, presented from environmental, economic, social, and political-institutional perspectives, which recall concepts of resource resilience and durability, territorial and social equity both in intra- and intergenerational terms;
- the theme of non-negotiable values of a local society, common and collective goods, whose respect and protection recall an ethical principle and non-avoidable social responsibility;
- the theme of the project for organizing inclusive space, directed at all, to any type of minority, to vulnerable subjects who require inclusive cities, spaces, and services;
- environmental-oriented management of the city and territory, which implies listening to the context and involving local societies in local development processes.
Area of Ecology, Geography, and Geology: The disciplines within this area provide the key elements of ecological issues in planning and the use of territory and urban environment. They also allow for the analysis and interpretation of territory through its geographical and economic-political dimension. Three-year graduates must know and understand the structure and functioning of territorial systems and, in particular, be able to analyze and evaluate biotic and abiotic components and soil both in structural terms (diversity), functional terms (processes), and management terms (conservation, restoration, problem identification and resolution of various environmental themes, particularly plant species and community aggregates). Graduates must acquire a systematic understanding of the functioning and organization of living plant organisms as well as the structure and processes of vegetation.
Area of Law, Economics, and Sociology: The teachings in this area provide disciplinary institutions of law, economics, and sociology with the deepening of preparatory aspects for the formation of the urban planning graduate. Within the discipline of economics, the main theories and experiences in the economic field for the safeguarding and valorization of collective goods are presented, with particular reference to the context and the project theme of the teaching block. Within the module related to law and sociology, in addition to essential disciplinary knowledge, the student acquires some interpretive tools for investigating the social landscapes of an urban context. The ability and skills in analyzing and interpreting legal norms allow the graduate to build normative knowledge of urban law to develop realistic and feasible project hypotheses.
Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities: Related training activities strengthen the educational path and fundamental knowledge for developing project hypotheses in laboratories. Among the disciplines, ancient typography makes explicit the settlement principle of a territory in relation to the environmental structure of the context, fundamental knowledge for initiating a deep understanding of the historical matrices of a city. Regarding environmental hygiene, the three-year graduate will acquire in-depth knowledge of the relationship between public health and the environment, reinforcing the understanding of planning's pivotal role as the primary form of protection for both. Territorial geology allows for the interpretation of structural elements of environmental context analysis and its dynamics. Project epistemology stimulates understanding and interactive dialogue on theoretical concepts that can form the basis of a project idea.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematics, Informatics, and Statistics: Modeling a problem through the language and tools of mathematics allows the urbanist to acquire a capacity for calculation, resolution, and approximation of solutions to complex problems. This provides the foundation for understanding the tools of technical disciplines addressed in subsequent years and for modeling urban phenomena.
Area of Representation: Students learn the knowledge necessary for forming a territorial analysis through graphical representation tools and through the stratification of coded territorial information, treatable, for example, with Geographic Information Systems. This allows them to apply both graphical and numerical techniques to propose the project idea and its implications on the environment and territory.
Area of Architecture and Engineering: The three-year urban planning graduate will be able to address the complexity of territorial and urban systems by applying acquired knowledge. They will be able to apply approaches, techniques, and tools within project laboratories that characterize each teaching module. The interdisciplinarity of the laboratories allows for the acquisition of understanding of the complexity of urban processes and promotes the practical skills and abilities of integrated design at various operational scales. The teaching project of the three-year degree promotes dialogue between distinct competencies that contribute, in practice, to solving urban problems. Group work stimulated in project laboratories fosters the acquisition of methodological and project skills with which to build hypotheses for urban transformation and regeneration. Through the project of urban space and territorial planning, even in infrastructural terms, the graduate develops sensitivity towards building conditions that improve urban quality and the environment. The three-year graduate will learn and develop capabilities on the principles and methods for addressing urban and environmental risks involving the organization of the city and territory. The operational comparison with a specific study context within project laboratories fosters the development of capabilities in framing, interpretation, and definition of action strategies and project interventions at appropriate levels of detail.
Area of Ecology, Geography, and Geology: The teaching approach provides that each theoretical element corresponds to an exemplification that students must apply autonomously within project laboratories. This stimulates the ability to choose and use appropriate equipment, tools, and methods to detect structural and functional diversity of the territory, to understand relevant approaches and theories for the investigated theme; combine theory and practice to solve information acquisition problems as well as conservation and protection.
Area of Law, Economics, and Sociology: Through the knowledge acquired in this area, the graduate will be able to prepare a preliminary assessment regarding the social and economic feasibility of planning and project interventions, to read and interpret social and normative dynamics that may hinder, favor, and integrate policies, plans, and projects.
Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities: The three-year graduate, through related activities, strengthens interdisciplinary capabilities to develop project ideas, make them feasible and implementable. For this, the acquired knowledge will allow them to anticipate and/or counter environmental issues, for example with evident impacts on public health, proposing prevention strategies inherent to planning at all possible levels (primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention). Regarding ancient topography, through acquired knowledge, the student must be able to initiate correct procedures for evaluating and interpreting current settlement landscapes; through geology, they will be able to understand the necessity of consistency between territory functioning and settlement and localization dynamics of a project. Epistemology offers the graduate the possibility to develop creative ideas that promote territorial innovation.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIANO Associated Competencies to the Function.
Junior Planner: For all functions, transversal and common competencies and abilities are the ability to dialogue with experts from other disciplines, to work within interdisciplinary groups and not.
For the performance of Function A - responsible for technical-administrative procedures in public administrations - knowledge of laws, decrees, etc., regulating technical-administrative processes, planning and project tools at various scales, procedures, and administrative steps for the drafting, approval, implementation, and monitoring of territorial, urban, landscape, and environmental plans and projects is required.
For the performance of Function B - independent professional with functions of analysis, monitoring, and evaluation - the graduate must possess analytical competencies and abilities, define indicators, requirements, and criteria for monitoring and evaluation oriented to planning, be able to use tools and techniques of analysis, monitoring, and evaluation, as well as institutional and legislative reference frameworks.
For the performance of Function C - independent professional analyst and data processor of territorial data, expert in territorial information systems - theoretical and practical foundations are required in the field of analysis, interpretation, and processing of territorial data and some models, techniques, and tools supporting such activities; for territorial information systems and cartographic representations, adequate theoretical and practical foundations are necessary, and the ability to use at least one software for creating territorial information systems.
For the performance of Function D - independent professional collaborator in the drafting of transformation, rehabilitation, recovery, and development programs - it is necessary to know in theory and practice techniques, methods, and tools for environmental and strategic evaluations, feasibility studies, and involving non-expert components in planning processes.
For the performance of Function E - independent professional collaborator in various planning activities at all scales - it is necessary to know the normative and institutional reference framework, planning tools at all scales, their hierarchy, definition, approval, implementation, and monitoring processes. Additionally, it is necessary to have capabilities in detecting, analyzing, and structuring problems related to the physical context of the activity and to be able to use techniques, methods, and tools supporting planning activities, including those oriented towards participation processes.
For the performance of Function F - independent professional promoter of local development - the graduate must possess the ability: to read and interpret the diverse specificities of local contexts but also to construct innovative project visions, capable of colliding the potentials expressed by territories with the needs traversing the contemporary. And at the same time, must be able to use devices and languages through which to involve the different actors and subjects inhabiting the territory.

Function in Work Context.
Junior Planner: The three-year graduate possesses basic competencies and knowledge that will allow them to continue studies in specialized paths in various sectors (Planning, Information Systems, Landscape Architecture, Environmental Sciences), to access first-level Master's programs (which require a three-year degree of the same class), or to carry out professional activities (after passing the State Exam for professional qualification and registration with the Professional Order of Architects, Planners, Landscape Architects, and Conservators - Section B of the register) in the fields of planning, evaluation, and urban management.
The main functions in a work context are:
A. responsible for technical-administrative procedures in public administrations for the realization of plans, policies, programs, territorial, urban, landscape, and environmental programs, also related to public works, for which they verify the existence of eligibility conditions, carry out acts and necessary technical verifications for various procedural stages, take care of communications, involvement, and interaction between various subjects involved in the administrative procedure, collaborate in the management of local development projects;
B. as an independent professional, develops territorial and urban analyses, systems, and procedures for environmental, urban, territorial, and landscape monitoring and evaluation (e.g., VIA, VAS, etc.);
C. as an independent professional, performs analyst functions, defines procedures for analyzing and processing data of various nature related to territory, landscape, environment, and city, produces forms of representation of the results of such analyses and processing (cartographic, textual, etc.), designs and manages territorial information systems;
D. as an independent professional, collaborates in activities for drafting programs of urban, territorial, environmental, and landscape transformation, rehabilitation, recovery, and development, and management of implementation processes derived from them;
E. as an independent professional, collaborates in the drafting of urban, territorial, environmental, landscape, or sectoral plans at various scales, with particular attention to analysis activities, without assuming overall responsibility for their production, collaborates in the management of local development projects;
F. as an independent professional, performs at various levels of administration a role of collaborator and promoter of innovative local development processes, within the framework of European and regional tenders aimed at rediscovering and reinterpreting the diverse local specificities through a project. Specificities intended not as simple heritage to be valorized, but as elements generating innovative projects, economies, and cultures around which to build innovation sites, even and through the involvement of broad social participation.

Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The Urbanism. Environmental Project of the City and Territory (CdS) provides theoretical, methodological, and technical tools encompassing cultural, historical, economic, social, and environmental context elements to analyze, represent, design, and manage settlement transformation processes involving the city, territory, landscape, and environment.
The educational path aims to train a professional capable of:
- analyze, interpret the dynamics of contemporary urban and territorial processes;
- confront with the different scales of complex problems traversing the urban ecosystem and current human condition (climate change and territorial risks, social inequalities and welfare system crises, forms of progress and processes of cultural homogenization induced by global economies, changes in world population…);
- develop effective and durable ideas, projects, and policies for planning, management, and governance of the territory, process information through information technologies.
The CdS aims to build fundamental competencies for city development and territory governance, but also to motivate students to build a learning environment capable of adequately responding to the problems and challenges of the ecological transition involving contemporary urban territories, which require interdisciplinary knowledge, competencies in terms of innovative and creative project approaches, a sense of responsibility, and an ethical approach towards the environment and living spaces. These are crucial objectives for a new model of urban territory development that confronts the diverse vulnerabilities of contexts not only local.
For this reason, the CdS prioritizes theoretical and project approaches that allow the student and thus the future urbanist to act under conditions of uncertainty and flexibility, complexity and innovation, process interscalarity and interdependence of involved actors. This is what qualifies the professional figure in relation to the needs emerging from social partners at the local level, which find important echoes also at the global level.
The interdisciplinary approach promoted by the CdS dedicates particular attention to the 'context' and, more specifically, to the many articulations of the Mediterranean landscape and environment, in order to promote an investigation and action method that students can extend to broader contexts in which they will operate in their future professional life. In relation to other planning and urbanism schools, the educational path promoted by the Degree Course - which is anchored to the specificity of the Sardinian territory where historically an idea of urban has developed not always coinciding with the idea of a delimited and circumscribed city - provides a baggage of knowledge and competencies that:
- pursue an orientation towards a project approach that overcomes the classic city/countryside dichotomies, to reveal the urban potential of the territory in its complexity;
- affirm a conception of territory as the center of the educational path and learning processes, as the deep matrix of living spaces;
- seek in the intertwining of different territorial scales alternatives to the dense city model and reorient the city towards a spatial reorganization where not only city and nature meet but environmental dominants and historically dense places acquire new meanings of centralities for the city.
These competencies allow the graduate to access master's degrees and develop professional capabilities for: a) collaborating in design and planning to manage transformation and regeneration processes of the city, territory, environment, and landscape; b) managing evaluation activities of projects, programs, plans, and urban, territorial, environmental, and landscape policies; c) managing scenario and policy construction processes with the involvement of social and economic actors; d) developing and managing territorial information systems.
The need for an internship path that gives the student greater ability to enter the workforce through field experience, also through Erasmus Placement programs that students carry out in Italy and abroad.
Basic subjects have a significant weight in the first two years of the course, to form a solid preparation that enables students to face the increasing complexity of project subjects in the final part of the path. In particular, basic subjects related to the study of the environment and its relationship with the territory (ecology discipline area) develop in an articulated path also in the second year, interacting in this case with project laboratories and characteristic subjects. The contribution of the representation discipline is relevant, fundamental for the competencies and skills required for urban space project. The space dedicated in the first year to historical and archaeological subjects related to planning and the study of the city and territory is motivated by the need to understand the historical, social, architectural, and cultural complexity of the urban and territorial context.
Description and Teaching Methods: The teaching of the educational path is delivered in a mixed mode. It predominantly uses distance learning for basic disciplines and theoretical lessons of characteristic courses. In particular, for basic disciplinary areas (mathematics, ecology and geography, representation), the mixed mode provides a balance between distance learning and in-person teaching, with a portion of in-person exercises. For characteristic disciplinary areas (architecture and engineering, law, economics, and sociology), in-person teaching is predominant over distance learning as it includes all project laboratories and practical exercises.
The course provides mixed-mode teaching because:
- involves a broader target of students and expands the pool of students from other regions;
- responds to proposals from social partners (ANCI, local administrations, professional world) regarding new guidelines on continuous training;
- responds to the needs outlined in the recently signed agreement between the University of Sassari and the Ministry of Public Administration to expand the knowledge and competencies of public employees (a target already present in the course).
The overall teaching offer, as specified in the University and Course Regulations, is organized into semesters in which teaching units and modules are structured, having a distinctive 'title' that recalls relevant themes of the city, environment, and landscape.
Teaching units (also called 'teaching blocks') generally focus on a key project theme around which, in some cases, different disciplines are integrated. Some courses develop independently from design activities (although in many cases they can deepen interdisciplinary aspects and specific investigations related to the project work).
The first year is dedicated to the basic study of the city, territory, environment, and landscape, i.e., to 'enter' the semantic fields of the profession's object. The second year is dedicated to deepening the methods and practices of project and environmental, urban, and territorial planning with increasing attention to themes related to territory safeguarding. The third year is a recapitulation and deepening, centered on a teaching unit addressing the relationship between plan and project, and on career-end paths (long internship and dissertation on that experience, design/planning laboratory, dissertation related to a research theme).
Project activities provide the presence of tutors, young professionals knowledgeable in the subject, who follow laboratory and project activities, and in some cases the didactic activities of frontal lessons. Intermediate learning verification activities are provided (written and oral tests, intermediate critiques of laboratory projects).
The objective of the CdS is also to constantly stimulate students to knowledge and use of foreign languages in written and oral form, both through the teaching of the English language, and indirectly through experiences organized by the CdS and the Department to foster an international and intercultural learning environment (open lectures and conferences, workshops and international summer schools, group work with Erasmus students from different contexts). In this sense, graduates must be able to fluently use at least the English language in written and oral form, referring also to national and international disciplinary lexicons.
During the three-year educational path, students develop autonomously chosen didactic activities: the degree course suggests some in-depth training activities that enrich and expand the offer of teaching units and modules. This semester also focuses on internship activities where the student develops applied research experiences and direct knowledge of the professional world; on career-end paths that have different structures according to the specific educational needs of the student.

The Bachelor's degree also aims to promote in graduates the ability to independently update their knowledge and develop experiences, with particular reference to learning issues that may arise during professional and work activities.

Autonomy of Judgment.
The degree program enables graduates to:
– develop critical abilities in interpreting economic phenomena, evaluating tourism market trends, organizing companies in the sector, and understanding institutional realities operating in tourism;
– collect, organize/manage, select, and interpret specific data of qualitative and quantitative nature, aimed at evaluating tourism companies and organizing tourism systems;
– autonomously organize a detailed reflection on specific business realities or tourism contexts, identifying existing critical issues and proposing practical solutions for the development of tourist destinations, improvement of business organization, orientation of service demand in the market, and development of homogeneous or integrated tourism offerings;
– plan choices, contribute collaboration, or assume a leadership position within work groups oriented towards developing tourism offerings, creating tourism products, managing services, tourism companies, and public and private infrastructure;
– make decisions and solve problems in the presence of non-homogeneous variables and incomplete information, adopting appropriate attitudes and behaviors aligned with the work environment and the reference professional profile;
– verify the level of technical preparation and the degree of autonomy achieved.
Students acquire full autonomy of judgment throughout the program through critical learning methods developed within traditional training activities, as well as through experiences of various nature encountered during teaching activities other than frontal lectures, which contribute to completing the acquisition process of the necessary methodology and tools for successfully entering the labor market.
Students are encouraged to continuously acquire and improve critical abilities and autonomy of judgment during study groups, practical exercises, project development, use of data banks, specialized programs, and simulation tools.
Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area The study program enables students to acquire:
a) knowledge, skills, and aptitudes sufficient to intervene in economic and financial planning, management control of tourism companies, and the definition of public policies for the tourism sector and related fields;
b) in-depth knowledge and adequate mastery of tools, systems, and management processes specific to tourism companies, public administration, and other entities and organizations operating in tourism, from a perspective oriented towards improving the efficiency and effectiveness of private and public actions;
c) adequate mastery of tools, methods, and skills necessary to create new entrepreneurial activities in the tourism sector or to continue economic and business studies in preparation for entering the professional world;
d) knowledge of at least one European Union language other than Italian, preferably English, enabling the ability to operate with application tools and use the most widely adopted management models internationally, through practical application within companies, organizations, and entities affiliated with the study program, as well as through specific simulation programs.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area Upon completion of the training path, graduates will be able to apply analytical, methodological, and interpretive tools of the economic framework, tourism market, and sector companies within specific operational realities and determined organizational sectors, utilizing the business, economic, legal, and quantitative competencies acquired during the program.
In particular:
a) specific abilities to understand business, economic, legal, and quantitative dynamics characterizing the tourism sector, with particular reference to market trends, company management, regulatory and institutional frameworks, and organization of territorial systems;
b) the ability to understand tourism sector problems and their development dynamics, the ability to interpret consumer needs and tourist behaviors, alongside the ability to contribute to the planning of public policies essential for improving supply systems, valorizing destinations, and addressing challenges related to environmental sustainability;
c) the ability to verify one's level of technical preparation and evaluate the degree of autonomy achieved in learning various disciplines and understanding the tourism system, dynamics, and phenomena;
d) skills in analyzing work organization, production, and business functions;
e) skills related to understanding organizational functioning;
f) skills in understanding and programming functions within a company, with specific reference to companies operating in the tourism sector;
g) the ability to define strategies and utilize marketing tools for tourism sector activities;
h) skills in understanding the competitive advantages of the company within the national and international economic context in which it operates.
To this end, appropriate teaching methodologies are provided, and numerous hours of exercises are conducted under the guidance of the official instructor for each course, with continuous support from academic tutors and, where applicable, sector experts.
The curricular internship (company internship), group exercises, continuous monitoring of acquired skills, problem-solving activities, simulation of management models, among others, represent additional ways in which students are enabled to acquire practical competencies and verify mastery of tools, methodologies, and critical autonomy.
The learning process is facilitated by the provision, organization, and delivery of a diverse portfolio of training activities aimed not only at promoting the learning of theoretical aspects of each discipline but also, if not primarily, at stimulating their practical application.
More specifically, the training activities, while respecting the specificity and nature of each discipline, are carried out through the following methods:
1) traditional lectures (frontal), always aimed at seeking and valuing active student participation;
2) practical exercises to stimulate the application of theoretical concepts;
3) discussion of articles from specialized press to stimulate students' ability to interpret and critically analyze topics related to regional, national, and international tourism phenomena;
4) company testimonials to help students understand how conceptual approaches guide strategic and operational reflection for those managing public and/or private organizations involved in the tourism supply chain;
5) company visits to allow students to directly appreciate within real organizational contexts the nature and scope of strategic and operational problems that tourism organizations face;
6) project work and/or active laboratories based on collaboration between university and companies, offering students the opportunity to tackle real business problems;
7) business games organized at national and/or international levels, where consistent with the disciplines and educational objectives of the study program.
Knowledge and understanding are assessed through oral interviews and/or written exams, sometimes supplemented by reports, exercises, group work, and evaluations of real problem-solving activities where students demonstrate mastery of theories, tools, and methodologies.

Generic Profile The degree program aims to train professional figures capable of effectively responding to labor market needs and successfully integrating into private companies, public entities, and other public and private organizations operating in the tourism sector.
The educational path also provides students with the necessary tools, methods, and competencies to create new entrepreneurial activities in the tourism sector or to continue economic and business studies in preparation for entering the professional world.
The degree program aims to build a solid and multidisciplinary cultural base suitable for training graduates capable of covering a variety of roles and functions in private and public institutions, including study, analysis, direction, and consulting within the tourism sector, or alternatively, to continue studies in first-level master's courses, specialized degrees, or second-level master's courses across various disciplines.
In particular, the degree program enables graduates to gain training experiences and acquire transferable skills applicable in various contexts where tourism companies and sector professionals operate, with particular reference to activities involving the organization and intermediation of travel (travel agencies, tour operators, communication companies, companies operating in electronic distribution and web marketing, for example) and the provision of individual tourism services (accommodation structures, transport companies, cruise companies, restaurants and catering companies, charter and nautical marina companies, beach enterprises; as well as professionals, guides, and escorts, conference, fair, and event organizers; to mention a few roles).
At the same time, the competencies acquired during the study path will enable graduates to perform consulting activities or hold responsible roles in public entities (municipalities, provinces, regions, as well as natural parks and protected marine areas, Chambers of Commerce, and other public bodies) and other public and private organizations (local tourism systems, sector associations, tourism consortia, non-profit organizations, for example), which are involved in organizing, planning, promoting, and developing the tourism market.
In this perspective, the degree program is particularly focused on providing students with a wide range of transversal competencies—transferable across various private and public organizational contexts—related to business organization and human resources, business strategy and tourism system management, tourism marketing and destination management, electronic distribution and revenue management, management of family businesses, and management control.
The degree program also offers a range of services, not secondary, aimed at facilitating the placement of young graduates in the business world, public administration, and professions, while developing concrete actions and organizing projects to support the startup of new companies and initiatives for creating new businesses by young graduates.
Lastly, graduates in Economics and Tourism Management benefit from a facilitated path for accessing the professions of travel and tourism agency technical director and tour guide, according to the new registration regulations for the respective regional registers established by Sardinia Region Law December 18, 2006, No. 20.
Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The degree program in Economics and Tourism Management aims to provide in-depth knowledge of the tourism sector through understanding the business, economic, legal, and quantitative dynamics characterizing the market reality, service organization, company and entity management, tourism supply system management, destination management, resource valorization, consumer choices, and tourism flow trends.
Therefore, the degree program is directed towards young individuals interested in acquiring high-level professional skills and in-depth knowledge of the tourism system, in preparation for labor market entry in private companies or important public entities; they are offered the opportunity to acquire specific tourism competencies and the methodological tools necessary for successfully entering the labor market.
Due to its interdisciplinary nature and the advanced knowledge it provides, the degree program is also aimed at private and public sector operators interested in obtaining new tools to correctly interpret tourism sector development trends and adapt their skills to the latest knowledge, thereby conferring new managerial competitiveness to private enterprises and ensuring new growth opportunities for the territory.
In this perspective, the training path is characterized first and foremost by providing a solid foundational preparation in the main areas of business management, coupled with adequate knowledge of economic, legal, mathematical-statistical disciplines, and at least one European Union language other than Italian.
On this foundation, a knowledge base is built focused on studying, from both a business and economic perspective, various tourism activities with organizational, intermediation, or service provision characteristics, as well as the actions of entities and organizations involved in planning and organizing tourism markets and systems.
Non-marginal attention is given to environmental profiles connected to the tourism phenomenon, particularly in forms of tourism where socioeconomic actions' sustainability and natural resources play a primary role.
The training process can be completed with a curricular internship to be carried out with sector operators, private companies, or public entities, enabling the concrete application of the methodological tools and knowledge acquired during the degree program.
