Judgment Autonomy.
Expected outcomes: the graduate will have awareness and judgment autonomy that enables them to acquire the necessary information and evaluate the implications inherent in forest and environmental management systems, to implement interventions aimed at improving and conserving environmental quality and planning sustainable development linked to the cultural aspects of the territory.
The assessment of the acquisition of judgment autonomy will occur through the evaluation of the results achieved in the core disciplines as well as in the optional subjects chosen by the student, and through the evaluation of the degree of autonomy and ability to work individually and in groups during practical activities and the completion of the assignment prepared for the final exam.

Learning Ability.
Expected outcomes: at the end of the three-year educational path, the graduate in Forest and Environmental Sciences will have acquired a solid basic education and competencies in forest and environmental disciplines, enabling them to pursue advanced studies with a high degree of autonomy, both in the management of forest and environmental systems and in the path of the master's degree LM-73. The bachelor's degree provides the essential cognitive tools for continuous knowledge updating in the specific sector, also using new communication technologies, remote sensing, and computer science, to apply their knowledge to solving the multiple problems related to the management of forest and environmental systems. Graduates will have developed the learning abilities that allow them to continue studies in a master's degree, a first-level master's, or directly enter the workforce.
The learning ability will be assessed through analysis of the individual student's academic record regarding grades in exams and the time elapsed between attending the course and passing the exam, as well as through evaluation of the self-learning abilities developed during the completion of the final exam-related activities.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area Expected outcomes: at the end of the educational path, graduates in Forest and Environmental Sciences will acquire basic knowledge of Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology.
In particular, they will have full knowledge of the physical processes related to the main management and planning issues in agroforestry and environmental management at both territorial and enterprise levels; they will know the atomic-molecular composition of materials and be able to understand the role of chemical bonds and structure on the properties of materials, as well as the main chemical and biochemical reactions occurring in the soil, living organisms, and natural biological cycles.
Graduates will have the knowledge for understanding the fundamental aspects of ecology and the biology of prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms. They will acquire knowledge of the investigation methods specific to Forest and Environmental Sciences and be able to approach the analysis of forest and environmental systems systematically, evaluating their complexity and biodiversity, applying the fundamental methods of scientific investigation for problem-solving in the forest and environmental sector.
They will possess theoretical, operational, and laboratory knowledge to carry out appropriate interventions in various sectors of forest and environmental activities, with particular reference to the protection, planning, and sustainable management of forest and agroforestry resources; improvement of forest and environmental systems; environmental monitoring and biodiversity conservation; prevention and treatment of forest species from attacks by phytophagous pests and cryptogams; protection and conservation of soil and mountainous environments, as well as environmental impact assessment.
The graduate in Forest and Environmental Sciences will also be able to perform technical, managerial, and support tasks in productive and technical activities, in laboratories, and in public and private service structures.
Teaching methods and tools: (Teaching methods and modalities)
The methodological and cultural, scientific, and professional knowledge will be acquired through theoretical courses and practical-oriented courses with exercises and laboratory activities. Courses will be structured into didactic units to allow the progressive achievement of objectives by the student.
A practical-applicative internship period is planned at cooperating Entities and Companies. The responsible personnel must provide an assessment on both the student's prior knowledge, for the purposes of the planned internship activities, and on the abilities and additional knowledge acquired during the internship.
The assessment of the acquisition of knowledge and understanding will occur through the successful completion of intermediate tests and final exams of the core and optional subjects chosen by the students.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area The professional activity of a graduate in Forest and Environmental Sciences is aimed at managing forest and mountainous territory or areas marginal to intensive agricultural use, as well as collaborating and managing planning interventions and their subsequent management in the same territorial areas.
The professional activity, as described in the previous points, requires both multidisciplinary knowledge and the correct correlation between what is learned in individual study subjects.
The strictly engineering aspects have in Mathematics and Applied Physics for Forest Sciences the basis for the subsequent understanding of Topography, Cartography, and Forest Constructions, Hydraulics, and Hydraulic-Forest Arrangements, and subsequently in the master's course, Forest Mechanization and Rural Territory Planning.
Economic-valuation skills also have Mathematics as the basis for understanding economic laws and procedures for valuing forest and environmental assets, estimating engineering works, and primary and secondary forest productions typical of Forest and Agricultural Valuation.
The biological component of a territory requires an holistic view of its components, both biological and abiotic. The vegetative biological aspects are learned in the courses of General Botany, Systematics, and Forestry; the animal component aspects are covered in the course of Forest Zoology. Finally, knowledge of Forest and Environmental Ecology allows the correlation between biological and abiotic components, particularly with the climatic component.
Knowledge of the physiology of plant and animal species is fundamental for understanding the biological processes underlying forest production. General and Inorganic Chemistry and Organic Chemistry are the prerequisite tools for understanding microbiological processes occurring within animal and plant tissues or in the soil. Processes described in the courses of Agricultural Biochemistry and Forest and Environmental Microbiology.
Forest productions, mountainous territories, and areas marginal to intensive agricultural use are acquired in the two courses of Silviculture and Agronomy and Herbaceous Crops. Courses whose understanding and correct application particularly require prerequisite knowledge of Pedology for soil knowledge and assessment of its productive potential, as well as Soil Chemistry regarding the relationships between soil, air, and water.

Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIAN Competencies associated with the function.
Generic Profile The graduate in Forest and Environmental Sciences acquires, during the study course, knowledge and competencies related to the compatible management of forest and mountainous territory in its biotic and abiotic components. Therefore, their professional function is to actively participate in the management of forest enterprises and collaborate in the planning and management of interventions in the territory at a large area level.

Function in the workplace context.
Generic Profile The following are among the professional profiles of a graduate in Forest and Environmental Sciences:
- Support and collaboration in the programming and management of rural territory, with particular reference to the analysis and monitoring of mountainous environments and forest ecosystems.
- Support, collaboration, and management of conservation and sustainable management of forest and agroforestry environments.
- Collaboration in the management of projects and works for soil protection and restoration of degraded and compromised environments.
- Consultancy, technical assistance, and dissemination in the agroforestry sector.
- Support for environmental protection, management of natural reserves, parks, and gardens.
- Valorization and conservation of biodiversity.
- Managing activities within the processes of transformation of wood and non-wood forest products.
Some of these activities require collaboration with other professionals operating in the environmental sector, such as biologists, naturalists, geologists, as well as architects, agronomists, and master's-level foresters in large-area territorial planning, and civil engineers in the design of structures such as roads, aqueducts, and buildings with complex structures.

Description of specific educational objectives.
The bachelor's degree in Forest and Environmental Sciences aims to ensure basic scientific and methodological knowledge in disciplines concerning rural territory and forest environment resources, as well as technological and economic aspects, the ability to carry out promotional and developmental activities for the conservation and valorization of forest, ecological resources, and sustainable development of mountainous and forest territories, acquisition of essential knowledge of technologies and forest and environmental engineering, and chemical and biological methods for monitoring forest and environmental systems.
It will enable graduates, in accordance with the qualifying educational objectives of class L-25, to:
- Acquire adequate knowledge of basic scientific and technical disciplines;
- Effectively use, in written and oral form, in addition to Italian, at least one European Union language, within their specific area of competence and for the exchange of general information;
- Develop appropriate tools for communication and information management, as well as for continuous knowledge updating;
- Acquire the fundamental methods of scientific investigation and be able to collaborate in experimental activities and apply knowledge to solving technical problems in the forest and environmental sector;
- Approach the analysis of forest and environmental systems systematically, valuing their complexity and biodiversity, within the context of sustainable management;
- Possess theoretical, operational, and laboratory knowledge in various sectors of forest activity, with particular reference to the protection, improvement, and sustainable management of forest and agroforestry resources;
- Perform technical, managerial, and support tasks in productive and technical activities, in laboratories, and in public and private service structures.

Degree course organization The normal duration of the bachelor's degree in Forest and Environmental Sciences is three years, and the required university credits for the degree are 180.
The educational path of each student is guided by a tutoring committee operating within the study course.
The proposed bachelor's degree includes theoretical courses and courses with a primarily practical purpose with exercises. Activities will be organized on a semester basis and various teaching methods (frontal lectures, exercises, practical activities, laboratories, seminars, internship) will be provided according to the cultural and educational characteristics of each course.
The hourly workload reserved for each CFU is regulated by the Department's Teaching Regulations.
Teaching courses may be single-disciplinary and/or integrated, according to the Department's Teaching Regulations.
Knowledge of the foreign language is assessed either through an exam or by recognizing a substitute certification issued by external bodies recognized by the University Language Center.
Information technology and telecommunication skills, as well as additional language knowledge, are assessed by a committee appointed by the CCL.
The credits reserved for the internship can be acquired, in agreement with the educational objectives declared by the student, either through a period of internship at an external entity or by spending a similar period at a Department structure. The final exam is based on the activities carried out during the practical internship or on the in-depth study of topics related to the educational objectives of the bachelor's degree.
Student-selected activities, while maintaining full freedom of choice among all courses offered by the University, must be consistent with the educational project of the bachelor's degree.

Training activities The didactic structure of the bachelor's degree includes a group of basic disciplines, followed by professional, general, and specialized disciplines. The course aims to provide graduates with adequate technical-scientific training, enabling them to quickly integrate into the workforce.
In particular, the didactic organization of the bachelor's degree is structured into six groups of training activities.
1 - Basic training activities aimed at acquiring basic theoretical-practical competencies, distributed across the disciplinary areas specified by the class: Mathematics, Informatics, Physics, Statistics, Chemistry, Biology.
2 - Core training activities aimed at acquiring competencies in the following disciplinary areas specified by the class: Economic-valuation and legal; Plant production; Forestry and Environmental; Animal Sciences; Agricultural, Forestry Engineering, and Representation and Defense.
3 - Affine or integrative training activities aimed at completing doctrinal knowledge on core disciplines, with integrative value in the fields of Defense, Plant Production, and Environmental Assessment.
4 - Free-choice training activities that students can select, even outside the training activities proposed by the competent teaching structure.
5 - Training activities related to the preparation of the final exam and the assessment of knowledge of at least one foreign language.
6 - Other planned training activities related to internship activities and additional information technology, telecommunication, and language skills.

COURSE: [A097] ECONOMICS AND MANAGEMENT
SECTION: Critical Judgment

Critical Judgment.
The graduate in the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Management is able to retrieve data, process it, develop analyses in order to propose solutions to specific economic and business problems, using an interdisciplinary approach.
Critical judgment is acquired by using the logical-formal framework and the technical-scientific knowledge acquired throughout the entire study path in order to develop critical analyses, evaluations, and proposals inspired by the principles of efficiency, effectiveness, and economy to which business activities are oriented;
the economic, patrimonial, and financial equilibrium conditions of companies;
the principles of rational choice and cost-benefit analysis in different decision-making contexts; the distinction between normative and positive propositions; the use where possible of reliable empirical evidence; integration and comparison with other disciplines interested in the same phenomena; analysis of the results of choices under the dual profile of economy, efficiency, effectiveness, and equity; weighing the relevant effects in the short and long term.
Students are encouraged to constantly acquire and improve critical abilities and critical judgment both during lectures and during individual study, responding to teachers' prompts oriented towards the analysis of specific issues, as well as during study groups, practical exercises, project development, and the use of specific software programs.

Learning Ability.
The graduate in Economics and Management has acquired adequate flexibility in approaching diverse topics and the ability to learn new knowledge with varying degrees of autonomy and responsibility during their studies.
The student thus possesses study methodologies and the ability for rigorous and in-depth understanding, enabling them to continue their studies at a higher level in both the managerial and economic fields.
The learning ability acquired during the degree program is not merely about study methods, but especially about the ability to use flexible approaches in relation to diverse topics, which represents an indispensable skill for working in various professional fields that require continuously evolving specialized competencies.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area The graduate in the degree program knows:
- basic mathematical and statistical tools for the detection, measurement, and quantitative analysis of economic phenomena: General Mathematics (9 CFU) SECS-S/06; Statistics in the first year (9 CFU) SECS-S/01 and Economic and Business Data Analysis in the second year (9 CFU) SECS-S/03-01; Financial Mathematics (6 CFU) SECS/S06 in the third year
- the basic and more advanced concepts of business economics disciplines (company theory, marketing, finance and accounting, with particular reference to the income statement, analytical accounting, and the budgeting and reporting system): Business Economics (9 CFU) SECS-P/07 in the first year; Financial and Economic Analysis and Accounting (9 CFU) SECS-P/07 and Business Economics and Management (9 CFU) SECS-P/08 in the second year; Planning and Control (9 CFU) SECS-P/07; Corporate Finance (9 CFU) SECS-P/09 in the third year
- the foundations of microeconomics and macroeconomics as tools for understanding the functioning of the modern economy, both at the level of economic policies and from the perspective of managerial decisions, as well as market operation models: Microeconomics (9 CFU) SECS-P/01 in the first year; Macroeconomics (9 CFU) SECS-P/01 in the second year, Public Finance (9 CFU) SECS-P/03 in the second year
- the legislation related to economic institutions with particular reference to the Constitution, the Civil Code, and related laws in order to learn the regulatory framework within which economic and entrepreneurial activities take place – Private Law (9 CFU) IUS/01-05 in the first year – Public Law (6 CFU) IUS/09 in the second year – Commercial Law (9 CFU) IUS/04 in the second year
- the English language: English Language (9 CFU) L-LIN/12
These knowledge areas are further enriched by additional courses related to the two curricula.
In particular, students who choose the Management curriculum will acquire specific competencies aimed at company management and related to:
- basic theoretical and practical tools for defining and managing organizational structures: Business Organization (6 CFU) SECS-P/10 in the third year
- methodologies and tools for managing production processes, as well as techniques for quality certification: Technology and Quality (9 CFU) SECS-P/13 in the third year
- tax regulations that economic institutions must adhere to in order to understand the constraints and opportunities underlying them – Tax Law (6 CFU) IUS/12 in the third year
Students, instead, who choose the Economics curriculum will acquire specific knowledge aimed at understanding the functioning of economic systems and related to:
- the analysis of some of the main macroeconomic phenomena (unemployment, inflation, real and financial crises, etc.), highlighting how they manifest and the main theories used for their interpretation, as well as the tools of economic policy (monetary, fiscal) in closed and open economies: Economic Policy (9 CFU) SECS-P/02 in the third year
- the main characteristics of the economic system, through innovation policies, demographic and geo-economic evolution, choosing two courses from the following in the third year: Industrial and Innovation Economics (6 CFU) SECS-P/06; Economic Geography (6 CFU) M-GRR/02; Demography (6 CFU) SECS-S/04
The knowledge and understanding abilities listed above are achieved through participation in frontal lectures, exercises, working groups, seminars, and, where possible, company visits that also include moments of critical discussion on various topics, the use of case studies and elements from reality, as well as through guided individual study, as provided by the activated training activities. The verification of the achievement of learning outcomes and understanding abilities primarily occurs through oral and/or written exams, written exercises, and other evaluation methods (mainly intermediate verification tests, but also, where possible, participation in study groups, case discussions, individual and group research), as well as through the discussion of the topic that is the subject of the final exam.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area The graduate in the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Management:
- is able to individually or in groups solve economic and business problems; has adequate operational knowledge of the topics covered during the study course and possesses methodological tools to conduct research on specialized topics related to economics and management, as well as problem-solving capabilities
- possesses a comprehensive view of business phenomena and economic systems, combined with mastery of analytical tools and techniques from an economic, patrimonial, and financial perspective
- knows how to apply accounting methodologies and operational tools to support decision-making processes and business planning and programming
- is able to apply principles and criteria for the optimal organization of companies and business processes
- possesses methodological tools for analyzing the attractiveness of competitive environments, market segments, and identifying potential targets for the development of appropriate production and commercial policies
The achievement of the abilities to apply knowledge and understanding listed above occurs through critical reflection stimulated in the classroom, as well as through in-depth study of the texts and materials proposed for individual study, together, where possible, with the study of business cases.
A valuable opportunity to acquire further knowledge and critical investigation abilities arises during the preparation of the final exam, where the topics often require a comparison with entrepreneurial and economic reality.
The various forms of assessment (written and/or oral exams, intermediate tests, reports, exercises, practical tests) are designed to test the student's mastery of competencies, tools, methodologies, critical autonomy, and analysis.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIANO Associated Competencies for the Role.
Generic Profile The course allows the acquisition of competencies to support the following roles:
- Accounting Clerk, through knowledge of the regulations and techniques that allow for proper maintenance of accounting records and the preparation of financial statements for civil and tax purposes
- Commercial Function Clerk, having acquired knowledge of all phases of the sales process and behavioral aspects of the customer with whom they will interact
- Procurement Function Clerk, having acquired knowledge of procurement and the accounting of purchases
- Planning, Programming, and Control Function Clerk, through a deep knowledge of the entire management accounting system related to analytical accounting, the budgeting and reporting system
- Financial Analyst, having acquired skills to "read" and reprocess data generated by the accounting information system and interpret the specific management realities they represent and their economic-financial solidity
- Business Consultant, having acquired the foundations of management inspired by the principles of effectiveness and efficiency, the graduate can support various management needs requested by entrepreneurs or, more generally, by companies
- Consultant for Local Authorities, through knowledge of the main economic policies and economic principles, can support the organization and decision-making process of local authorities

Role in the Workplace Context.
Generic Profile The Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Management allows for the acquisition of a solid interdisciplinary education in economic, legal, and quantitative fields, opening up a plurality of career opportunities. In particular, the graduate in Economics and Management can perform numerous coordination and operational tasks in the administrative and management functions of private and public companies. They can perform diverse tasks in the administration, finance, and management control function, dealing with the entire accounting information system, both to meet regulatory obligations with the proper maintenance of general accounting for the preparation of the annual financial statement and to provide the necessary information to support the decision-making process, continuously interacting with the company's top management levels.
The graduate may also perform tasks in more operational functions: in the procurement function, managing purchase orders and supplier relationships; in the commercial function managing sales orders and customer relationships; in the human resources function dealing with both administrative and managerial aspects related to personnel.
The graduate in Economics and Management may also perform economic analysis and forecasting in real and financial markets within various organizations, such as banks, supervisory and regulatory authorities, research centers, industry associations, development agencies, and local authorities, directing the design and implementation of public and management policies carried out by such organizations.
Finally, candidates who obtain the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Management, and after passing the state exam and registration with the professional register, can practice the free profession of Certified Accountant.

Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Management aims to provide a solid foundational preparation in the sciences of economics and business management, allowing students to acquire fundamental methodological and analytical tools necessary to understand both the management and main functions of a modern company, as well as the functioning of the economic system and its institutions.
To this end, the study path integrates the classic set of foundational knowledge in business, legal, quantitative, and economic areas (microeconomics, business economics, private law, mathematics, and statistics) with a set of characteristic subjects and other training activities useful for qualifying different professional profiles, thereby enabling students to acquire specific economic-business knowledge tailored to various functional contexts (marketing, organization, planning and control, quality, finance, etc.).
The knowledge acquired in the first two years and part of the third year is necessary to occupy first-level managerial positions in public and private organizations, to practice the free profession, or to start entrepreneurial activities.
In particular, the first two years focus on the core of institutional courses (business economics, political economy, private law, mathematics, and statistics) and are further enriched by the study of economic history, macroeconomics, commercial law, public finance, marketing, and public law, as well as the acquisition of knowledge such as English language and economic data analysis, considered essential and widely required by the economic and entrepreneurial world.
During the third year of the three-year program, the student has the opportunity to choose between two curricula to complete the study path in line with their inclinations and personal expectations developed during the first two years.
Those who wish to deepen the study of business economics and management will have the opportunity to consolidate knowledge related to company dynamics in a variety of directions, such as organization, production process organization, and tax law. At the same time, by appropriately combining the study of fiscal topics and business mathematics with other optional subjects, they can enhance their profile for the free profession (Certified Accountant, Consultant).
Those who prefer the study of economic sciences will acquire further competencies on the functioning of the economy and the main economic policies, learning the essential operational methods and analytical tools to interpret economic systems in a competitive context particularly focused on innovation and to analyze information regarding different markets and the behaviors of economic actors. Thanks to this training, the student will be able to work as an analyst, project manager at banks, authorities, local authorities, and other organizations, both national and international.

Communication skills.
Graduates are able to effectively manage communication regarding the premises and purposes of their choices and project interventions, calibrating and modulating it according to the various objectives to be achieved, contexts, and audiences. The blended teaching approach helps students learn new communication methods and thus digital communication skills, as required by the challenges of the digital era.
They are therefore able to adjust the level of depth—and also the linguistic and lexical register—according to the recipient, situation, objectives, and interfaces.
In particular, students must be able to effortlessly use argumentative structures within a framework of communication organization based on the requirements of rational argumentation, while considering the need for public acts to be understandable even to non-experts and transparent.
These objectives are achieved through constant didactic and pedagogical attention aimed at enhancing the ability to justify each choice with effective argumentative structures, to make implicit or tacit premises explicit or perceptible, to be aware of the strengths and weaknesses of positions, and to be able to adopt new perspectives very different from the starting point.
In this context, the relationship rich in interactions with teachers, experts, and tutors, as well as with classmates from their own and other classes, with international students at our campus or in other campuses through Erasmus exchanges, and with graduates (an open learning community), is extremely important. Equally important is the continuous critical discussion carried out in class and in laboratories. For this reason, project laboratories often include in-process and/or final critical discussions of student work by representatives of institutions, organizations, and stakeholders interested in the project developed in the laboratory, thus simulating a real planning and design context.
The practice of languages other than Italian, familiarity with digital languages, and different communication registers used not only in face-to-face interactions but also in virtual contexts complete the construction of graduates' communication skills, which must be able to engage with differing opinions, cultures, ideologies, and cultural approaches, and potentially understand the nature of disagreements to intervene effectively through mediation, negotiation, and resolution of misunderstandings, conflict management.
In addition to the tools indicated in the previous descriptors, a constant activity will be verifying communication skills, both verbal, written, and representational, in exams and in-course assessments; in particular, a portion of the dissertation score is attributed to communication skills.
Learning abilities.
Graduates are able to synthesize acquired knowledge to form a valid basis for subsequent in-depth study, and are able to formulate independent judgments on various issues, with knowledge or awareness of major theoretical orientations and project or planning practices.
They have developed a learning methodology throughout their studies that enables them to tackle further studies by optimally using acquired skills within a framework of increasing autonomy and growing conceptual and theoretical complexity. Every opportunity for professional growth naturally becomes a moment for knowledge and theoretical deepening. They have critical awareness to identify, among their experiences, which have relevance for motivating continued university education, or to understand the needs for updating and training that arise in their professional activities.
In addition to the tools indicated in the previous descriptors and particularly individual interpretation and analysis exercises of laboratory and course materials, it is the very process of "learning by doing" through numerous assessments and constant interaction with teachers, experts, and tutors that constitutes the decisive moment for evaluating learning abilities.

UNIVERSITY: University of Sassari
COURSE: [A145] URBAN PLANNING. ENVIRONMENTAL PROJECT OF THE CITY AND TERRITORY
SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://uniss.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10901?annoOrdinamento=2022

Autonomy of Judgment.
Graduates are able to formulate relevant and insightful judgments on various disciplinary and transdisciplinary issues, using acquired knowledge correctly and rationally, demonstrating the ability to well organize, use, and adapt concepts, techniques, tools, and theories, and to 'gather' knowledge in the context of cognitive and operational objectives influenced by the context.
Their judgment capacity is open to the multiplicity of possible approaches, structured by awareness of the complexity of issues and distant from a merely solution-oriented conception of the project and plan.
The judgments typically formulated by graduates must be flexible and 'original', but must always be anchored to the fundamental ability to explore and understand the world, so that even the formulation of a judgment becomes, always, an additional heuristic and a hypothesis to test.
Graduates subject every judgment to their own ability to discuss and doubt, supporting it both with argumentative reasoning and quantitative analyses.
It is particularly important to highlight, at every opportunity, the cultural, social, philosophical, historical, and technical-scientific aspects that deepen and give substance to any project-related issue.
These results are pursued through:
- integrated teaching modules where the same comparison between professors forces students to continuous work of translation and comparison between personal and disciplinary viewpoints;
- project laboratories inspired by complexity and interdisciplinarity;
constant didactic reference to the adoption of new theoretical perspectives and the need to provide reasoned justifications for actual and possible choices;
- interpersonal comparison, achieved through group work and critical class discussions;
- collaborative methods supported by e-learning tools;
- cultivation of autonomy of judgment.
In addition to the tools indicated in the previous descriptors, periodic assessments, structured and coordinated also by tutors, will be carried out on theoretical and project-related topics and issues chosen autonomously by students and interpreted by them using the methods and techniques they deem appropriate.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematics, Computer Science, and Statistics The basic languages, concepts, and theorems of linear algebra, mathematical analysis, and geometry provide fundamental knowledge for using the tools of technical disciplines addressed in subsequent years and for modeling urban phenomena.
Area of Representation Students acquire, also practical, knowledge of the basic tools for graphical representation of cartography, even digital; they must be able to filter and manage data structure, representation levels, and graphical coding of a representative dataset's visualization; use communication tools and graphical languages to present project solutions and large-scale and/or local planning. In particular, they acquire: knowledge and understanding of drawing as an expressive act and visual communication of the project idea; knowledge of representation and communication tools for the plan at different operational scales; graphical languages and tools to build a territorial knowledge base for urban, territorial, and environmental planning; tools for processing digital cartography in a GIS environment.
Area of Architecture and Engineering The three-year urban planning graduate will have acquired basic knowledge of the evolution of urban thought, urban technique, environmental and territorial planning, planning tools, and urban, territorial, and landscape policies through continuous comparison between Italian, international experiences, and case studies.
Within urban planning and territorial planning, the three-year graduate acquires knowledge of city history, urban theory, experiences related to urban projects and territorial planning, basic requirements for sustainability of plans and projects, and sustainable mobility. This allows them to acquire the ability to critically analyze phenomena and the dynamics of evolution of urban, territorial, and landscape systems.
The three-year graduate will learn knowledge on the principles and methods for addressing planning and design of space and transportation systems as a structural component of territorial organization.
The graduate will acquire particular sensitivity and develop particular attention regarding some cross-cutting knowledge of the architecture and urban planning area:
- the theme of sustainability and urban and environmental risks, presented from environmental, economic, social, and political-institutional perspectives, which recall concepts of resource resilience and durability, territorial and social equity both in intra- and intergenerational terms;
- the theme of non-negotiable values of a local society, common and collective goods, whose respect and protection recall an ethical principle and non-avoidable social responsibility;
- the theme for the project of organizing inclusive space, directed at all, to any type of minority, to vulnerable subjects requiring inclusive cities, spaces, and services;
- environmental-oriented management of the city and territory, implying listening to the context and involving local societies in local development processes.

Area of Ecology, Geography, and Geology The disciplines within this area provide the key elements of ecological issues in planning and the use of territory and urban environment. They also allow for analyzing and interpreting territory through its geographical and economic-political dimension.
Three-year graduates must know and understand the structure and functioning of territorial systems and, in particular, be able to analyze and evaluate biotic and abiotic components and soil both in structural terms (diversity), functional terms (processes), and management terms (conservation, restoration, problem identification and resolution of various environmental themes, particularly plant species and community aggregates). Graduates must acquire a systematic understanding of the functioning and organization of living plant organisms as well as the structure and processes of vegetation.

Area of Law, Economics, and Sociology The teachings in this area provide disciplinary institutions of law, economics, and sociology with the deepening of preparatory aspects for the formation of the urban planning graduate.
Within the discipline of economics, the main theories and experiences in economic field for safeguarding collective goods and their valorization are presented, with particular reference to the context and the project theme of the teaching block.
Within the module related to law and sociology, in addition to essential disciplinary knowledge, the student acquires some interpretive tools for investigating social landscapes in an urban context. The ability and competencies in analyzing and interpreting legal norms allow the graduate to build normative knowledge of urban law to develop realistic and feasible project hypotheses.

Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities Related training activities strengthen the educational path and fundamental knowledge for developing project hypotheses in laboratories. Among the disciplines, ancient typography makes explicit the settlement principle of a territory in relation to the environmental structure of the context, fundamental knowledge for initiating a deep understanding of the historical matrices of a city. Regarding environmental hygiene, the three-year graduate will acquire in-depth knowledge of the relationship between public health and the environment, reinforcing the understanding of planning's pivotal role as the primary form of protection for both. Territorial geology allows for interpreting the structural elements of environmental context analysis and its dynamics. The epistemology of the project stimulates understanding and interactive dialogue on theoretical concepts that can form the basis of a project idea.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematics, Computer Science, and Statistics Modeling a problem through the language and tools of mathematics allows the urbanist to acquire the ability to calculate, solve, and approximate solutions to complex problems. This provides the foundation for understanding the tools of technical disciplines addressed in subsequent years and for modeling urban phenomena.
Area of Representation Students learn the necessary knowledge for forming a territorial analysis through graphical representation tools and through the stratification of coded territorial information, treatable, for example, with Geographic Information Systems. This allows them to apply both graphical and numerical techniques to propose the project idea and its implications on the environment and territory.
Area of Architecture and Engineering The three-year urban planning graduate will be able to address the complexity of territorial and urban systems by applying acquired knowledge. They will be able to apply approaches, techniques, and tools within the project laboratories that characterize each teaching module. The interdisciplinarity of the laboratories allows for acquiring the ability to understand the complexity of urban processes and promotes the practical skills of integrated design at different operational scales.
The teaching project of the three-year degree promotes dialogue between distinct competencies that, in practice, contribute to solving urban problems. Group work stimulated in project laboratories fosters the acquisition of methodological and project skills to build hypotheses of urban transformation and regeneration. Through the design of urban space and territorial planning, even in infrastructural terms, the graduate develops sensitivity towards building conditions that improve urban quality and the environment.
The three-year graduate will learn and develop capabilities on the principles and methods for addressing urban and environmental risks involving the organization of the city and territory. The operational comparison with a specific study context within project laboratories fosters the development of skills in framing, interpretation, and definition of action strategies and project interventions at appropriate detail scales.
Area of Ecology, Geography, and Geology The teaching approach provides that each theoretical element corresponds to an exemplification that students must apply autonomously within project laboratories. This stimulates the ability to choose and use appropriate equipment, tools, and methods to detect structural and functional diversity of the territory, to understand relevant approaches and theories for the investigated theme; combine theory and practice to solve problems of information acquisition as well as conservation and protection.
Area of Law, Economics, and Sociology Through the knowledge acquired in this area, the graduate will be able to prepare a preliminary assessment regarding the social and economic feasibility of planning and project interventions, to read and interpret social and normative dynamics that may hinder, favor, and integrate policies, plans, and projects.
Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities The three-year graduate, through related activities, strengthens interdisciplinary capabilities to develop project ideas, make them feasible and implementable. For this, the acquired knowledge will allow them to anticipate and/or counter environmental issues, for example with evident impacts on public health, proposing prevention strategies inherent to planning at all possible levels (primary, secondary, and tertiary). Regarding ancient topography, through acquired knowledge, the student must be able to initiate correct procedures for evaluating and interpreting current settlement landscapes; through geology, they will be able to understand the necessity of consistency between territory functioning and settlement and localization dynamics of a project. Epistemology offers the graduate the possibility to develop creative ideas that promote territorial innovation.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN

Competencies Associated with the Function.
Junior Planner For all functions, common and cross-cutting competencies and abilities are the ability to dialogue with experts from other disciplines, to work within interdisciplinary groups.
For the performance of Function A - responsible for technical-administrative procedures in public administrations - knowledge of laws, decrees, etc., regulating technical-administrative processes, planning and project tools at various scales, procedures, and administrative steps for drafting, approval, implementation, and monitoring of territorial, urban, landscape, and environmental plans and projects.
For the performance of Function B - freelance professional with analysis, monitoring, and evaluation functions - the graduate must possess analytical competencies and abilities, define indicators, requirements, and criteria for monitoring and evaluation oriented to planning, be able to use tools and techniques of analysis, monitoring, and evaluation, as well as institutional and legislative reference frameworks.
For the performance of Function C - freelance professional analyst and data processor of territorial data, expert in territorial information systems - theoretical and practical foundations are required in the field of analysis, interpretation, and processing of territorial data and some models, techniques, and tools supporting such activities; for territorial information systems and cartographic representations, adequate theoretical and practical foundations are necessary, and the ability to use at least one software for creating territorial information systems.
For the performance of Function D - freelance professional collaborator in the drafting of transformation, rehabilitation, recovery, and development programs - it is necessary to know in theory and practice techniques, methods, and tools for environmental and strategic evaluations, feasibility studies, and involving non-expert components in planning processes.
For the performance of Function E - freelance professional collaborator in various planning activities at all scales - it is necessary to know the normative and institutional reference framework, planning tools at all scales, their hierarchy, definition, approval, implementation, and monitoring processes. Additionally, it is necessary to have the ability to detect, analyze, and structure problems related to the physical context of the activity and to use techniques, methods, and tools supporting planning activities, including those oriented towards participation processes.
For the performance of Function F - freelance professional promoter of local development - the graduate must possess the ability: to read and interpret the diverse specificities of local contexts but also to construct innovative project visions capable of merging the potentials expressed by territories with the needs traversing the contemporary. At the same time, they must be able to use devices and languages to involve the different actors and subjects inhabiting the territory.

Function in the Workplace Context.
Junior Planner The three-year graduate possesses basic competencies and knowledge that will allow them to continue studies in specialized paths in various fields (Planning, Information Systems, Landscape Architecture, Environmental Sciences), to access first-level Master's programs (requiring a three-year degree of the same class), or to perform professional activities (after passing the State Exam for professional qualification and registration with the Professional Order of Architects, Planners, Landscape Architects, and Conservators - Section B of the register) in the fields of planning, evaluation, and urban management.
The main functions in a workplace context are:
A. responsible for technical-administrative procedures in public administrations for the realization of plans, policies, programs, territorial, urban, landscape, and environmental programs, also related to public works, for which they verify the existence of eligibility conditions, carry out acts and necessary technical verifications for various procedural stages, handle communications, involvement, and interaction between various subjects involved in the administrative procedure, collaborate in managing local development projects;
B. as a freelance professional develops territorial and urban analyses, monitoring and evaluation systems and procedures for environmental, urban, territorial, and landscape aspects (e.g., VIA, VAS, etc.),
C. as a freelance professional performs analyst functions, defines procedures for analyzing and processing data of various nature related to territory, landscape, environment, and city, produces representation forms of such analysis and processing results (cartographic, textual, etc.), designs and manages territorial information systems;
D. as a freelance professional collaborates in activities of drafting transformation, rehabilitation, recovery, and development programs for urban, territorial, environmental, and landscape areas, and managing the implementation processes derived from them;
E. as a freelance professional collaborates in drafting urban, territorial, environmental, landscape, or sectoral plans at various scales, with particular attention to analysis activities, without assuming overall responsibility for their production, collaborates in managing local development projects;
F. as a freelance professional performs a role of collaborator and promoter of innovative local development processes at various administrative levels, within European and regional funding programs aimed at rediscovering and reinterpreting the diverse local specificities through a project. Specificities are not intended as simple heritage to be valorized, but as elements generating innovative projects, economies, and cultures around which to build innovation sites, even and through the involvement of broad social participation.

Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The Urban Planning. Environmental Project of the City and Territory (CdS) provides theoretical, methodological, and technical tools encompassing cultural, historical, economic, social, and environmental context elements to analyze, represent, design, and manage settlement transformation processes involving the city, territory, landscape, and environment.
The educational path aims to train a professional capable of:
- analyze, interpret the dynamics of contemporary urban and territorial processes;
- confront complex problems at various scales that traverse the urban ecosystem and current human condition (climate change and territorial risks, societal inequalities and welfare system crises, forms of progress and cultural homogenization processes induced by global economies, changes in global population...);
- develop effective and durable ideas, projects, and policies for planning, management, and governance of the territory, process information through information technologies.
The CdS aims to build fundamental competencies for city development and territory governance, but also to motivate students to build a learning environment capable of adequately responding to the problems and challenges of the ecological transition involving contemporary urban territories, which require interdisciplinary knowledge, competencies in terms of innovative and creative project approaches, a sense of responsibility, and an ethical approach towards the environment and living spaces. These are crucial objectives for a new model of urban territory development that confronts the diverse vulnerabilities of contexts not only local.
For this, the CdS prioritizes theoretical and project approaches that allow the student and thus the future urbanist to act under conditions of uncertainty and flexibility, complexity and innovation, process interscalarity and interdependence of involved actors. This is what qualifies the professional figure in relation to the needs emerging from social partners at the local level, which find important reflections also at the global level.
The interdisciplinary approach promoted by the CdS dedicates particular attention to the 'context' and, more specifically, to the many articulations of the Mediterranean landscape and environment, to promote a method of investigation and action that students can extend to broader contexts where they will operate in their future professional careers. In relation to other planning and urbanism schools, the educational path promoted by the Degree Course - which is anchored to the specificity of the Sardinian territory where, historically, an idea of urban space not always coinciding with the idea of a delimited and circumscribed city has developed - provides a set of knowledge and competencies that:
- pursue an orientation towards a project approach that overcomes the classic city/countryside dichotomies, revealing the urban potential of the territory in its complexity;
- affirm a conception of territory as the center of the educational path and learning processes, as the deep matrix of living spaces;
- seek in the interweaving of different territorial scales possible alternatives to the dense city model and redirect the city towards a spatial reorganization where not only city and nature meet, but environmental dominants and historically dense places acquire new meanings of centralities for the city.
These competencies allow the graduate to access master's degrees and develop professional capabilities for: a) collaborating in design and planning to manage transformation and rehabilitation processes of the city, territory, environment, and landscape; b) managing evaluation activities of projects, programs, plans, and policies of urban, territorial, environmental, and landscape aspects; c) managing scenario and policy construction processes with the involvement of social and economic actors; d) developing and managing territorial information systems.
The need for an internship path that gives the student greater ability to enter the workforce through field experience, also through Erasmus Placement programs students undertake in Italy and abroad.
Basic subjects have a significant weight in the first two years of the course to form a solid preparation that enables students to face the increasing complexity of project subjects in the final part of the path. In particular, basic subjects related to the study of the environment and its relationship with the territory (ecology discipline area) develop in an articulated path also in the second year, interacting with project laboratories and characteristic subjects. The contribution of the representation discipline is relevant, fundamental for the skills required for urban space design. The space dedicated in the first year to historical and archaeological subjects related to planning and the study of the city and territory is motivated by the need to understand the historical, social, architectural, and cultural complexity of the urban and territorial context.

Description and Teaching Methods The teaching of the educational path is delivered in a mixed mode. It primarily uses distance learning for basic disciplines and theoretical lessons of characteristic courses. In particular, for basic disciplinary areas (mathematics, ecology and geography, representation), the mixed mode provides a balance between distance learning and in-person teaching, with a portion of in-person exercises.
For characteristic disciplinary areas (architecture and engineering, law, economics, and sociology), in-person teaching is predominant over distance learning as it includes all design laboratories and practical exercises.
The course provides mixed-mode teaching because:
- involves a broader target of students and expands the pool of students from other regions;
- responds to proposals from social partners (ANCI, local administrations, professional world) regarding new guidelines on continuous training;
- responds to the needs outlined in the recently signed agreement between the University of Sassari and the Ministry of Public Administration to expand the knowledge and competencies of public employees (a target already present in the course of study).
The overall teaching offer, as specified in the University and Course Regulations, is organized into semesters where teaching units and modules are structured, having a distinctive 'title' that recalls relevant themes of the city, environment, and landscape.
Teaching units (also called 'teaching blocks') generally focus on a key project theme around which, in some cases, different disciplines are integrated. Some courses develop independently from design activities (although in many cases they can deepen interdisciplinary aspects and specific investigations related to the project work).
The first year is dedicated to the basic study of the city, territory, environment, and landscape, i.e., to 'enter' the semantic fields of the profession's object. The second year is dedicated to deepening the methods and practices of project and environmental, urban, and territorial planning with increasing attention to themes related to territory safeguarding. The third year is a recapitulation and deepening, centered on a teaching unit addressing the relationship between plan and project, and on career-end paths (long internship and dissertation on that experience, design/planning laboratory, dissertation related to a research theme).
Design activities include the presence of tutors, young professionals knowledgeable in the field, who follow laboratory and project activities, and in some cases, front-class teaching activities. Intermediate learning verification activities are provided (written and oral tests, intermediate critiques of laboratory projects).
The CdS's goal is also to constantly stimulate students to knowledge and use of foreign languages in written and oral form, both through the teaching of the English language, and indirectly through experiences organized by the CdS and Department to foster an international and intercultural learning environment (open lectures and conferences, workshops and international summer schools, group work with Erasmus students from different contexts). In this sense, graduates must be able to fluently use at least the English language in written and oral form, referring also to national and international disciplinary lexicons.
During the three-year educational path, students develop autonomously chosen teaching activities: the degree course suggests some in-depth training activities that enrich and expand the offer of teaching units and modules. This semester also focuses on internship activities where the student develops applied research experiences and direct knowledge of the professional world; on career-end paths that have different structures according to the student's specific educational needs.

Junior Architect The graduate, upon obtaining the degree and passing the professional examination, naturally finds placement in the job market in technical offices of public bodies and private companies, in architecture and engineering firms operating in the field of architectural design or production of construction processes and building products.
In detail, the graduate may find employment in:
- private design structures organized also as engineering companies;
- technical offices of public bodies integrated in design and management roles for the procurement process of works assigned to the procurement authority;
- technical offices of public bodies integrated in roles of officials responsible for processing matters related to territorial control from the perspective of general building activity;
- private companies linked to the production and marketing of building products, artifacts, and related services.
Final exam characteristics.
The final exam consists of submitting a portfolio of activities carried out during the degree program and discussing a final project in public session, prepared under the guidance of a supervising professor, in the form of a graphic-design elaboration or monographic essay, which may also be written in English.
The graphic-design elaboration consists of a maximum of 3 sheets (maximum format A0) and/or a video presentation of the graphic elaborations. Explanatory models may be used to accompany the graphic elaborations.
The short monographic essay may be up to 40,000 characters, excluding notes and bibliography, and may be discussed through a video presentation. The text may be written in English.
The CFU allocated for the final exam are 3.
The total points awarded for the final exam are 9, of which
- 6 for the discussion of the final project
- 3 for international mobility.
Required knowledge for admission.
Those acquired in all recognized upper secondary schools.
It is also necessary to have passed the admission test for degree programs leading to the qualification of architect, according to the current ministerial guidelines for each academic year.
For students admitted to the course with a score below 1/3 of the total points available, additional mandatory educational obligations must be fulfilled within the first year of the course, as defined in the course's didactic regulations, which are referred to.
The admission test will determine the ranking for course admission, which will occur according to the procedures specified in the course's didactic regulations.

Communication Skills.
Graduates have the ability to effectively manage communication of the premises and objectives of their design interventions, calibrating and modulating it according to the various goals to be achieved, and being able to adjust the level of depth—as well as the linguistic and lexical register—in relation to the recipient, the situation, and other relevant parameters. In particular, students must be able to use argumentative structures with ease, within a framework of communication organization based on the requirements of rational argumentation.
These objectives are achieved through constant didactic and assessment attention directed at enhancing the ability to justify each choice with rational argumentative structures, to clarify implicit premises and implications, to be aware of the strengths and weaknesses of possible positions, and to be able to adopt new perspectives, even those not congruent with one's own. Within this framework, the rich interaction with teachers and peers, as well as the continuous critical discussion work carried out in class and in laboratories, is of utmost importance. The practice of languages other than Italian and familiarity with digital languages, as well as with different communication registers used not only in real situations but also in virtual ones, completes the construction of graduates' communication skills, which must be able to engage with differing opinions, cultures, ideologies, and cultural approaches, and eventually understand the nature of disagreements to intervene effectively through mediation, negotiation, and the elimination of misunderstandings.
In addition to the evaluation criteria indicated for the previous indicators, teachers and tutors will be ready to evaluate—for each specific educational activity: design, theoretical-critical discussion, pre-design analysis, group work, proposal construction, project presentation—the degree of communication skills exhibited by the student. Written and oral exercises will be dedicated to the main purpose of cultivating and refining argumentative skills. Particular emphasis in the evaluation of the dissertation will be placed on the evaluation of expressive and especially argumentative abilities.
