Autonomy of Judgment.
Graduates are able to formulate relevant and insightful judgments on various issues, both disciplinary and transdisciplinary, using acquired knowledge in a correct and reasoned manner, demonstrating the ability to skillfully manipulate concepts and theories, and to apply knowledge in the service of the moment's cognitive and operational objectives. The judgment ability they possess is vigilant and open to the multiplicity of possible approaches, structured by an awareness of the complexity of issues and distant from a merely solution-oriented conception of architectural or urbanistic projects. Typically formulated judgments by graduates contain notable elements of originality, but are always anchored to the fundamental ability to explore and understand the world, so that even the formulation of a judgment becomes, always, an additional heuristic and a hypothesis to be tested. Moreover, graduates subject every judgment to their own ability to discuss and doubt, and support it with argumentative reasoning. It is particularly important to highlight, at every opportunity, the cultural, social, philosophical, historical, and technical-scientific aspects that deepen and give substance to any design issue. These results are pursued through:
- integrated teaching blocks where the very comparison among teachers forces students to continuous work of translation and comparison between personal and disciplinary viewpoints;
- project laboratories inspired by complexity and interdisciplinarity;
- constant didactic reference to the adoption of new theoretical perspectives and the need to provide reasoned justifications for actual and possible choices;
- interpersonal comparison, achieved through group work and critical classroom discussions;
- cultivation of autonomy of judgment.
The evaluation tools here, in addition to those indicated in the previous descriptors, consist in the constant verification by teachers and tutors of students' ability to work in groups with a critical spirit and autonomous judgment capacity. It will be important, both during the examination and dissertation verification, to require and reward autonomy of judgment; and, in collective teaching activities, to evaluate that the dynamics between individual and group (both in discussions and in project collaborations) serve both synergy and the valorization of innovative and reasoned personal contributions.

Learning Ability.
Graduates are able to synthesize acquired knowledge so that it constitutes a valid basis for subsequent in-depth study, and are capable of formulating autonomous judgments on various issues—although guided by main theoretical orientations. They have derived from the study course a learning methodology that enables them to tackle further studies by optimally using acquired competencies within a framework of increasing autonomy and progressively greater conceptual and theoretical complexity. Every opportunity for professional growth naturally becomes for them a moment of knowledge and theoretical deepening. They possess critical awareness to identify, among their experiences, those that are relevant to motivate theoretical research, which represents the continuation of university training during subsequent professional engagement. The project laboratory—with its multiple ongoing evaluation moments—is the primary tool for evaluating students' ability to select the most important educational experiences for the new tasks they gradually face. Teachers and tutors have the opportunity to observe the growth over time of learning abilities through constant contact during project activities, continuous interaction, and progressive requests for feedback.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematical Disciplines for Architecture Knowledge and understanding of the languages, concepts, and theorems of basic disciplines in linear algebra, mathematical analysis, and information processing systems.
Area of Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture Fundamental knowledge that enables students to link design choices with energy control techniques and environmental comfort. Understanding of the fundamentals of heat transmission, principles of environmental conditioning, and essential concepts of acoustics and lighting technology applied to construction.
Area of Historical Disciplines for Architecture Students must
- critically define the historical context that generated architecture and highlight in it styles, needs, characters, craftsmanship, and elements of the construction vocabulary;
- recognize the main structural elements of architecture;
- understand the nature of issues related to building functionality;
- view the architectural object as connected to the environment, its territory, history, and the complexity of the context;
- extract from styles and design experiences the logical and non-rigid schemes for approaching and interacting with problems.
Area of Architecture and Environment Representation Students must acquire:
- Knowledge and understanding of graphic languages useful for developing design ideas and drawing the project;
- Knowledge and understanding of techniques and tools for representing space, 3D modeling software, and project communication;
- Knowledge and understanding of drawing as an expressive and visual communication act of the design idea;
- Knowledge and understanding of theories, methods, techniques, and tools for representing and communicating the project at various operational scales;
- Knowledge and understanding of technical norms regarding representation and project.
Area of Urban Architectural Design Understand the meaning of architectural design and the necessary knowledge to address it, through design exercises starting from the elementary cell of housing and its various aggregations and articulations. The project must be understood by the student as a drawn prefiguration of construction.
Area of Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration Students must possess a good knowledge of all disciplines contributing to the structuring of the restoration project, particularly urban and historical contexts, i.e., they must be able to:
- define the historical context that generated architecture and highlight in it styles, needs, characters, craftsmanship, and elements of the construction vocabulary;
- recognize the main structural elements of historical architecture and their traditional materials, with particular attention to the system of street fronts of historical urban facades;
- organize the geometric dimensional survey of an architectural complex and its graphical restitution;
- understand the nature of issues related to the structural functioning of a building;
- view the architectural object as connected to the environment, its territory, history, and the complexity of the context;
- extract from styles and design experiences the logical and non-rigid schemes for approaching and interacting with problems.
Area of Structural Analysis and Design for Architecture The graduate must acquire solid knowledge in the fields of structural design and modeling of structural materials, knowledge of the main methodologies for calculating displacements and stresses in one-dimensional structures, and mastery of methods for verifying sections and structures.
Area of Urban Planning and Territorial Planning Within urban planning and territorial planning, the undergraduate graduate must know the constitutive elements of urban and territorial systems; must develop a basic understanding of urban theory, know the basic urban planning techniques and tools, and acquire the ability to critically analyze phenomena and dynamics of urban system evolution. The graduate will thus be able to design public, communal, and collective spaces at the urban and territorial scale following context-appropriate design concepts. Experience will be gained within interdisciplinary laboratories that will provide a basic understanding of the disciplinary field and stimulate integrated design.
Area of Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Construction Students will learn fundamental knowledge in the fields of materials and construction techniques, and functional coupling criteria for technical elements. Students will also learn about environmental factors influencing building design and potential degradation actions during the building's lifecycle. They will learn the methods and tools for representing the technical project, from broad scale to detailed construction. Therefore, at the end of the training path, students will be autonomous in choosing between different technological project solutions and construction materials.
Area of Estimation Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Students will learn theories, principles, and methods of valuation. They will be able to identify the various economic aspects characterizing a property, the corresponding values, and the criteria for their determination. They will deepen their knowledge of the real estate market and the construction market.
Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities
- Knowledge and understanding of the theme of environmental sustainability and the ecosystemic aspects of architecture, settlement, and territory;
- Knowledge and understanding of the theme of safeguarding and conserving cultural heritage and built heritage at the scale of architecture, city, and territory;
- Knowledge and understanding of the engineering and technological aspects of construction and development of competencies in the field of traditional and innovative materials within architectural design;
- Knowledge and understanding of the philosophical, epistemological, and interdisciplinary aspects of design.

Application of Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematical Disciplines for Architecture Ability to model problems through the language and tools of mathematics. Ability to calculate, solve, and approximate solutions to basic geometric and analytical problems, with particular reference to disciplines characterizing architecture, design, and urban planning. Ability to formalize and implement automatic solutions to typical processing problems.
Area of Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture Ability to apply acquired knowledge and quantify studied phenomena through practical exercises in energy, climate control, acoustics, and lighting technology. Verification of understanding and acquired competencies, but especially the ability to elaborate and apply them in a design context.
Area of Historical Disciplines for Architecture Students must be able to apply their knowledge to new and unprecedented situations—skill not responding to rigid and predefined rules nor intuitive or instinctive, but rather responding to a historical study and analysis methodology. They must integrate and enrich every application through awareness of the cultural dimensions of the intervention developed for analysis, and properly integrated for construction and complexity management. They can develop their technical-scientific and historical-critical competencies in new or innovative contexts, in situations never faced before, under conditions of partial or vague knowledge of relevant information. Finally, they can relate the awareness of the need for critical and historical deepening to the needs, trends, and complexity of architectural design.
Area of Architecture and Environment Representation Students must be able to apply:
- knowledge and understanding of acquired graphic languages to concrete experiences of ideation and representation of solutions to problems at different scales and contexts;
- drawing as an expressive and visual communication act of the design idea to the communication of design ideas related to different themes and application fields;
- ability to choose, use, and combine representation and communication methods, techniques, and tools appropriate to different phases of the design process and experiences;
- ability to use and apply technical norms and knowledge regarding representation and project.
Area of Urban Architectural Design The project must also be understood as a moment of synthesis of the various disciplinary contributions present in other courses. Drawing on these, the student in the project exercise can clearly express the maturity achieved and the degree of knowledge acquired.
Area of Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration Students must be able to apply their knowledge to new and unprecedented situations—skill not responding to rigid and predefined rules nor intuitive or instinctive, but rather responding to a rigorous design methodology underlying architectural and urban restoration. They must adapt this method to the surrounding historical built reality, developing a process that connects all their knowledge from the geometric reality of the asset, to its material, to its conservation status, up to restoration hypotheses. They must integrate and enrich every application through awareness of the cultural dimensions of the intervention developed for analysis, and properly integrated for construction and complexity management. They can develop their technical-scientific and historical-critical competencies in new or innovative contexts, in situations never faced before, under conditions of partial or vague knowledge of relevant information. Finally, they can relate the awareness of the need for safeguarding and conserving historic city architecture to current and historical cultural trends, in light of the regulatory and professional framework.
Area of Structural Analysis and Design for Architecture The graduate in Architecture must have acquired the ability to apply classical methods and tools of structural design to the study of civil buildings.
Area of Urban Planning and Territorial Planning The undergraduate graduate, regarding urban planning and territorial planning, will be able to address the complexity of territorial and urban systems by applying acquired methods, techniques, and tools. They will be able to critically and consciously identify interventions following principles and strategies appropriate to different scales.
Area of Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Construction The student, starting from the characteristics of known materials, must be able to analyze cataloged technical elements and then design new ones, limited to the complexities that their acquired knowledge allows them to address. Moreover, what is learned, viewed through an eco-compatible lens, will enable the student to adopt construction and technological project choices aimed at reducing the environmental impact of construction on the surrounding territory.
Area of Estimation Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning Students will be able to apply in practice market value, cost value, transformation value, complementary value, and substitution value estimation.
Area of Related or Integrative Training Activities
- Ability to apply knowledge gained in the field of environmental sustainability and ecosystemic aspects of architecture, settlement, and territory to the project;
- Ability to apply knowledge gained in the field of safeguarding and conserving cultural heritage and built heritage at the scale of architecture, city, and territory to the project;
- Ability to apply knowledge gained in the field of engineering and technological aspects of construction and development of competencies in the field of traditional and innovative materials within architectural design to the project;
- Ability to apply knowledge gained in the field of philosophical, epistemological, and interdisciplinary aspects of design to the project.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN Associated Professional Competencies.
Junior Architect The undergraduate graduate in Architecture may perform autonomous professional activities after registering with the Architects' Association, Section B.
The graduate may also carry out design, direction, and management of works, measurement, supervision, accounting, and settlement of simple civil constructions realized with standardized methodologies.
Additionally, professional activities include instrumental and direct surveys on current and historical construction.
Professional Function in Work Context.
Junior Architect After passing the relevant state exam, the graduate may register with the Register of Architects, Planners, Landscape Architects, and Conservators as a Junior Architect and perform professional activities, contributing and collaborating in programming, design, and implementation activities for the organization and transformation of the built environment at various scales.
In particular, the graduate will have the following competencies:
- knowledge of methodological-operational aspects related to the disciplines characterizing the study course and ability to identify and solve architecture and construction problems using updated methods, techniques, and tools;
- adequate knowledge of aspects concerning technical and economic feasibility, cost calculation, and the production and realization process of architectural and construction artifacts, as well as aspects related to their safety;
- ability to use the techniques and tools of architectural and construction artifact design.
These competencies may enable autonomous design or collaborative capacity:
- in applied research in the fields of architecture and civil engineering;
- in the design of buildings and civil artifacts and related ideational and procedural processes;
- in processes useful for surveying, representing, designing, supervising construction, and maintaining artifacts and equipment related to safety systems;
- in the analysis of architectural process prices and economic aspects of construction works.

Specific Educational Objectives Description.
The Bachelor's degree in Sciences of Architecture and Design pursues the following educational objectives:
- know methods and have the ability to use techniques for analyzing and defining architecture, space, and objects within it, territory, and landscape;
- be able to set up conservation and transformation programs from the object to the territory, both in reference to various disciplines and to the organizational and competence methodologies of design teams;
- master the contents of legal frameworks regulating the protection and transformation of architecture, cities, and landscape in relation to design levels and expected outcomes;
- ability to interact with complex clients (both public and private) and interdisciplinary work groups.
The study course is oriented towards training professional figures capable of recognizing and understanding architectural works, both in their logical-formal, compositional, typological-distributive, structural, constructive, technological aspects, and in their relationships with historical, physical, institutional, and environmental contexts. In this field, the specific competencies of the graduate relate to activities connected with architectural and urban design in different fields and at various application scales. The study course is structured in credit intervals, prepared for a distinct curriculum articulation if required by local market needs, as well as to harmonize and make the first-cycle training path as congruent as possible with a potential future differentiation of the second-cycle training offer.
The study course's didactic regulation provides, in relation to specific objectives, the possibility of external activities, such as training internships at companies, enterprises, and public bodies, and internships at other Italian and foreign universities, also within international agreements.

Description of Offer and Teaching Methods.
The Bachelor's degree is organized with an innovative conception based substantially on the following aspects:
- learning by doing: not only are all acquired theoretical notions systematically verified against reality, but the comparison itself with real conditions becomes an additional topic for developing critical reasoning;
- consequently, the study plans are structured around projects from the first year, allowing direct application of theoretical course content; thus, the ability to transform learned concepts into elaborations is acquired, and students become accustomed to the rhythms and deadlines imposed by professional activity;
- pluralistic training achieved both through the cooperation of different disciplines on each individual project and through teaching by professors from different schools, Italian and foreign;
- language learning during work, also through blocks where teaching is conducted in English, to develop not only language knowledge but also specific disciplinary vocabulary;
- the possibility of conducting an intermediate and final professional internship abroad supported by specific Erasmus projects;
- an optimal ratio between the number of teachers and students, allowing students to be consistently followed during lectures and laboratory sessions;
- extensive and creative use of new technologies as both a study and work environment, as well as for learning and using new professional tools.
This course organization (innovative for Italy, but already successfully adopted by some foreign schools) arises from a careful analysis and in-depth evaluation of major international experiences in relation to the evolution of disciplines, learning methods, and professional activities. Each academic year is divided into two semesters, with the distribution of university credits (CFU).
The training activity, according to the University's Didactic Regulation and the Department of Architecture, Design, and Urbanism's Regulation, is structured in:
- project and in-depth teaching blocks;
- single-discipline courses;
- student-selected activities and internships;
- foreign language (English);
- final exam.
Project teaching blocks are characterized by a design theme developed through disciplines chosen among those most important for the theoretical and practical development of the project. In each block and for each discipline, frontal lessons, exercises, and integrated project laboratories with teachers and tutors are carried out. Throughout the academic year, prolonged development courses and single-discipline courses are also held. The widespread use of new technologies characterizes the study plan programs, creating a creative study and work environment and enabling the learning and use of new professional tools. The exam schedule is divided into three sessions: February, July, and September. The third year, in its first part, follows the usual block structure, while the second part contains an area for free credits, a block for final exam preparation, and the final exam, also in view of completing the training path for the Master's degree in Architecture at the same Department.
The CFU for final exam preparation may be dedicated to internships, allowing sufficient duration for an Erasmus Placement activation, or to acquiring other knowledge useful for drafting a project or other elaboration to be discussed in the final exam, which will be further defined in the Regulation. This organization is represented in the curriculum grid as a credit interval that can be assigned to either "Training and Orientation Internships" or "Other knowledge useful for entering the workforce." The activation of one or both credit intervals will occur during the definition of the Study Plan, together with the definition of "other useful knowledge," to ensure the necessary flexibility for a study course that must offer both the possibility of entering the workforce and training oriented towards continuing in the Master's degree.

Junior Architect The graduate, upon obtaining the degree and passing the professional exam, naturally finds placement in the job market in technical offices of public bodies and private companies, in architecture and engineering studios operating in the field of architectural design or production of building processes and products.
In detail, the graduate may find employment in:
- private design structures organized also as engineering companies;
- technical offices of public bodies integrated in design and management roles of the tendering process for works assigned to the contracting authority;
- technical offices of public bodies integrated in roles of officials responsible for procedures related to various aspects of territorial control from the perspective of building activities in a general sense;
- private companies linked to the production and marketing of building products, artifacts, and related services.
Characteristics of final exam.
The final exam consists of submitting a portfolio of activities carried out during the degree course and discussing a final thesis in public session, drafted under the guidance of a supervising professor, in the form of graphic-design work or monographic essay, which may also be written in English.
The graphic-design work consists of a maximum of 3 sheets (maximum size A0) and/or video presentation of graphic works. Explanatory models may be used to accompany the graphic works.
The short monographic essay may be up to 40,000 characters, excluding notes and bibliography, and may be discussed through a video presentation. The text may be written in English.
The CFU planned for the final exam are 3.
The total points assigned to the final exam are 9, of which
- 6 for the discussion of the final thesis
- 3 for international mobility.
Required knowledge for admission.
These are those acquired in all recognized upper secondary schools.
It is also necessary to have passed the admission test for bachelor's degree courses leading to the qualification of architect, according to the current annual ministerial guidelines.
For students admitted to the course with a grade lower than 1/3 of the total points available, additional training obligations must be fulfilled within the first year of study, as defined in the Teaching Regulations of the course, which is referred to.
The admission test will determine the ranking for course access, which will occur according to the procedures specified in the Teaching Regulations of the study course.
Degree awarded.
Bachelor's degree in SCIENCES OF ARCHITECTURE AND DESIGN Employment and professional opportunities for graduates.

- technical offices of public bodies integrated in roles of officials responsible for procedures related to various aspects of territorial control from the perspective of building activities in a general sense;
- private companies linked to the production and marketing of building products, artifacts, and related services.

SECTION: Communication Skills

Communication Skills.
Graduates have the ability to effectively manage communication regarding the premises and purposes of their design interventions, calibrating and modulating it according to various objectives to be achieved, and being able to adjust the level of depth—as well as the linguistic and lexical register—in relation to the recipient, the situation, and other relevant parameters. Specifically, students must be able to use argumentative structures with ease within a framework of communication organization based on the requirements of rational argumentation. These objectives are achieved through constant didactic and assessment attention directed at enhancing the ability to justify each choice with rational argumentative structures, to explicitly state implicit premises and implications, to be aware of the strengths and weaknesses of possible positions, and to adopt new perspectives, even those not congruent with their own. In this context, the rich interaction with teachers and peers, as well as the continuous critical discussion work carried out in class and in laboratories, is of utmost importance. Practicing languages other than Italian and familiarity with digital languages, as well as with different communication registers used not only in real situations but also in virtual ones, completes the construction of graduates' communication skills, which must be able to engage with differing opinions, cultures, ideologies, and cultural approaches, and eventually understand the nature of disagreements to intervene effectively through mediation, negotiation, and the elimination of misunderstandings. In addition to the evaluation criteria indicated for the previous indicators, teachers and tutors will be ready to evaluate—for each specific educational activity: design, theoretical-critical discussion, pre-design analysis, group work, proposal construction, project presentation—the degree of communication skills exhibited by the student. Written and oral exercises will be dedicated primarily to nurturing and refining argumentative skills. Particular emphasis in the evaluation of the dissertation will be placed on the assessment of expressive and especially argumentative abilities.

UNIVERSITY: University of Sassari
COURSE: [1212] SCIENCES OF ARCHITECTURE AND DESIGN
SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://uniss.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10402?annoOrdinamento=2021

Autonomy of Judgment.
Graduates are able to formulate relevant and insightful judgments on various disciplinary and transdisciplinary issues, using acquired knowledge correctly and rationally, demonstrating the ability to effectively manipulate concepts and theories, and to apply knowledge in the service of cognitive and operational objectives at the moment. The judgment capacity they possess is vigilant and open to the multiplicity of possible approaches, structured by awareness of the complexity of issues and distant from a merely solution-oriented conception of architectural or urbanistic projects. The judgments typically formulated by graduates contain notable elements of originality, but are always grounded in the fundamental ability to explore and understand the world, so that even the formulation of a judgment becomes, always, an additional heuristic and a hypothesis to be tested. Furthermore, graduates subject every judgment to their own capacity for discussion and doubt, supporting it with argumentative reasoning. It is particularly important to highlight, in every opportunity, the cultural, social, philosophical, historical, and technical-scientific aspects that deepen and give substance to any design issue. These outcomes are pursued through:
- integrated teaching blocks where the same comparison among teachers forces students to continuously translate and compare personal and disciplinary viewpoints;
- project laboratories inspired by complexity and interdisciplinarity;
- constant didactic reference to the adoption of new theoretical perspectives and the necessity of providing reasoned justifications for actual and possible choices;
- interpersonal comparison, achieved through group work and critical classroom discussions;
- cultivation of autonomy of judgment.
Assessment tools, in addition to those indicated in previous descriptors, consist of continuous verification by teachers and tutors of students' ability to work in groups with critical spirit and autonomous judgment. It is important, both during exam and thesis assessment, to require and reward autonomy of judgment; and, in collective teaching activities, to evaluate whether dynamics between individual and group (both in discussions and in project collaborations) serve both synergy and the valorization of innovative and reasoned personal contributions.
Learning Ability.
Graduates are able to synthesize acquired knowledge to form a valid basis for further in-depth study, and are able to formulate autonomous judgments on various issues—though guided by main theoretical orientations. They have derived from the study course a learning methodology that enables them to address further studies by optimally using acquired skills within a framework of increasing autonomy and progressively greater conceptual and theoretical complexity. Every opportunity for professional growth naturally becomes a moment for knowledge and theoretical deepening. They possess critical awareness to identify, among their experiences, those that have relevance to motivate a theoretical research representing the continuation of university training during subsequent professional engagement.
The project laboratory—with its multiple moments of ongoing assessment—is the primary tool for assessing students' ability to select the most important teaching experiences for new tasks they gradually face. Teachers and tutors can observe the growth over time of learning abilities through constant contact during project activities, continuous interaction, and progressive requests for feedback.
Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematical Disciplines for Architecture: Knowledge and understanding of the languages, concepts, and theorems of the basic disciplines of linear algebra, mathematical analysis, and information processing systems.
Area of Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture: Fundamental knowledge enabling students to link design choices with energy control techniques and environmental comfort. Understanding of the fundamentals of heat transfer, principles of environmental conditioning, and essential concepts of acoustics and lighting technology applied to construction.
Area of Historical Disciplines for Architecture: Students must
- define with critical depth the historical framework that generated architecture and highlight in it styles, needs, characters, craftsmanship, and elements of the construction vocabulary;
- recognize the main structural elements of architecture;
- understand the nature of issues related to building functionality;
- view the architectural object as connected to its environment, territory, history, and contextual complexity;
- extract logical and non-rigid patterns of approach and interaction with problems from styles and design experiences.
Area of Architecture and Environment Representation: Students must acquire:
- Knowledge and understanding of graphic languages useful for developing design ideas and drawing the project.
- Knowledge and understanding of techniques and tools for representing space, 3D modeling software, and project communication.
- Knowledge and understanding of drawing as an expressive and visual communication act of the design idea.
- Knowledge and understanding of theories, methods, techniques, and tools for representing and communicating the project at different operational scales.
- Knowledge and understanding of technical norms regarding representation and project.
Area of Urban Architectural Design: Understanding the meaning of architectural design and the necessary knowledge to address it, through design exercises starting from the elementary unit of housing and its various aggregations and articulations. The project must be understood by the student as a drawn prefiguration of construction.
Area of Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration: Students must possess good knowledge of all disciplines contributing to the structuring of a restoration project, with particular reference to urban and historical contexts, meaning they must be able to:
- define the historical framework that generated architecture and highlight in it styles, needs, characters, craftsmanship, and elements of the construction vocabulary;
- recognize the main structural elements of historical architecture and their traditional materials, with particular attention to the system of street fronts and urban facades;
- organize the geometric and dimensional survey of an architectural complex and its graphical restitution;
- understand the nature of issues related to the structural functionality of a building;
- view the architectural object as connected to its environment, territory, history, and contextual complexity;
- extract logical and non-rigid patterns of approach and interaction with problems from styles and design experiences.
Area of Structural Analysis and Design for Architecture: Graduates must acquire solid knowledge in the fields of structural design and modeling of structural materials, know the main methodologies for calculating displacements and stresses in one-dimensional structures, and master the methods for verifying sections and structures.
Area of Urban Planning and Territorial Planning: Within urban planning and territorial planning, the undergraduate graduate must know the constitutive elements of urban and territorial systems; must develop a basic knowledge of urban theory, know the basic techniques and tools of urban planning, and acquire the ability to critically analyze phenomena and dynamics of urban system evolution. The graduate will thus be able to design public, communal, and collective spaces at urban and territorial scales following design concepts appropriate to the reference context. Experience will be gained within interdisciplinary laboratories that will provide a basic understanding of the disciplinary field and stimulate integrated design.
Area of Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Construction: Students will learn fundamental knowledge in the fields of materials and construction techniques, and functional coupling criteria for technical elements. Students will also learn environmental factors influencing building design and potential degradation actions during the building's life cycle. They will learn the methods and tools for representing the technical project, from broad scale to detailed construction. Therefore, at the end of the training path, students will also be autonomous in choosing between different technological project solutions and construction materials.
Area of Valuation Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning: Students will learn theories, principles, and methods of valuation. They will be able to identify the different economic aspects characterizing a property, the corresponding values, and the criteria for their determination. They will deepen their knowledge of the real estate market and the construction market.
Area of Related or Integrated Training Activities
- Knowledge and understanding of the theme of environmental sustainability and the ecosystemic aspects of architecture, settlement, and territory;
- Knowledge and understanding of the theme of protection and conservation of cultural heritage and built heritage at the scale of architecture, city, and territory;
- Knowledge and understanding of engineering and technological aspects of construction and development of competencies in the field of traditional and innovative materials within architectural design;
- Knowledge and understanding of philosophical, epistemological, and interdisciplinary aspects of design.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Area of Mathematical Disciplines for Architecture: Ability to model problems through the language and tools of mathematics. Ability to calculate, solve, and approximate solutions to basic geometric and analytical problems, with particular reference to disciplines characterizing architecture, design, and urban planning. Ability to formalize and implement automatic solutions to typical processing problems.
Area of Physical-Technical and Engineering Disciplines for Architecture: Ability to apply acquired knowledge and quantify studied phenomena through practical exercises in energy, climate control, acoustics, and lighting technology. Verification of understanding and acquired competencies, but especially the ability to elaborate and apply them in a design context.
Area of Historical Disciplines for Architecture: Students must be able to apply their knowledge to new and unprecedented situations—ability not responding to rigid and predefined rules nor intuitive or instinctive, but rather responding to a historical study and analysis methodology.
In this, they must integrate and enrich every application through awareness of the cultural dimensions of the intervention developed for analysis, and properly integrated for construction and complexity management.
They are able to develop their technical-scientific and historical-critical competencies in new or innovative contexts, in situations never faced before, under conditions of partial or vague knowledge of relevant information.
Finally, they are able to relate the awareness of the need for critical and historical deepening to the needs, trends, and complexity of architectural design.
Area of Architecture and Environment Representation: Students must be able to apply:
- knowledge and understanding of acquired graphic languages to concrete experiences of ideation and representation of solutions to problems at different scales and contexts.
- drawing as an expressive and visual communication act of the design idea to the communication of design ideas related to different themes and application fields.
- ability to choose, use, and combine representation and communication methods, techniques, and tools appropriate to different phases of the design process and experiences.
- ability to use and apply technical norms and knowledge regarding representation and project.
Area of Urban Architectural Design: The project must also be understood as a moment of synthesis of the various disciplinary contributions present in other courses. Drawing on these, the student in the project exercise will be able to clearly express the maturity achieved and the degree of knowledge acquired.
Area of Theories and Techniques for Architectural Restoration: Students must be able to apply their knowledge to new and unprecedented situations—ability not responding to rigid and predefined rules nor intuitive or instinctive, but rather responding to a rigorous design methodology at the basis of architectural and urban restoration.
They must be able to adapt this method to the surrounding historical built reality, developing a process that connects all their knowledge from the geometric reality of the asset, to its material, to its conservation status, up to restoration hypotheses.
In this, they must integrate and enrich every application through awareness of the cultural dimensions of the intervention developed for analysis, and properly integrated for construction and complexity management.
They are able to develop their technical-scientific and historical-critical competencies in new or innovative contexts, in situations never faced before, under conditions of partial or vague knowledge of relevant information.
Finally, they are able to relate the awareness of the need for protection and conservation of historic city architecture to current and historical cultural trends, in light of the regulatory and professional framework.
Area of Structural Analysis and Design for Architecture: Graduates in Architecture must have acquired the ability to apply classical methods and tools of structural design to the study of civil buildings.
Area of Urban Planning and Territorial Planning: The undergraduate graduate, regarding the field of urban planning and territorial planning, will be able to address the complexity of territorial and urban systems by applying acquired methods, techniques, and tools. They will be able to critically and consciously identify interventions following principles and strategies appropriate to different scales.
Area of Technological Disciplines for Architecture and Construction: Students, starting from the characteristics of known materials, must be able to analyze cataloged technical elements and then design new ones, limited to the complexities that their acquired knowledge allows them to address. Moreover, what is learned, viewed through an eco-compatible lens, will enable students to adopt construction and technological project choices aimed at reducing the environmental impact of construction on the surrounding territory.
Area of Valuation Disciplines for Architecture and Urban Planning: Students will be able to apply in practice the valuation of Market Value, Cost Value, Transformation Value, Complementary Value, and Surrogate Value.
Area of Related or Integrated Training Activities
- Ability to apply to the project knowledge acquired in the field of environmental sustainability and ecosystemic aspects of architecture, settlement, and territory.
- Ability to apply to the project knowledge acquired in the field of protection and conservation of cultural heritage and built heritage at the scale of architecture, city, and territory.
- Ability to apply to the project knowledge acquired in the field of engineering and technological aspects of construction and development of competencies in the field of traditional and innovative materials within architectural design.
- Ability to apply to the project knowledge acquired in the field of philosophical, epistemological, and interdisciplinary aspects of design.

High school diploma Tuition and fees Regulations on careers - Fees Roles President NICOLÒ GIACOMO BERNARDO CECCARELLI Program, texts and objectives Professional title conferred by the degree.
Designer The three-year graduate is able to interpret different contexts with versatility, looking beyond immediate perspectives to anticipate behaviors and future responses. They can therefore engage with companies, organizations, and production realities at regional, national, and international levels, bringing strategic visions, creativity, and innovative approaches.
Their employment prospects are diverse: from the freelance professional called upon to offer design projects, direct solutions, and contributions as a consultant moving freely in the creative design market, to that of an operator capable of guiding team work and actively integrating into companies' internal offices as a design technician, but also as an analyst and process facilitator.
Final project characteristics.
The final project plays an important role in our training program: as a stimulus and assumption of responsibility by students, before being a evaluation of the maturity acquired by the student throughout their training path.
The final project may take place along two main directions: one path involves a detailed and comprehensive presentation of the activities carried out during the internship; alternatively, students may agree with a tutor professor on a topic to be explored, which may be design-oriented or research-based, also within a path combining the internship and activities in the final synthesis laboratories. Particular attention will be given to the candidates' ability to approach the chosen topic problematically. Students are required to demonstrate analytical and synthesis skills, according to a model inspired by a multidimensional approach (therefore controlling both the overall scale in terms of process, and the detail, i.e., proposing specific and precise solutions).
Students must also demonstrate full familiarity with the topic addressed, proving, through the choice of appropriate modes and languages for its transmission, to have acquired adequate communication skills.
The achievement of autonomous methodological control, the overall quality of the final outcomes, their coherence, and the acquisition of full awareness of the work carried out represent additional evaluation criteria.
Required knowledge for admission.
To be admitted to the study program, one must hold a secondary school diploma of the second level or another equivalent foreign degree recognized as suitable. The required initial knowledge and preparation concern analytical, expressive, and communication skills; synthesis and systemic vision; reading and processing of visual and textual content, as well as general cultural level, verified through a specific admission test that will result in a score.
For students admitted to the study program with a score below the predetermined threshold, specific additional training obligations will be indicated in the didactic regulations to be fulfilled within the first year of study.
Expected employment and professional opportunities for graduates.
Designer The three-year graduate is able to interpret different contexts with versatility, looking beyond immediate perspectives to anticipate behaviors and future responses. They can therefore engage with companies, organizations, and production realities at regional, national, and international levels, bringing strategic visions, creativity, and innovative approaches.
Their employment prospects are diverse: from the freelance professional called upon to offer design projects, direct solutions, and contributions as a consultant moving freely in the creative design market, to that of an operator capable of guiding team work and actively integrating into companies' internal offices as a design technician, but also as an analyst and process facilitator.

COURSE: [A144] DESIGN
SECTION: Communication Skills

Communication Skills.
The exercise of communication skills plays a key role in the educational project. This is to enable graduates to acquire tools and strategies with which, during the practical design process, the future designer can interface and engage with their interlocutors, whether they be clients, experts and collaborators, stakeholders, individual users or groups. In this direction, the main lines of work encompass the two fundamental communication dimensions for the designer:
· those related to the operational level (in a multitude of interpretations and expressions), i.e., aimed at both the strict design process – through conceptual models and schematizations of reality – and at the production, technical, and execution aspects;
· those linked to the strategic level and project promotion, through appropriate languages and formulas to convey the guiding ideas and reference scenarios, using conceptual representations, visualizations, narratives, and illustrations of imaginaries.
All of this, always navigating with agility within the current communication and media landscape.
The educational project places particular emphasis on acquiring these skills, structuring their learning throughout the entire three-year period in a series of incremental teaching moments. The entire educational program also bases its foundation on a plurality of practice and verification moments for the ability to argue design choices: in revisions and intermediate presentations, internships, final project plenary presentations, as well as in opportunities for discussion and interaction, even outside the community of our school, with a variety of external subjects (stakeholders, experts, visiting professors and researchers).
Learning Ability.
Third-year graduates must have developed the ability to apply both 'indirect' knowledge – of a speculative nature – acquired through the educational process, and 'direct' knowledge – based on design discussion, trial-and-error experience, analysis of case studies and experiences conducted by others – to filter future experiences and problems, deriving new knowledge from them. This within the framework of acquiring a personal model of non-abstract methodological processing and analysis, along with the maturation of one's own value system to interpret a multitude of demands, identifying their synthesis through an overall view of the process and the ability to harmoniously balance the variables in play.
A key component of responsible design is the designer's ability to assume responsibility: meaning not only to make choices, but also to put oneself in a position to do so consciously, to give meaning and complete form to the solution of specific problems, within the context of the needs of the era.
The educational model underlying this vision of knowledge construction draws inspiration from the 'basic design' model and is structured into a series of intermediate learning opportunities: the preparation for practical skills occurs through a series of incremental steps, whose sequence is primarily aimed at building an overall design attitude. The positive 'interference' between concentrated small-scale experiences (intensive workshops, cross-class workshops, with external subjects) and broader design tasks (semester-long design laboratories) also represents an intentional element of problematic growth and maturation.
The results achieved by students in the design laboratories – particularly in the integrated ones, where dialogue between different disciplines is intended to introduce, as learning opportunities, different models of knowledge construction and reality interpretation, transversal to the educational project – as well as in the final synthesis laboratories and in the conduct of the final assessment, represent the moments of verification of this objective.

Autonomy of Judgment.
The ability of the problem-solver – one of the key qualities traditionally associated with the designer's figure – is accompanied by that of the decision-maker. The designer, in fact, guides and coordinates the collection of project data, confronts the problems that inform them and the demands of the various involved actors, but ultimately, they are primarily called upon to make decisions through their design choices, assuming responsibility for their economic, social, ethical, and environmental implications. To stimulate students' development of autonomy of judgment, the educational project involves engaging with a structured set of experiences, promoting a complex and problem-oriented perspective that provides tools for critically interpreting reality based on analytical and methodological elements, as well as – through the exercise of lateral thinking – according to their personal viewpoint. The educational program therefore assigns a key role from the first year to the assumption of individual responsibility by those following it: students are thus encouraged to make informed decisions regarding the opportunities offered by the Course of Study in terms of structuring their educational path. Throughout the entire three-year period – in selecting the thematic pathways of annual interdisciplinary workshops, identifying internship activities and other elective activities, and in defining the theme around which to structure the final project – they are, to some extent, called upon to outline the 'design' of their personal educational path. The coherence of choices and the overall results achieved – verifiable at multiple levels: from design laboratories to individual courses; from responses to individual project themes to the ability to harmonize the overall design – will serve as evidence of students' acquired autonomous judgment capability.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Scientific Training: Graduates in design are trained in the intuitive and analytical understanding of geometric space, its conceptualization practices, and the modes of its relationships and transformations.
Technological Training: Graduates in design are familiar with the set of industrial product production methods in relation to possible options in resource, material, and processing choices, structural characteristics, realization contexts, and various economic-production options.
Foundational Project Training: Consistent with the reference productive, social, and cultural contexts, graduates possess a comprehensive view of design as a system to address and solve design problems within the scope of consumer goods, communication artifacts, and services.
Humanistic Training: The graduate possesses the foundations to frame the historical progression of design in light of its intersections with culture, technology, and society.
Foundational Representation Training: Graduates are familiar with the set of representation systems and have acquired the necessary control of the technical-expressive graphic dimension required to develop and communicate design ideas.
Design and Multimedia Communications: Graduates in design are able to exercise control over how the design expertise inherent to the designer unfolds across various different application fields. They are able to manage the use of digital tools and techniques for information processing around the project; they control methodologies and procedures for the design, transformation, and production of material goods; they are capable of addressing design themes related to the experience and use of space, also for translating and presenting information content to the public; they are familiar with contemporary "immaterial" declinations of design for digital communication applications, artifacts, networks, and social networks. Graduates control the theoretical-practical dimension underlying multimedia and audiovisual artifacts populating the current communication landscape, and are finally capable of framing design as strategic activity for the design of innovative services and as a tool for social innovation.
Technological and Engineering Disciplines: Graduates in design have a solid preparation regarding the technologies of processing methods with which, at various scales and in different productive contexts and in line with environmental emergencies, design dialogues for the realization and distribution of new material products and immaterial services. They are also familiar with the set of diverse graphic expression forms, intended as technical representation elements of the project functional to its design evolution. Regarding these technical forms, even in the perspective of their historical-technological evolution, they know how to use them as distinct languages: design technical, illustrative, artistic.
Economic and Social Sciences: Graduates in design are able to integrate knowledge from economic and social sciences into their design awareness and sensitivity, deriving additional knowledge elements from interdisciplinary comparison. They are able to profitably grasp the contributions of this disciplinary area, which broadens their cognitive horizons and contributes to the maturation of analytical and critical abilities, through which the designer can position themselves as an interpreter and mediator of diverse demands.
Related or Integrative Training Activities: Graduates in design integrate and/or complete their educational path through engagement with themes useful for dialectically framing their aptitude and approaches more specifically related to design. They know how to position the design of material goods, immaterial artifacts, communication, and services in relation to the needs of environmental balance and within a dimension that encompasses both territorial and residential scales, highlighting the reasons and logics between local and global.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Scientific Training: The acquired knowledge translates into the ability to employ the language and tools of geometry as a basis for articulating an idea of form and translating it, having understood its constructive, procedural, and semantic potentials. The course refers to SSD MAT/03.
Technological Training: The direct confrontation offered by the design exercise regarding possible formal solutions, the integration of structural and accessory elements, and the concreteness of realization constraints allows the application of knowledge to production processes and understanding of problematic aspects (referable to SSD ICAR/08) through which to make choices in terms of scale economy and sustainability.
Foundational Project Training: Based on a general framework of methodological knowledge and practical experiences, graduates are able to apply a broad and problem-oriented understanding of the essence of design to a variety of themes and needs. They are also capable of developing appropriate solutions for managing the design and realization process.
Humanistic Training: The problem-oriented confrontation with the subject will enable students to transform their historical-critical reading ability into a dynamic tool for interpreting the present reality. The attainment of full awareness of the historical experiences in which design has been articulated constitutes a key element of applying the acquired knowledge and understanding how to structure one's own critical reference framework, even strictly design-related.
Foundational Representation Training: Graduates are able to apply the disciplinary knowledge framework to their design tasks through identifying the most suitable expressive solutions and personal use of the language of images.
Design and Multimedia Communications: A characteristic of the designer is the ability to intertwine theoretical and practical dimensions, constantly applying the acquired knowledge across a variety of disciplinary fields and occasions during the design process. The direct confrontation with multiple and diverse declinations of the design activity is the essential condition for verifying the ability to transfer knowledge to the practical plane, developing problem-oriented models of reality understanding and generating new knowledge.
Technological and Engineering Disciplines: The confrontation with practical opportunities and concrete issues proposed by the experience of design laboratories, in the context of real cases, allows design graduates to refine their ability to apply knowledge and understanding of the correspondence between design objectives, costs, production conditions, and possible target markets. Regarding graphic expression techniques, familiarity – combined with a critical approach and not merely instrumental – with this thematic language system allows design graduates to apply their knowledge and understanding of the methods to convey the most appropriate graphic information for a given communication context.
Economic and Social Sciences: A key objective of the entire educational model, graduates' propensity for interdisciplinary integration is also realized in relation to courses pertaining to economic and social sciences, referable to SDD M-DEA 01, SECS-P/08, and SPS/08. The exercise of the project, aimed at stimulating the aptitude for lateral thinking, thus offers concrete opportunities to apply the knowledge and understanding acquired through confrontation with these disciplines.
Related or Integrative Training Activities: The comparison of design methodologies with different themes, cases, and intervention scales is an opportunity to apply disciplinary knowledge and verify its understanding, in relation to issues and intervention scales referable to SSD BIO/07, ICAR 14, ICAR 20, and M-FIL/02.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIANO Associated Competencies.
Designer: The three-year designer is able to propose innovative solutions in line with the ideational, realization, and distribution processes of service and product design, and with the techniques, languages, and current communication methods, adapting to different work contexts. Integrated into a company, but also proposing themselves as independent designers/consultants, the three-year graduate is able to control the basic aspects of strategy, realization, and production of graphic and identity communication projects, the preparation of specifications, and the final realization care, the development of audiovisual, interactive artifacts, and graphic contributions for web/social platforms. They are also able to intervene in product design, equipping themselves with the appropriate tools to interface with production managers and finalize the engineering and realization aspects of the products they have conceived, providing them with all necessary execution materials.

Work Context Function.
Designer: Upon completion of the Three-Year Degree, the student's preparation encompasses the abilities traditionally associated with the designer profile: innovative charge; analytical and synthetic capacity; autonomous and mature exercise of design thinking. Operating both autonomously as an external consultant and as an active participant in internal company teams, the three-year designer is able to conduct research to position new products and services in the market; indicate guidelines for promotion strategies; and finally, provide design contributions across a variety of fields: graphic and product design, multimedia artifacts, and network communication.

Specific Educational Objectives Description.
The three-year study plan encompasses product and communication design, while also touching on the various fields in which contemporary designer professionalism is articulated: strategic design, service design, audiovisual and multimedia design, the ideation of events and cultural experiences, info-design, and integrated promotion and communication on new media. On this basis, the central objective of the educational project is to train a designer familiar with the ideational, realization, and distribution processes of service and product design, as well as with the techniques, languages, and communication methods of the current scenario. A hybrid figure that, based on a preparation combining specific competencies, design methodology, and vision capacity, is able to interpret a multiplicity of diverse demands, identifying their synthesis and solution in relation with companies, institutions, and social actors at regional, national, and international levels.

The educational organization is structured by thematic semesters, unfolding along the three-year path into a sequence of training experiences, according to a model that starts with a general framework, gradually focusing on specific reference areas. In the first semester of the first year of study, the perspective frames the dimension of emerging global problems (course Design for the Planet), particularly emphasizing the urgency of addressing major environmental issues. The courses Images I (Drawing), History of Design, and courses aimed at providing additional foundational competencies (Geometry, Philosophy of Art) complete this introductory cycle. In the second semester, with the course Design and Places, attention shifts to the territorial dimension, highlighting the need for constant human interaction with their surroundings. The course of Design Cultures, in its structure (including a Photography module), is tasked with introducing students to the methodological aspects of design and the cultural mediation function that design can perform in society. A course in Cultural Anthropology serves as integration and complement. The first semester of the second year includes courses related to communication practices characterizing the current media landscape: Digital Culture Design (Info Design and Digital Design), Theory of Audiovisual Languages, along with the course Images II (dedicated to Graphic Languages). In the second semester, the design teaching shifts to themes of material culture and product (Material Culture Design), updated to the practices of new craftsmanship and digital fabrication. The courses in Technology of Processing Methods, Models and Materials Technologies for Design, and Marketing reinforce the path. In the third year, the Exhibit Design laboratory presents students with the complex interplay between communication languages and space organization, while the course Design for Society outlines the scenarios of relationships and interactions between design disciplines and the design of processes and services. The second and final semester is dedicated to synthesis and completion activities of the learning process: professional internships, personal portfolio development, elective courses, English language improvement, and preparation of the final project. The educational project assigns a particularly significant task for developing the project aptitude to the series of annual interdisciplinary workshops, designed for direct confrontation with problems expressed by territories and the working world. Workshop activities are based on dialogue with external subjects (institutions, companies, artisans, entrepreneurial initiatives) that bring design practice experiences to confront real-world themes and issues. The predominant workshop directions follow thematic lines of heritage design, the valorization of territorial products, and the relationship between design and craftsmanship, but may include cross-cutting fields such as fashion, entertainment, technical, social, and scientific communication. Interdisciplinary workshops are the backbone of an educational project aimed at empowering students in building their personal, cultural, and professional maturation. The three main thematic strands, which form 'passing' corridors throughout the three years of the Course, offer them opportunities for discovery and choice, allowing them to trace individual paths autonomously through the basic study plan. These paths may further be enriched through participation in planned parallel activities (summer schools, free-credit courses), the selection of a targeted internship, attendance at a final synthesis laboratory, and the elaboration of the final project. The overall path – in line with our Department's tradition – will also be characterized by an articulated program of professional internships, both within and outside Sardinia, with a strong orientation towards internationalization.

Program, texts, and objectives Professional status conferred by the title.
Professional operators in private, public, national, supranational, and multinational organizations, in administrations, bodies, non-governmental organizations, third sector, and companies within the processes of social inclusion, preventive-promotional, organizational, educational-training, and research.
The expected professional outcome is that of a social worker, a figure that for over sixty years in Europe has been the main reference point for the implementation of policies and services for people in the public welfare sector (Single or associated local authorities, ASL, AO, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Labor, Ministry of the Interior, INAIL, etc.), in the social private sector (associations, social cooperation, foundations, research bodies, observatories, social enterprises), in the for-profit private sector, as well as in international cooperation (Governmental and non-governmental organizations) and international bodies.
The Regional Order of Social Workers reports that "in 2008, the Council of the Sardinian Order conducted a study regarding the presence of social workers in the municipalities of Sardinia (...) The situation varies by province, with maximum presence in Cagliari, Medio Campidano, and Carbonia-Iglesias, and minimum presence in the Province of Sassari, where social workers are present in only 29 out of 66 municipalities. This aspect is of fundamental importance given the regional situation reported by ISTAT analyses, which highlight that 191 out of 377 Sardinian municipalities (51%) are in a 'highly deprived' condition in the material deprivation index, 45% at the lowest level in the social deprivation study, and 57% of these municipalities belong to areas of greatest socio-health need, having been found very disadvantaged in the distribution of the disadvantaged index." The action of the Regional Order of Social Workers "will therefore be oriented (...) to support basic, specialized, and advanced training."
The Regional Order of Social Workers therefore predicts that "in the next decade (2010/2020), the implementation of social policies and normal turnover will require the entry of approximately one thousand social workers into the labor market." It also considers that the number of social workers currently registered on the Sardinian Register, if "compared to the labor needs within provinces, municipalities, ASL, and social private sector, is absolutely insufficient to cover the labor market demand."
Final exam characteristics.
The final thesis for the student consists of presenting a written paper, agreed upon in form and content with a tutor professor, on topics related to the disciplines studied, or the deepening of an area where the internship was conducted.
A tutor professor is a course professor (structured or contractual) or an external expert who assumes the role of guiding the graduate and accompanying them in the preparation of the paper.
Knowledge required for access.
To be admitted to the European Social Service Bachelor's program, one must possess an appropriate academic qualification – a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as appropriate – for admission to the Bachelor's program. Additionally, a sufficient general culture and logical ability are required, which will be verified through a written and oral test.
The methods for verifying initial preparation and the assignment of any additional educational obligations (OFA) are regulated by the Course's Academic Regulations.

Communication Skills.
The objective of the Bachelor's Degree Course is to train graduates capable of effectively implementing their interventions to promote the full self-determination, potential, and autonomy of individuals, as active subjects in the assistance project. The communication of problems and solutions is based on the principles of subsidiarity and empowerment and is carried out using conceptual tools and interpretive methods that refer to the theoretical heritage of social service, as well as other social sciences as specified in the SSD SPS/07-08, M-PSI/01-04, M-DEA/01. The development of these skills is also pursued through the knowledge of at least one foreign language, useful for understanding multiculturalism present in the social contexts of reference; the ability to inform and communicate is also achieved through the acquisition of basic computer skills. The teaching tools that will allow the achievement of the expected learning outcomes, in addition to frontal lectures including those given by visiting professors, include internships, activities related to the ERASMUS+ program, guided visits, study trips, and group work. For formative and summative assessment purposes, writing workshops and workshops for developing relational-communication skills, interviews, and practical tests may be scheduled.
