Judgment Autonomy.
The objective of the Bachelor's Degree Course is to train graduates capable of interpreting problematic situations by applying the principles of social service design; to collect and interpret data in light of theories, methodologies, and techniques of social sciences; of the principles, foundations, and applied theories of Social Service; to develop reflection on social and scientific issues, with regard to the code of ethics of the social assistant. The methods by which expected learning outcomes can be achieved are based on the circularity of the theory-practice approach and utilize teaching tools such as the internship, integrated courses, career day, and meetings organized with the professional world, thematic seminars, group work, participation in study conferences, and debate forms that actualize the topics addressed. Oral and practical assessments are provided as evaluation methods.

Learning Ability.
The objective of the Bachelor's Degree Course is to train graduates capable of recognizing the uniqueness and variability of needs, in order to identify original and appropriate assistance solutions for individual intervention cases. The development of learning abilities, useful for continuing studies with a high degree of autonomy, occurs through a didactic approach based on the circularity of theory-practice, as learned from internship operational contexts and re-elaborated through reflective action, guided within the university context. Teaching tools to achieve these learning outcomes, alongside the internship, include integrated courses, thematic seminars, laboratory meetings, and group work. Oral discussions, practical tests, and evaluation seminars are provided.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Sociological and Social Service Field The objective of this field is to provide knowledge and skills inherent to sociological disciplines and Social Service, enabling graduates to understand social dynamics, ongoing transformations, and the emergence of new and old needs, both individual and collective.

Legal, Political-Economic, and Statistical Field The objective of this field is to provide foundational concepts of legal disciplines, enabling students to understand legislative content regulating citizens' lives and social policies. An additional objective is to provide main statistical tools for understanding and processing quantitative data in the socio-assistive field and prepare for using computer procedures for data processing.

Psychological, Medical, and Anthropological Field The objective of this field is to provide foundational concepts of psychological, medical, and anthropological disciplines, enabling students to understand different worldviews and value orientations inherent to cultures and social groups, and recognize main pathologies existing in our society, regardless of cultural specifics.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Sociological and Social Service Field The objective of this field is to develop abilities enabling students to plan actions, interventions, promotional activities, and assistance projects. Such knowledge will contribute to taking charge of, supporting, and accompanying individuals and groups experiencing distress and difficulties toward resolution.

Legal, Political-Economic, and Statistical Field The objective of this field is to develop abilities to use and apply legal norms for the social assistant professional to take charge of individuals, families, and groups facing critical and distressing situations. An additional objective is to develop abilities to use and apply statistical data for programming activities, quality assessment of services provided, analysis of user needs, analysis of socio-economic context and protection networks, and report writing.

Psychological, Medical, and Anthropological Field The objective of this field is to develop abilities to implement effective support and intervention actions in relation to the specificities of distress affecting individuals, families, groups, and communities, regardless of their cultural specifics.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN Associated competencies for the role.
Professional operators in private, public, national, supranational, and multinational organizations, administrations, bodies, non-governmental organizations, third sector, and enterprises within social inclusion, preventive-promotional, organizational, educational, and research processes.

Graduates in the degree courses of this class must:
possess adequate knowledge and mastery of basic disciplines, methods, and techniques of Social Service;
possess disciplinary and methodological knowledge appropriately useful for programming and implementing integrated interventions across various operational fields;
possess competencies in the field of detecting and processing social distress situations for individuals, families, groups, and communities;
possess adequate competencies for communication and information management, particularly regarding citizenship rights and accompanying individuals in difficulty;
possess competencies and abilities to interact with cultures, including gender and immigrant populations, in the perspective of multicultural and multiethnic social relations;
be able to activate preventive actions for social distress, promotional actions for the well-being of individuals, families, groups, and communities; social emergency intervention and support in accessing resources and services;
possess adequate mastery of the social research method;
possess abilities to operate within groups and in work groups;
effectively know, in written and oral form, at least one European Union language, in addition to Italian.

Role in Work Context.
Professional operators in private, public, national, supranational, and multinational organizations, administrations, bodies, non-governmental organizations, third sector, and enterprises within social inclusion, preventive-promotional, organizational, educational, and research processes.

Social Service Assistant.
Specific Training Objectives Description.
It is considered that, for the formation of a figure capable of supporting the construction of a modern welfare system, training activities related to the theoretical body of social sciences (SPS/07 or 08, MDEA/01, M-PSI/01), legal sciences (IUS/09, IUS/01, IUS/17), and statistical sciences (SECS-S/05) are necessary, all included within the 'basic' type. In particular, Social Service disciplines, included in SSD SPS/07, will contribute to creating knowledge and practice commensurate with the tasks required by territorial welfare systems, considering the problems and increasing demands for cohesion and integration from society.

The regulated profession of social assistant is recognized within the European Union and allows for professional mobility consistent with its guiding principles.

Particular attention is dedicated to theoretical-practical training through internship activities, supervised exclusively by qualified social assistants. A filtering system is provided for accessing different internship levels: in addition to some prerequisites that must be respected (quantity and quality of mandatory courses already taken; exams passed and number of credits obtained; internship placement following a specific report with the organization). Regarding ongoing internship evaluations, laboratories and seminars, logbook, and portfolio are required, to be submitted to a specific department office linked to student secretariat for formalizing the internship at the end of the experience. The demand for enrollment from the territory is constant and substantial, but is moderated by the programmed number, including a careful entrance test. It should be noted that with the implementation of Law 328/2000 by the Autonomous Region of Sardinia (L.R. 23/2005), services in the socio-health sector have increased and the role of the third sector in programming and delivering personal services has expanded. This is responded to with adequate training of figures deemed capable of meeting the challenges of new welfare, to be competent professionals in personal services.

Research activities, seminars, conferences, publications, etc., carried out by the course instructors strengthen the trend and carry out in-service updating and training activities for social assistants, in coordination with the Order, but also in dialogue with other professions.

In the state examination for social assistant, graduates from the University of Sassari have so far achieved a high promotion rate at the highest qualification levels.

Their employment prospects are diverse: from the freelance professional called to offer design proposals, direct solutions, and contributions as a consultant moving freely in the creative design market, to that of an operator capable of guiding team work and actively integrating into companies' internal offices as a design technician, but also as an analyst and process facilitator.
Characteristics of the final assessment.
The final assessment plays an important role in our training project: as a stimulus and assumption of responsibility by students, before being a evaluation of the maturity acquired by the student throughout their training path.
The final assessment may take place along two main directions: one path involves a detailed and exhaustive presentation of activities carried out during the internship; alternatively, students may agree with a faculty supervisor on a topic to explore, which may be design-oriented or research-based, also within a path combining the internship and activities in the final synthesis laboratories. Particular attention will be given to the candidates' ability to approach the chosen topic problematically. Students are required to demonstrate analytical and synthesis skills, according to a model inspired by a multidimensional approach (thus controlling both the overall scale in terms of process, and the detail, i.e., proposing specific and precise solutions).
Students must also demonstrate full familiarity with the topic addressed, proving, through the choice of appropriate modes and languages for its transmission, that they have acquired adequate communication skills.
Achieving autonomous methodological control, the overall quality of the final outcomes, their coherence, and the full awareness of the work carried out represent additional evaluation criteria.
Required knowledge for admission.
To be admitted to the study program, one must hold a secondary school diploma of the second level or another equivalent foreign degree recognized as suitable. The required initial knowledge and preparation concern analytical, expressive, and communication skills; synthesis and systemic vision; reading and processing of visual and textual content, as well as general cultural level, verified through a specific admission test that will result in a score.
For students admitted to the study program with a score below the predetermined threshold, specific additional training obligations will be indicated in the teaching regulations to be fulfilled within the first year of study.
Expected employment and professional opportunities for graduates.
Designer The three-year graduate is able to interpret different contexts with versatility, looking beyond immediate perspectives to anticipate behaviors and future responses. They can therefore engage with companies, organizations, and productive realities at regional, national, and international levels, bringing strategic visions, creativity, and innovative approaches.
Their employment prospects are diverse: from the freelance professional called to offer design proposals, direct solutions, and contributions as a consultant moving freely in the creative design market, to that of an operator capable of guiding team work and actively integrating into companies' internal offices as a design technician, but also as an analyst and process facilitator.

COURSE: [A144] DESIGN
SECTION: Communication Skills
URL: https://uniss.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10900?annoOrdinamento=2022

Communication Skills.
The exercise of communication skills plays a key role in the educational project. This is to enable graduates to acquire tools and strategies with which, during the practical design process, the future designer will be able to interface and engage with their interlocutors, whether they be clients, experts and collaborators, stakeholders, individual users or groups. In this direction, the main lines of work encompass the two fundamental communication dimensions for the designer:
· those related to the operational level (in a multitude of interpretations and expressions) and thus aimed at both the strict design process – through conceptual models and schematizations of reality – and at the productive, technical, and execution aspects;
· those related to the strategic level and the promotion of the project, through appropriate languages and formulas to convey its guiding ideas and reference scenarios, through conceptual representations, visualizations, narratives, and illustrations of imaginaries.
All of this, always navigating with agility within the current communication and media landscape.
The educational project places particular emphasis on acquiring these skills, structuring their learning throughout the entire three-year period, in a series of incremental teaching moments. The entire educational program, moreover, is based on a plurality of practice and verification moments for the ability to argue design choices: in revisions and intermediate presentations, in internships, in final project plenary presentations, as well as in opportunities for discussion and interaction, even outside our school community, with a variety of external subjects (stakeholders, experts, visiting professors and researchers).
Learning Ability.
Third-year graduates must have developed the ability to apply both 'indirect' knowledge – of a speculative nature – acquired during the educational path, and 'direct' knowledge – based on project-based comparison, trial-and-error experience, analysis of case studies and experiences conducted by others – to filter future experiences and problems, deriving new knowledge from them. This within the framework of the personal acquisition of a non-abstract methodological processing and analysis model, along with the maturation of one's own value system to interpret a multitude of demands, identifying their synthesis through an overall view of the process and the ability to harmoniously balance the variables at play. A key component of responsible design is the designer's ability to take responsibility: meaning not only to make choices, but also to put oneself in a position to do so consciously, to give meaning and complete form to the solution of specific problems, within the context of contemporary needs. The educational model underlying this vision of knowledge construction draws inspiration from the 'basic design' model and is structured into a series of intermediate learning opportunities: preparation for practical skills occurs through a series of incremental steps, whose sequence is primarily aimed at building an overall design attitude. The positive 'interference' between concentrated small experiences (intensive workshops, cross-class workshops, with external subjects) and broader project tasks (semester-long design workshops) also represents an intentional element of problematic growth and maturation. The results achieved by students in the design workshops – particularly in the integrated ones, where dialogue between different disciplines is intended to introduce, as learning opportunities, different models of knowledge construction and reality interpretation, transversal to the educational project – as well as in the final synthesis workshops and the conduct of the final assessment, represent the moments of verification of this objective.

SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment

Autonomy of Judgment.
The ability of the problem-solver – one of the key qualities traditionally associated with the designer's figure – is accompanied by that of the decision-maker. The designer, in fact, guides and coordinates the collection of project data, confronts the problems that inform them and the demands of the various involved actors, but ultimately, they are primarily called upon to make decisions through their design choices, assuming responsibility for their economic, social, ethical, and environmental implications. To stimulate students' development of autonomous judgment maturity, the educational project provides confrontation with a structured set of experiences, designed to promote a complex and problem-oriented vision, offering tools to critically interpret reality based on analytical and methodological elements, as well as – through the exercise of lateral thinking – according to one's personal perspective. The educational program therefore assigns a key role, from the first year, to the assumption of individual responsibility by those following it: students are thus encouraged to make informed decisions regarding the opportunities offered by the Course of Study in terms of structuring their educational path. Throughout the entire three-year period – in the selection of thematic trajectories of annual interdisciplinary workshops, in identifying internship activities and other elective activities, in the elaboration of the theme on which to structure the final exam – they are to some extent called upon to outline the 'design' of their personal educational path. The coherence of choices and the overall results achieved – verifiable at multiple levels: from project laboratories to individual courses; from responses to individual project themes to the ability to harmonize their overall design – will be evidence of students' acquisition of the component of an autonomous judgment capacity.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Scientific Training Graduates in design are trained in the intuitive and analytical understanding of geometric space, its conceptualization practices, and the modes of its relationships and transformations. They are also able to translate the fields of spatial development and plastic composition into useful and applicable solutions for concrete needs.

Technological Training Graduates in design are familiar with the set of industrial product production methods in relation to possible options in the selection of resources, materials, and processing, structural characteristics, realization contexts, and various economic-production options.

Basic Project Training Consistently with the reference productive, social, and cultural contexts, graduates possess a comprehensive vision of design as a system to address and solve design problems within the scope of consumer goods, communication artifacts, and services. They are able to collect and process the elements informing the project in relation to its development and production, usability, and the capacity to express values beyond strict functionality. Graduates in design are also capable of controlling the various phases of the project: in relation to clients, interaction with a variety of collaborators, and communication and transmission of design ideas.

Humanistic Training Graduates possess the foundation to frame the historical progression of design in light of its intersections with culture, technology, and society. They are therefore able to correctly frame the spatial-temporal dimension of artifacts, objects, and environments, recognizing styles, influences, and references to contexts.

Basic Representation Training Graduates are familiar with the set of representation systems and have acquired the necessary control of the technical-expressive graphic dimension required to elaborate and communicate design ideas. In particular, they are accustomed to using a variety of drawing and graphic rendering techniques for the expression and communication of design concepts.

Design and Multimedia Communications Graduates in design are able to control how the design expertise of the designer unfolds across various application fields. They are able to manage the use of digital tools and techniques for information processing around the project; control methodologies and procedures for the design, transformation, and production of material goods; are capable of addressing design themes related to the experience and consumption of space, also for the translation and presentation of informational content to the public; are familiar with contemporary "immaterial" declinations of design for digital communication applications, networks, and social networks. Graduates control the theoretical-practical dimension underlying multimedia and audiovisual artifacts populating the current communication landscape and are capable of framing design in terms of strategic activity, for the design of innovative services and as a tool for social innovation.

Technological and Engineering Disciplines Graduates in design have a solid foundation in the technologies of processing methods with which, at various scales and in different production contexts, in line with environmental concerns, design dialogues for the realization and distribution of new material products and immaterial services. They are also familiar with the set of diverse graphic expression forms, understood as technical elements of project representation conducive to its evolutionary development. Of these technical forms, they are able to use them as languages: project, illustrative, and artistic.

Economic and Social Sciences Graduates in design are able to integrate knowledge from economic and social sciences into their design awareness and sensitivity, deriving additional knowledge through interdisciplinary comparison. They are able to profitably grasp contributions from this disciplinary area, which broadens their knowledge horizons and contributes to the maturation of analytical and critical abilities, enabling the designer to propose themselves as an interpreter and mediator of diverse demands.

Related or Integrative Training Activities Graduates in design integrate and/or complete their educational path through confrontation with themes useful for dialectically framing their more strictly design-oriented aptitudes and approaches. They are able to position the design of material goods, immaterial artifacts, communication, and services in relation to the needs of environmental balance within a dimension embracing both territorial and residential scales, highlighting the reasons and logics between local and global.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Scientific Training The acquired knowledge translates into the ability to employ the language and tools of geometry, as a basis for articulating an idea of form and translating it, having understood its constructive, procedural, and semantic potentials. The course refers to SSD MAT/03.

Technological Training The direct confrontation offered by the design exercise regarding possible formal solutions, the integration of structural and accessory elements, and the concreteness of realization constraints allows the application of knowledge to production processes and the understanding of problematic aspects (referable to SSD ICAR/08) through which to make choices in terms of scale economy and sustainability.

Basic Project Training Based on a general framework of methodological knowledge and practical experiences, graduates are able to apply a broad and problem-oriented understanding of the meaning of designing to a variety of themes and needs. They are also capable of developing appropriate solutions for managing the design and realization process.

Humanistic Training The problem-oriented confrontation with the subject will enable students to transform their historical-critical reading ability into a dynamic tool for interpreting present reality. Achieving full awareness of the experiences through which design has been articulated historically constitutes a key element in applying acquired knowledge and understanding how to articulate one's own critical reference framework, even strictly design-oriented.

Basic Representation Training Graduates are able to apply the disciplinary knowledge framework to their design tasks through the identification of the most suitable expressive solutions and the personal use of the language of images.

Design and Multimedia Communications A characteristic of the designer is the ability to intertwine theoretical and practical dimensions, constantly applying acquired knowledge across various disciplinary fields and occasions. Direct confrontation with multiple and diverse design activity declinations is the essential condition for verifying the ability to transfer knowledge to the practical plane, developing problem-oriented models for understanding reality and generating new knowledge.

Technological and Engineering Disciplines The confrontation with application opportunities and concrete problematic aspects proposed by the experience of design laboratories, facing real cases, allows design graduates to refine their ability to apply knowledge and understanding of the correspondence between design objectives, costs, production conditions, and potential reference markets. Regarding graphic expression techniques, familiarity combined with a critical approach, not merely instrumental, with this system of thematic languages allows design graduates to apply their knowledge and understanding of the modes to convey the most appropriate graphic information for a given communication context.

Economic and Social Sciences A key objective of the entire educational model, the graduates' propensity for interdisciplinary integration is also realized in relation to courses pertaining to economic and social sciences, referable to SSDs M-DEA 01, SECS-P/08, and SPS/08. The design exercise, aimed at stimulating lateral thinking, offers concrete opportunities to apply the knowledge and understanding gained through comparison with these disciplines.

Related or Integrative Training Activities The confrontation of design methodologies with different themes, cases, and intervention scales is an opportunity to apply disciplinary knowledge and verify understanding in relation to problems and scales referable to SSDs BIO/07, ICAR 14, ICAR 20, and M-FIL/02.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN Competencies Associated with the Function.
Designer The three-year designer is able to propose innovative solutions in line with the ideation, realization, and distribution processes of design for goods and services, and with the techniques, languages, and current communication modalities, adapting to different work contexts. Inserted within a company, but also proposing themselves as autonomous design consultants, the three-year graduate is able to control the basic aspects of the strategy, realization, and production of graphic and identity communication design, the preparation of specifications, and the care in final realization, the development of audiovisual and interactive artifacts, and contributions for web/social platforms.

They are also able to intervene in product design, equipping themselves with the appropriate tools to interface with production managers and finalize the engineering and realization aspects of the products they have conceived, providing all necessary execution materials.

Function in the Workplace Context.
Designer Upon completion of the three-year degree, the student's preparation encompasses the abilities traditionally associated with the designer profile: innovative charge; analytical and synthetic capacity; exercise of autonomous and mature design thinking.

Operating both independently, as an external consultant, and as an active participant in internal company teams, the three-year designer is able to conduct research to position new products and services in the market; indicate lines of orientation for promotion strategies; finally, they are able to provide design contributions across a plurality of fields: graphic and product design, multimedia artifacts, and network communication.

Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The three-year study plan encompasses product and communication design, while simultaneously touching on the various fields in which contemporary designer professionalism is articulated: strategic design, service design, audiovisual and multimedia design, the ideation of events and cultural experiences, information design, and integrated promotion and communication on new media. On this basis, the central objective of the educational project is to train a designer familiar with the ideation, realization, and distribution processes of design for goods and services, and with the techniques, languages, and communication modalities of the current scenario. A hybrid figure that, based on a preparation combining specific skills, design methodology, and vision capacity, is able to interpret a multiplicity of diverse demands, identifying their synthesis and solution in relation to companies, institutions, and social actors at regional, national, and international levels.

The educational organization is structured into thematic semesters, unfolding along the three-year path as a sequence of formative experiences, following a model that begins with a general framework and progressively focuses on specific reference areas.

In the first semester of the first year, the perspective frames the dimension of emerging global problems (course Design for the Planet), particularly emphasizing the urgency of addressing major environmental issues. Courses Images I (Drawing), History of Design, and courses aimed at providing additional foundational competencies (Geometry, Philosophy of Art) complete this introductory cycle.

In the second semester, with the course Design and Places, attention shifts to the territorial dimension, highlighting the need for constant human interaction with their surroundings. The course Culture of Design, in its articulation (including a Photography module), is tasked with introducing students to the methodological aspects of design and the cultural mediation function that design can perform in society. A course in Cultural Anthropology serves as integration and complement.

The first semester of the second year includes courses related to communication practices characterizing the current media landscape: Design of Digital Culture (Info Design and Digital Design), Theory of Audiovisual Languages, alongside the course Images II (dedicated to Graphic Languages).

In the second semester, the focus of design shifts to the themes of material culture and product (Design of Material Culture), updated to the practices of new craftsmanship and digital fabrication. Courses in Technology of Processing Methods, Models and Technologies of Materials for Design, and Marketing reinforce the path.

In the third year, the Exhibit Design laboratory introduces students to the complex interplay between communication languages and spatial organization, while the course Design for Society outlines the scenarios of relationships and interactions between design disciplines and the design of processes and services.

The second and final semester is dedicated to the synthesis and completion of the learning process: professional internships, personal portfolio development, elective courses, English language improvement, and preparation of the final career project.

The educational project assigns particular importance to the development of design aptitude through a series of annual interdisciplinary workshops, designed for direct confrontation with issues expressed by territories and the working world. Workshop activities are based on dialogue with external subjects (institutions, companies, artisans, entrepreneurial initiatives) that bring design practice experiences into contact with real-world themes and problems. The predominant workshop directions follow thematic lines of heritage design, territorial product valorization, and the relationship between design and craftsmanship, but may include cross-cutting fields such as fashion, performance, technical, social, and scientific communication.

Interdisciplinary workshops form the backbone of an educational project aimed at empowering students in the construction of their personal, cultural, and professional maturation. The three main thematic threads, which configure 'passing' corridors throughout the three years of the course, offer them opportunities for discovery and choice, allowing them to independently chart individual paths through the core study plan.

These paths may further enrich through participation in planned parallel activities (summer schools, credit-based courses), selection of a targeted internship, attendance at a final synthesis laboratory, and preparation of the final career project.

The overall path – in line with the tradition of our Department – will also be characterized by an articulated program of professional internships, both within and outside Sardinia, with a strong orientation towards internationalization.

Characteristics of final exam.
The exam consists of preparing a theoretical-critical, experimental or applied paper chosen by the candidate and its critical discussion. Through this exam, the acquisition of learning, maturity, communication skills, and the ability to independently process acquired knowledge are assessed.
More specifically, the final exam aims to verify the achievement of critical reflection capabilities on acquired knowledge and their potential application in both scientific and practical contexts. Finally, it aims to assess the achievement of the appropriate level of autonomy necessary to address the complexity of a scientific or applied topic.
Required knowledge for access.
To be admitted to the degree course, one must hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign degree recognized as suitable.
For admission to the degree course, knowledge and skills in Italian and English language, logical-analytical reasoning abilities, basic scientific knowledge, and linguistic knowledge are required. In particular, the assessment of such knowledge occurs through the admission test using TOLC-PSI (consisting of 50 questions divided into 5 sections: Text comprehension, Basic mathematics, Verbal reasoning, Numerical reasoning, and Biology; plus 30 questions from the module for verifying English language knowledge).
No additional educational obligation (OFA) will be assigned to candidates who, ranked in a suitable position in the merit ranking for admission to the degree course, answered at least 50% of the questions correctly.
Students who achieve insufficient results will be assigned additional educational obligations, which must be fulfilled by December 31 of the academic year following enrollment. Further details may be specified in the Course Didactic Regulations.

Communication Skills.
The acquisition of communication skills is a fundamental and qualifying element, since the profession of a psychologist is characterized by constant contact with social operators and with people working in public and private organizations interested in analyzing opinions, attitudes, and lifestyle surveys. This ability includes non-verbal and verbal communication of an oral type, but also written, that is, carried out on computer platforms that allow the use of statistical software, thanks to which data from conducted research can be effectively communicated graphically. For the achievement of such skills, exercises and learning and application moments specifically designed and coordinated with the different transactional contexts are provided. The ability to process and communicate the acquired knowledge will be specifically evaluated during the in-course assessments, through oral and/or written tests and through the final exam.

Autonomy of Judgment.
The training activities as a whole are aimed at developing competencies that foster the necessary professional autonomy to address critical conditions in human and social contexts and in the types of collaboration in research, consulting, and community intervention promotion and development activities. This means that the student must acquire the ability to use scientific, psychometric, educational, and psychological and neuropsychological intervention tools. They must also acquire the ability to read and interpret statistical and experimental data derived from research activities. Finally, they must be capable of navigating within the ethical and legal norms governing interactions with clients and, in perspective, the profession of the psychologist.
The Autonomy of Judgment is achieved through the exercise of critical ability, both during lectures and exercises, and in applications carried out through laboratory and internship activities. This ability is appropriately assessed and acquired through oral and/or written exams during the examination assessments.

Learning Ability.
The graduate must have acquired knowledge and mastery of the fundamental theories and techniques of psychological sciences, both for potential integration into the workforce and in the perspective of continuing studies in master's degrees. Additionally, they must demonstrate the ability to learn from experience and modify, update, and enrich their professional competencies, which do not exclude the ability to use computer and linguistic tools (libraries, databases, application or analytical software). The evaluation of these abilities and their acquisition, in addition to being assessed through the performance achieved in individual courses based on oral and/or written exams, occurs specifically through the work underlying the preparation of the final thesis.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Analytical-Experimental Field The objective of this field is to provide the basic knowledge and methodological skills inherent to psychological disciplines and (more generally) scientific disciplines, on a purely experimental plane and oriented towards basic and applied research. To this end, the main tools of experimental methodology, psychometrics, neuropsychology, and neuroscience, experimental research techniques, and psychophysical methods are provided to understand and process quantitative data in all possible fields belonging to the sphere of psychological science. This objective is complemented by the use of computer procedures for data processing necessary to enable the practical application of acquired knowledge.

Socio-Evolutionary Field The objective of this field is to provide the foundational concepts of psychological and social disciplines, also in light of discoveries in neuroscience, enabling students to understand the bases of different explanatory potentials of personality, its development, and its manifestations in normal and pathological behaviors.

Clinical-Diagnostic Field The objective of this field is to provide the foundational concepts of applying psychological disciplines in clinical and diagnostic contexts, enabling students to understand the different explanatory potentials of personality and its development in pathological behaviors.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Analytical-Experimental Field The objective of this field is to develop capabilities that make concrete interventions effective in various fields, not only in basic research but also in applied research. The logical-experimental field described above constitutes the foundation of the following two fields.
The assessment of acquired knowledge and competencies and their relative application capability by the student involves specific oral and/or written exams for each training activity, through which the student can demonstrate mastery in using the tools and methodologies learned. For some training activities that involve learning practical skills and their professional application, either in the field or through practical exercises, assessment may be conducted through practical evaluations. Assessments, in addition to being conducted at the end of the training activity, may also be carried out during the activity at the discretion of the instructor designated for the specific training activity. Didactic regulations and syllabi for each training activity detail the specific assessment methods.

Socio-Evolutionary Field The objective of this field is to develop the ability to use and apply acquired knowledge in social dynamics, transformations occurring in the individual, family, and society. This objective is complemented by the development of abilities to use and apply statistical data for programming, quality assessment of activities, needs analysis, and socio-economic context analysis.
The assessment of acquired knowledge and competencies and their relative application capability by the student involves specific oral and/or written exams for each training activity, through which the student can demonstrate mastery in using the tools and methodologies learned. For some training activities that involve learning practical skills and their professional application, either in the field or through practical exercises, assessment may be conducted through practical evaluations. Assessments, in addition to being conducted at the end of the training activity, may also be carried out during the activity at the discretion of the instructor designated for the specific training activity. Didactic regulations and syllabi for each training activity detail the specific assessment methods.

Clinical-Diagnostic Field The objective of this field is to develop the necessary knowledge to implement effective diagnostic, support, and intervention actions in relation to the specific nature of difficulties affecting individuals, families, groups, and the community.
The assessment of acquired knowledge and competencies and their relative application capability by the student involves specific oral and/or written exams for each training activity, through which the student can demonstrate mastery in using the tools and methodologies learned. Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN Associated Competencies.
Bachelor in Psychological Techniques
- Ability to access scientific and specialist literature;
- Competence in using tools for scientific and disciplinary updating;
- Application of statistical data analysis techniques in various fields of psychology;
- Correct use and interpretation of the most significant diagnostic tests;
- Knowledge of research and psychometric investigation techniques;
- Ability to observe and scientifically analyze human behavior;

- Ability to provide psychological support throughout the life cycle.
The competencies acquired in the three-year L-24 course prepare students for subsequent master's degrees and the formation of an expert who can operate as a support figure to a master's-level psychologist registered in Section A of the Register.
Professional Role in the Workplace.
Bachelor in Psychological Techniques The Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of Cognitive Processes, in accordance with the national and European scientific and professional community of psychologists, enables the qualification for independent psychological practice, Section B of the Professional Register of Psychologists, following completion of the Practical Evaluation Internship (ex DM 654 of July 5, 2022).
Graduates of the three-year program, and after registration in Section B of the Professional Register of Psychologists (passing the State Exam) and under the supervision of a registered psychologist, can effectively operate within services directed at individuals, families, groups, and communities.
This role aims at promoting well-being, enhancing the effectiveness of educational interventions, and strengthening individual and social resources.
Workplace Functions: active participation in planning and evaluating psychological and psycho-social interventions; implementation of psycho-educational interventions; application of ergonomic knowledge for designing technologies and improving interaction between individuals and specific activity contexts; use of psychological tools (interview, tests, observation) for assessing personality, social interactions, opinions, and attitudes; implementation of school and career orientation activities and human resource management; collection and statistical processing of psychological and psychophysical data for research purposes; use of psychological tools to recover cognitive, emotional, relational, and practical skills in disabled individuals; implementation of surveys and investigations using web-assisted questionnaires.
It is essential to emphasize that these functions can only be carried out exclusively within a professional team context and as a support figure to a psychologist registered in Section A of the Register of Psychologists.

Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of Cognitive Processes aims primarily to train students by combining psychological research and cognitive neuroscience with human sciences, education, and rehabilitation, through the acquisition of essential technical-scientific tools for professional activity in psychosocial, neuropsychological, ergonomic, psychometric and neuroscientific assessment, human resource management, training, assistance, and health promotion contexts, to be carried out in both public and private structures, in companies, and in the third sector.
More specifically, knowledge and competencies will gradually develop throughout the three-year program through various activities. The knowledge and competencies that graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of Cognitive Processes will acquire during the three years are as follows:
- Basic and characterizing subjects aimed at understanding psychological and neuro-biological disciplines and interdisciplinary fields fundamental for building solid technical and cultural competencies;
- Characterizing and related knowledge and competencies aimed at using techniques, methods, and procedures of neuro-scientific, neuropsychological, and clinical investigation;
- Knowledge aimed at mastering the main statistical and applied techniques in various sectors and work contexts;
- Knowledge and competencies in communication and information management;
- Advanced competencies in using at least one European Union language, in addition to Italian, both in written and oral form.
Upon completion of studies, graduates of the L-24 class can perform professional activities in public and private, scientific, applied, and health institutions, educational institutions, companies, and third-sector organizations. They can carry out activities in services directed at individuals, groups, organizations, and communities, as well as in services for assistance and health promotion. These activities also relate to psychometric, neuropsychological, psycho-social, developmental assessment, and human resource management across the life cycle.
To achieve these objectives, the courses include activities aimed at acquiring theoretical foundations and technical-methodological elements of general psychology and development, investigation methodologies, statistical methods, and computer procedures for data processing, psychophysiological and neural mechanisms underlying behavior, and dynamics of normal and pathological human relationships.
The courses will also aim to adequately contextualize psychological disciplines within the broader framework of natural, biological, and neuroscience.
For this purpose, supplementary training activities in various disciplinary fields, such as seminars, laboratory activities, and practical experiences in real or simulated situations, are also provided. These are complemented by Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) and orientation activities, as well as student-selected credits.
According to current regulations, the additional professionalizing training activities, amounting to 10 CFU, are carried out during the Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques - L-24 class. The specific articulation of these professionalizing training activities, defined by the university's didactic regulations for L-24 study programs, includes:
a) Activities for acquiring basic professional competencies related to empirical methods characteristic of all areas of psychology and techniques for evaluating the functioning of the mind and behavior, including their psychobiological correlates, in relation to different age groups and social and life contexts;
b) Activities for acquiring basic professional competencies related to psychological assessment and the main forms of intervention on interpersonal, intragroup, and intergroup relationships in various social contexts, at the level of dyads, families, small groups, and organizations;
c) Analysis of the main forms of alteration in psychological processes and human behavior, in relation to different age groups and social and life contexts. The training of students carrying out TPV activities and the evaluation of these activities are entrusted to professionals/teachers-tutors registered with the Order for at least three years, whose training and evaluation activities are conducted in accordance with the tutorial teaching regulations of the study programs.
The course also includes, in relation to specific objectives, extracurricular activities and study stays at Italian and foreign universities, also within the framework of international agreements.

Critical Judgment.
Graduates must have acquired the ability to compare the key themes emerging from psycho-pedagogical thought with events, problems, and phenomena originating from other fields of knowledge, their applications, and the various life situations, demonstrating critical mastery and independence of judgment.
After the training path, consisting of theoretical study, exercises, group work, internship activities, and in-depth studies, the graduate must be able to critically, consciously, and creatively address educational and psycho-pedagogical issues, hypothesizing and implementing targeted actions for promoting the person and supporting individuals in difficulty.
The achievement of these expected outcomes will be promoted within specific disciplines and, transversally, through the various teaching and learning activities proposed in the degree program (lectures, workshops, seminars and conferences, internship, and final thesis). Their evaluation will be conducted both through in-course and final exams of individual courses and the curricular internship activity, as well as overall at the end of the program, through the student's elaboration and discussion of a final thesis.
Knowledge and Understanding.
Pedagogical Disciplines: Knowledge of the main theoretical models, themes, and issues in the pedagogical-educational-didactic field, including their historical evolution.
Knowledge of the main working methodologies and operational strategies in the educational field, for different intervention sectors.
Psychological Disciplines: Mastery of the main psychological theories and themes, both general and social, as well as developmental psychology, also in relation to educational psychology.
Didactic and Disability Integration Disciplines: Knowledge of the main issues related to the cognitive, affective, and psychosocial sphere from an evolutionary perspective.
Sociological and Anthropological Disciplines: Basic knowledge of the main approaches, methodologies, and themes in the sociological field and the main theoretical orientations and themes in the anthropological field.
Historical Disciplines: Basic knowledge of the main historical phenomena and historiographical aspects in various eras, with particular attention to the modern and contemporary periods.
Geographical Disciplines: Basic knowledge of the connections between environments and economies using the theoretical tools of economic and political geography as reading keys.
Philosophical Disciplines: Knowledge of themes in contemporary philosophy, the history of philosophical thought, and philosophical historiography.
Language Skills: Good written and oral knowledge of at least one European language, and preferably other foreign languages.
Computer Skills: Knowledge of the main computer tools relevant to processing cultural content: electronic text processing, electronic communication, mastery of techniques for consulting electronic databases, etc.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Pedagogical Disciplines: Ability to argue the main themes and issues in the pedagogical-didactic field.
Ability to apply theoretical assumptions acquired in the pedagogical field to practical educational interventions, including their design and evaluation.
Ability to interpret and respond to educational questions of the territory, in order to develop personalized educational projects.
Psychological Disciplines: Ability to apply theoretical knowledge and skills acquired in the educational context, with particular reference to motivational, emotional, cognitive, and social processes.
Didactic and Disability Integration Disciplines: Ability to integrate and apply theoretical knowledge within specific rehabilitation and educational intervention contexts.
Sociological and Anthropological Disciplines: Ability to read and interpret major social phenomena.
Ability to read and interpret individual and collective human behavior from an anthropological perspective.
Historical Disciplines: Analytical and argumentative skills regarding major historical phenomena and events, also in relation to pedagogical thought.
Geographical Disciplines: Application of acquired skills in designing educational interventions within territorial policies.
Philosophical Disciplines: Ability for critical analysis and argumentation, with particular attention to developing the capacity to identify interdisciplinary connections for understanding the complexity of reality.
Language Skills: Regarding the languages studied during the course, the student must have acquired the following competencies: (a) understanding of scientific literature in the original language, especially on content related to the disciplines of the course; (b) use of at least one foreign language for effective communication of content related to the disciplines of the course; (c) ability to conduct written exchanges in a foreign language; (d) ability to engage in oral conversations in a foreign language.
Computer Skills: Ability to process humanistic content (including multimedia) using electronic computers and communicate them via the Internet through the appropriate use of specific application programs.

Design, develop, and manage networked interventions in the areas of personal and educational services, with the aim of promoting the development of individual growth potential and social integration of people (minors and adults) in a state of distress, difficulty, marginalization, and/or deviance.

Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The specific educational objective for graduates of the Course is the acquisition of a solid cultural preparation in the field of education sciences through in-depth study of pedagogical, psychological, philosophical, and socio-anthropological disciplines. These multidisciplinary competencies and knowledge are essential both for entering the workforce and for continuing studies (enrollment in master's degrees). They appear indispensable for the educator's activity in responding to the diverse needs of the territory regarding educational needs in various fields. Therefore, additional specific educational objectives are:
- Acquisition of theoretical and operational competencies for understanding and analyzing socio-cultural contexts, achieved through the study of anthropological-social, historical, and economic-social geography disciplines, foreign languages, and contemporary multimedia languages;
- Acquisition of competencies related to the educator's field of activity, developed through specialized education sciences courses and the mandatory curricular internships at institutions, educational and training bodies, companies, and public administration structures, and possibly including stays at other Italian and foreign universities, also within international agreements. The final thesis is also related to fieldwork.
The didactic methodology used in the three-year degree will primarily be classroom-based (also with the support of multimedia, interactive, and online tools), taking the form of frontal communication, in-depth discussion of key issues (group activities, exercises, and workshops), reading and comparing sources, documents, original texts, tables, catalogs, case studies, etc., also using new multimedia online technologies. Study and thematic in-depth seminars will also be held, supported by external experts, as well as internship activities aimed at acquiring and refining professional competencies.
Regarding the training path, theoretical competencies are acquired predominantly in the first and second years, while specialized courses are entrusted to the second and third years. Theoretical reflection on professional opportunities occurs at various times throughout the three years, while field experience is gained through internships assigned to the second and/or third year. The thesis concludes the L-19 path but is preceded by bibliographic research and research techniques, treated as integrative aspects of various disciplines and also within the teaching aimed at acquiring the methodology of research in the educational field.

Characteristics of the final exam.
The exam consists of preparing a theoretical-critical, experimental or applied paper chosen by the candidate and its critical discussion. Through this exam, the acquisition of learning, maturity, communication skills, as well as the ability for independent processing of acquired knowledge by the student are evaluated.
More specifically, the final exam aims to verify the achievement of critical reflection capabilities on acquired knowledge and their potential application in both scientific and practical contexts. Finally, it aims to evaluate the achievement of the appropriate level of autonomy necessary to address the complexity of a scientific or applied topic.
Required knowledge for admission.
To be admitted to the degree course, one must hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign degree recognized as equivalent.
For admission to the degree course, knowledge and skills in Italian and English language, logical-analytical reasoning abilities, basic scientific knowledge, and linguistic knowledge are required. In particular, the assessment of such knowledge occurs through the admission test using TOLC-PSI (consisting of 50 questions divided into 5 sections: Text comprehension, Basic mathematics, Verbal reasoning, Numerical reasoning, and Biology; plus 30 questions from the module for verifying English language knowledge).
No additional educational obligation (OFA) will be assigned to candidates who, ranked in a suitable position in the merit ranking for admission to the degree course, answer at least 50% of the questions correctly.
Students who achieve insufficient results will be assigned additional educational obligations, which must be fulfilled by December 31 of the academic year following enrollment. Further details may be specified in the Course Didactic Regulation.

Communication Skills.
The acquisition of communication skills is a fundamental and qualifying element, since the profession of psychologist is characterized by constant contact with social operators and individuals working in public and private entities interested in analyzing opinions, attitudes, and lifestyle patterns. This ability encompasses both non-verbal and verbal oral communication, as well as written communication achieved through computer platforms that allow the use of statistical software, enabling effective graphical communication of research data. Specific exercises and learning and application moments, specifically designed and coordinated with different transactional contexts, are provided to acquire these skills. The ability to process and communicate acquired knowledge will be specifically assessed during in-course assessments through oral and/or written tests and through the final examination.

Judgment Autonomy.
The educational activities as a whole are aimed at developing competencies that foster the necessary professional autonomy to address critical conditions in human and social contexts and in the types of collaboration in research, consulting, and the promotion and development of community interventions. This means that the student must acquire the ability to use scientific, psychometric, educational, and psychological and neuropsychological intervention tools. They must also acquire the ability to read and interpret statistical and experimental data derived from research activities. Finally, they must be able to navigate within the ethical and legal norms governing interactions with clients and, in perspective, the profession of psychology.
Judgment autonomy is achieved through the exercise of critical ability, both during lectures and practical sessions, and in the applications carried out through laboratory and internship activities. This ability is appropriately assessed and acquired through oral and/or written exams during the assessment process.
Learning Ability.
The graduate must have acquired knowledge and mastery of the fundamental theories and techniques of psychological sciences, both for potential integration into the workforce and in the perspective of continuing studies in master's degrees. Additionally, they must demonstrate the ability to learn from acquired experience and to modify, update, and enrich their professional competencies, which do not exclude the ability to use computer and linguistic tools (libraries, databases, application or analytical software). The assessment of these abilities and their acquisition, in addition to being based on the results obtained in individual courses through oral and/or written exams, occurs specifically through the work underlying the preparation of the final thesis.
Knowledge and Understanding.
Analytical-Experimental Domain The objective of this domain is to provide the basic knowledge and methodological skills inherent to psychological disciplines (and more generally scientific disciplines), on a purely experimental plane oriented towards basic and applied research. To this end, the main tools of experimental methodology, psychometrics, neuropsychology, and neuroscience, as well as experimental research techniques and psychophysical methods for understanding and processing quantitative data in all possible domains of psychological science are provided. This objective is complemented by the use of computer procedures for data processing necessary to enable the real application of acquired knowledge.
Socio-Evolutionary Domain The objective of this domain is to provide the foundational concepts of psychological and social disciplines, also in light of discoveries in neuroscience, enabling students to understand the bases of different explanatory potentials of personality, its development, and its manifestations in normal and pathological behaviors.
Clinical-Diagnostic Domain The objective of this domain is to provide the basic concepts of applying psychological disciplines in clinical and diagnostic contexts, enabling students to understand the different explanatory potentials of personality and its development in pathological behaviors.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Analytical-Experimental Domain The objective of this domain is to develop abilities that enable effective interventions in various domains, not only in basic research but also in applied research. The logical-experimental domain described above forms the foundation for the following two domains.
The assessment of acquired knowledge and competencies and their relative application ability by the student involves specific oral and/or written tests for each educational activity, through which the student can demonstrate mastery of the tools and methodologies learned. For some educational activities that involve learning practical skills and their professional application, either in the field or through practical exercises, verification may be conducted through practical tests with evaluation. Assessments, in addition to being conducted at the end of the educational activity, may also be carried out during the activity at the discretion of the instructor designated for the specific educational activity. Didactic regulations and syllabi for each educational activity detail the specific assessment methods.
Socio-Evolutionary Domain The objective of this domain is to develop abilities to use and apply acquired knowledge in social dynamics, transformations occurring in the individual, family, and society. This objective is complemented by developing abilities to use and apply statistical data for planning, quality evaluation of activities, needs analysis, and socio-economic context analysis.
The assessment of acquired knowledge and competencies and their relative application ability by the student involves specific oral and/or written tests for each educational activity, through which the student can demonstrate mastery of the tools and methodologies learned. For some educational activities that involve learning practical skills and their professional application, either in the field or through practical exercises, verification may be conducted through practical tests with evaluation. Assessments, in addition to being conducted at the end of the educational activity, may also be carried out during the activity at the discretion of the instructor designated for the specific educational activity. Didactic regulations and syllabi for each educational activity detail the specific assessment methods.
Clinical-Diagnostic Domain The objective of this domain is to develop the necessary knowledge to implement effective diagnostic, support, and intervention actions in relation to the specificities of difficulties affecting individuals, families, groups, and the community.
The assessment of acquired knowledge and competencies and their relative application ability by the student involves specific oral and/or written tests for each educational activity, through which the student can demonstrate mastery of the tools and methodologies learned. For some educational activities that involve learning practical skills and their professional application, either in the field or through practical exercises, verification may be conducted through practical tests with evaluation. Assessments, in addition to being conducted at the end of the educational activity, may also be carried out during the activity at the discretion of the instructor designated for the specific educational activity. Didactic regulations and syllabi for each educational activity detail the specific assessment methods.

ITALIAN Associated Competencies for the Role.
Bachelor in Psychological Techniques
- Ability to access scientific and specialized literature;
- Competence in using tools for scientific and disciplinary updating;
- Application of statistical data analysis techniques in various domains of psychology;
- Correct use and interpretation of the most significant diagnostic tests;
- Knowledge of psychological research and psychometric investigation techniques;
- Ability to observe and scientifically analyze human behavior;
- Ability to conduct and interpret a psychological interview;

The competencies acquired in the three-year L-24 course prepare students for subsequent master's degrees and the formation of an expert who can operate as a support figure for a master's-level psychologist registered in Section A of the Register.
Role in the Workplace Context.
Bachelor in Psychological Techniques The Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of Cognitive Processes, in accordance with the national and European scientific and professional community of psychologists, enables the qualification for independent psychological practice, Section B of the Professional Register of Psychologists, following the completion of the Practical Evaluation Internship (ex DM 654 of July 5, 2022).
Graduates of the three-year program, and after registration in Section B of the Professional Register of Psychologists (passing the State Exam) and under the supervision of a registered psychologist, can effectively operate within services directed at individuals, families, groups, and communities.
This role aims at promoting well-being, enhancing the effectiveness of educational interventions, and strengthening individual and social resources.
Workplace Functions: Active participation in planning and evaluating psychological and psychosocial interventions; implementation of psychosocial educational interventions; application of ergonomic knowledge for designing technologies and improving interaction between individuals and specific activity contexts; use of psychological tools (interview, tests, observation) for evaluating personality, social interactions, opinions, and attitudes; implementation of school and career orientation activities and human resource management; collection and statistical processing of psychological and psychophysical data for research purposes; use of psychological tools to recover cognitive, emotional, relational, and practical competencies in disabled individuals; implementation of web-assisted surveys and investigations.
It is essential to emphasize that these functions can only be carried out exclusively within a professional team context and as a support figure for a psychologist registered in Section A of the Register.
Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of Cognitive Processes aims primarily to train students by combining psychological research and cognitive neuroscience with human sciences, education, and rehabilitation, through the acquisition of essential technical-scientific tools for professional activity in psychosocial, neuropsychological, ergonomic, psychometric and neuroscientific evaluation, human resource management, training, assistance, and health promotion, to be carried out in both public and private structures, in companies, and in the third sector.
More specifically, knowledge and competencies will gradually develop throughout the three years through the range of activities. The knowledge and competencies that graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of Cognitive Processes will acquire during the three years are as follows:
- Basic and characterizing subjects aimed at understanding psychological and neuro-biological disciplines and those related to interdisciplinary training, fundamental for building solid technical and cultural competencies;
- Characterizing and related knowledge and competencies aimed at using techniques, methods, and procedures of neuro-scientific, neuropsychological, and clinical investigation;
- Knowledge aimed at mastering the main statistical and applied techniques in various sectors and work contexts;
- Knowledge and competencies in communication and information management;
- Advanced competencies in using at least one European Union language, in addition to Italian, both in written and oral form.
At the end of their studies, L-24 graduates can perform professional activities in public and private, scientific, applied, and health institutions, educational institutions, companies, and third-sector organizations. They can carry out activities in services directed at individuals, groups, organizations, and communities, as well as in services for assistance and health promotion. These activities also relate to psychometric, neuropsychological, psychosocial, and developmental evaluation, as well as human resource management throughout the life cycle.
To achieve these objectives, the courses include activities aimed at acquiring theoretical foundations and technical-methodological elements of general psychology and development, investigation methodologies, statistical methods, and computer procedures for data processing, psychophysiological and neural mechanisms underlying behavior, and dynamics of normal and pathological human relationships.
The courses will also be oriented towards achieving an adequate contextualization of psychological disciplines within the broader framework of natural, biological, and neuroscience.
For this purpose, supplementary educational activities in various disciplinary fields, such as seminars, laboratory activities, and practical experiences in real or simulated situations, are also provided. These are complemented by Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) and orientation activities, as well as student-choice credits.
According to current regulations, the additional professionalizing activities, amounting to 10 CFU, are carried out during the Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques - Class L-24. The specific articulation of these professionalizing activities, defined by the university didactic regulations for L-24 courses, includes:
a) Activities for acquiring basic professional competencies related to empirical methods characteristic of all areas of psychology and techniques for evaluating the functioning of the mind and behavior, including their psychobiological correlates, in relation to different age groups and social and life contexts;
b) Activities for acquiring basic professional competencies related to psychological evaluation and the main forms of intervention on interpersonal, intragroup, and intergroup relationships in different social contexts, at the level of dyads, families, small groups, and organizations;
c) Analysis of the main forms of alteration of psychological processes and human behavior, in relation to different age groups and social and life contexts. The training of students carrying out TPV activities and the evaluation of such activities are entrusted to professional tutors registered with the Order for at least three years, whose educational and evaluative activities are conducted in accordance with the tutorial teaching regulations of the courses.
The course also includes, in relation to specific objectives, extracurricular activities and study stays at Italian and foreign universities, also within the framework of international agreements.
