Critical Judgment.
The graduate in Languages, Cultures and Techniques for Tourism acquires the ability to collect, select, and interpret market requests, directing them to the specific end-user (children, adults, people with disabilities, elderly, tourists from diverse linguistic-cultural areas and socio-cultural contexts) and to the specific entity/client. The acquired skill in selecting both relevant data for tourism offerings and interdisciplinary information, combined with the ability to reflect on socio-touristic and eco-compatible themes, contributes to the capacity to develop independent judgments, support complex arguments, and solve management problems related to the professional field of cultural tourism. The acquisition and verification of these competencies occur on-site through participation in laboratory activities (Audiovisual Laboratory, Cartographic Laboratory, Art Curation Laboratory, Archaeology Laboratory) and internship activities based on agreements with public and/or private leading entities within the regional, national, and international territory. Additionally, tutoring and career monitoring activities provided by the Course of Study (CdS) allow for continuous interaction between teachers and students, fostering a productive exchange aimed at maturing and verifying the acquired judgment capabilities.

Knowledge and Understanding.
Cultural and Territorial Area The graduate possesses a body of knowledge in areas related to the study of the territory, geographical, archaeological, historical, and anthropological heritage that characterize the cultural and social landscape, enabling the understanding and application of strategies useful for the valorization of tourism resources. The study of Tourism Geography, Economic and Political Geography, Geopolitics, and the Territorial Laboratory provides the graduate with a good awareness of complex phenomena related to contemporary reality, both in relation to the local territory's peculiarities and in the context of globalization, now indispensable. To these competencies are added knowledge regarding natural and urban landscapes and their changes, which are studied both from a cultural perspective (Social Anthropology and Audiovisual Landscapes) and from an ecological perspective (Integrated Quality and Environmental Management Systems for Tourism Operators, Topography and Cartography, Valorization of Landscape and Cultural Assets, Landscape Analysis). Thanks to the study of literature and the publishing system in the modern and contemporary age, the graduate has a good preparation in the field of literary publications, with reference also to the context of cultural tourism and its valorization. Additionally, the graduate possesses good preparation in the archaeological and historical field, both in the ancient aspect (Prehistoric and Protohistoric Archaeology Itineraries, Roman History) and in the modern and contemporary aspect (Museology); such knowledge enables them to understand the richness of territories and the development and valorization potential of cultural assets present therein.

Economic Area The graduate possesses good knowledge in the economic field as well as useful statistical notions that enable them to navigate the complex territory of tourism planning. The graduate in Languages, Cultures and Techniques for Tourism is indeed a hybrid figure, trained in interdisciplinarity, as they must necessarily combine traditional humanistic knowledge relevant to the Cultural and Territorial Area described above with a more technical body of knowledge. Thanks to the study of Business Economics, Economics and Management of Tourism Services, and Statistics, they possess good abilities to interpret processes of corporate value creation and issues that may affect the management of tourism companies, as well as the ability to read and interpret data and economic flows related to tourism and its induced sectors, and are also capable of applying innovative implementation and sustainable development strategies, deepened within the Tourism Management course.

Linguistic and Communication Area The graduate, in addition to a good knowledge of the Italian language, masters linguistic disciplines through the study of two foreign languages for two academic years, chosen from English, French, Spanish, and German. The study of languages ensures the acquisition of a good general and sector-specific preparation, and the ability to use the chosen languages fluently in the exchange of current information, as well as through the use of new communication techniques specific to the tourism sector. The acquisition of these competencies is ensured not only by institutional Language and Linguistics courses, but also by opportunities for study abroad through student mobility (Erasmus and Erasmus Placement Programs), and through self-training at the multimedia language laboratories of the Department of Humanities and Social Sciences. Connected to the ability to communicate is also the acquisition of psychological knowledge necessary to understand orientations and relationship mechanisms with others. Within the framework of communication skills, the graduate finally possesses good preparation in the field of modern and contemporary publishing, computer science, and new technologies, since social communication, careful use of network resources, and the ability to engage with basic computer tools are indispensable skills in a training path aimed at the valorization of cultural and sustainable tourism.

Legal Area The graduate possesses good knowledge in the legal field that enables them to navigate within the regulations governing tourism offerings. The graduate in Languages, Cultures and Techniques for Tourism, thanks to the study of legal disciplines, possesses the necessary competencies to navigate the opportunities offered by European measures and national and regional policies within the field of cultural and sustainable tourism (Public Tourism Law).

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Cultural and Territorial Area The graduate is capable of applying the acquired cultural and territorial knowledge in the concrete scenario of cultural and sustainable tourism. Indeed, they are capable of imagining alternative archaeological, historical, artistic, cultural, geographical, and natural itineraries that valorize the territory's cultural heritage, particularly but not exclusively local, in order to expand and enrich the tourism offer from the perspective of culture and environmental sustainability.

Economic Area The graduate is capable of applying the acquired economic knowledge within the vast and complex field of tourism planning and is able to identify useful tools for the managerial governance of enterprises and for the design of initiatives to enhance the tourism offer. Additionally, they are capable of analyzing data and information related to the territory and applying appropriate management strategies for the valorization, promotion, and development of cultural and sustainable tourism.

Linguistic and Communication Area The graduate is capable of applying the acquired linguistic and communication knowledge within the broad panorama of tourism communication. Therefore, they are able to produce texts related to the territory and tourism valorization, both in Italian and in the chosen foreign languages; they are also able to communicate content related to the tourism field appropriately, effectively, and fluently in conversation in Italian and the chosen foreign languages. The acquired computer skills finally enable them to navigate the web and produce content useful for the promotion and valorization of sustainable and cultural tourism on the web, social networks, and the main information dissemination channels.

Legal Area The graduate is able to employ the acquired legal competencies to navigate and operate within the regional and community legislative landscape. They are capable of interpreting fundamental public law norms and institutions, analyzing and identifying the main forms of legal organization of enterprises, and analyzing the legal relationships between parties involved in the enterprise-labor context.

Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN

Competencies Associated with the Function.
Tourism Operator in Various Contexts The work of planning and organization in the various fields connected to cultural tourism can be successfully carried out by the graduate thanks to the competencies acquired during their university training. Indeed, the graduate possesses strong linguistic competencies that enable them to move with confidence in an international work environment, geographical knowledge, as well as extensive knowledge regarding the valorization of natural and cultural resources, which are indispensable for the roles they will undertake. These competencies, combined with the historical, artistic, literary, and archaeological knowledge gained during their studies, will enable them to design alternative tourism proposals and navigate with awareness in the increasingly complex scenario of the cultural tourism market. The graduate indeed possesses technical competencies, so to speak, related to the field of tourism economics and management and tourism legislation, enabling them to navigate the concrete planning and programming of various events and initiatives related to cultural tourism. Regarding the communication field, which is certainly strategic in this context, the graduate possesses extensive capabilities matured both in the study of computer science and audiovisuals, as well as in linguistic training, since they will be able to communicate fluently in at least one foreign language (among the main European languages).

Function in the Workplace Context.
Tourism Operator in Various Contexts The graduate will be able to perform functions of a planning, organizational, and managerial nature within the field of cultural tourism and the valorization of territorial resources. Their training will enable them to interact most effectively in a team work context, collaborating with professionals from diverse backgrounds and training, particularly with communication experts, Blue and Green economy experts, and various professional figures related to the sustainable development of territories and the valorization of natural, cultural, artistic, and archaeological resources. In this scenario, they will be able to work, also in coordination roles, on the planning, programming, and direction of tourist itineraries; they will be able to design and realize cultural events aimed at the valorization of the territory; additionally, they will be able to design and organize tailor-made tourism programs for conferences, congresses, and fairs. In the field of education, the graduate will be able to design, plan, and create educational and cartographic material related to cultural and sustainable tourism; they will be able to plan and organize educational trips for schools of all levels, taking into account specific needs (trips for children, elderly, and/or people with disabilities); additionally, they will be able to design and organize trips requiring in-depth knowledge of specific cultural-touristic itineraries. In the communication field, the graduate will be able to collaborate with sector magazines, newspapers, and all channels present on web platforms through the production of texts and materials related to cultural and sustainable tourism and the valorization of territorial resources.

Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The Course of Study (CdS) proposes itself as a training response to the peculiarities of the territory that constitutes the main user base of the University of Sassari, characterized by a strong tourism vocation with high quality standards determined by the great relevance of the historical, archaeological, natural, and ethnographic heritage. The objective is to train cultural operators focused on the management, promotion, and valorization of territorial resources and the tourism sector in general, who, alongside adequate theoretical preparation, also possess the necessary operational skills and linguistic competencies that enable projection towards an international work dimension. To this end, the Course provides specific competencies on subjects related to cultural planning, both from a theoretical-methodological perspective and specific knowledge on prehistoric and historical archaeological heritage (L-ANT/01, 03), the valorization of environmental and cultural assets (L-ANT/10), museum heritage (L-ART/04), landscape analysis (M-GGR/01), tourism geography (M-GGR/02), cartography and topography (ICAR/06), social anthropology (M-DEA/01), linguistics (L-LIN/01), literature and the publishing system in modern and contemporary Italy (L-FIL-LET/11), audiovisual landscapes (L-ART/06), . Mastery of the main European languages is guaranteed by two academic years of a chosen language among French, English, Spanish, and German. These aspects are necessarily associated with a solid competence in the legal, economic, and statistical fields, which constitutes the indispensable basis for the management and organization of enterprises, companies, entities, and administrations active in the tourism sector (SECS-P/13; SECS-S/01), as well as the relevant legislative tools (IUS/09) and economic, financial, and tourism management tools (SECS-P/07, SECS-P/08). Equally important, for the success of a training project of this magnitude, is an adequate knowledge of the organizational culture of work contexts and psychological aspects (M-PSI/05), which ensures practical competence and places young graduates in a position to make choices regarding the orientation of the tourism offer itself. Within the framework of communication skills, there is also good preparation in the field of computer science (INF/01) and new audiovisual technologies (ensured by the Audiovisual Production Laboratory within the Department), since social communication, careful use of network resources, and the ability to engage with computer tools are indispensable skills for a training path aimed at the valorization of cultural and sustainable tourism. The training path guarantees the acquisition of communication skills and theoretical cultural preparation, functional to the construction of a solid professional preparation acquired through frontal lessons, laboratory courses, classroom courses, and which finds its practical completion through the mandatory attendance of a training internship carried out at public or private entities active in the tourism sector.

The graduate in Letters must acquire the ability to independently and critically evaluate and process the knowledge and methodologies acquired, with particular sensitivity to their ethical and social growth function.

Learning Ability.
The rigorous cultural training of the Letters graduate will lay the foundation for continuing studies to obtain the master's degree, as well as, eventually, university master's degrees and research doctorates. Specific Educational Objectives Description.
The Bachelor's Degree in Letters aims primarily and generally to provide foundational knowledge in the disciplines of the humanities field from antiquity to the present day, aiming to combine secure mastery of the national language, spoken and written, with knowledge of contemporary European and extra-European culture, primarily through languages and literatures. The marked attention to modern European and peri-European languages and literatures, which complements attention to the main disciplines of the humanistic tradition, can even be considered distinctive of the Course. Adequate training in humanistic informatics is also guaranteed.
Since this is a bachelor's degree with a predominant methodological vocation, the preferred occupational outcome for three-year graduates, namely teaching the so-called humanistic subjects in secondary schools, passes through continuing studies in the master's degree. Compared to the master's degree, the three-year degree provides largely the basic disciplinary competencies that will form the cultural backbone of the future teacher.
The three-year degree will also ensure participation in public competitions that require it as an indispensable requirement; in the private sector, it will ensure adequate training for operators with a broad and qualified humanistic spectrum in the fields of editorial activities and cultural promotion in a broad sense.
Specific educational objectives of the course are:
a) acquisition of basic knowledge in historical, artistic, geographical, and philosophical fields, with ability to read texts in the original;
b) acquisition of specific knowledge in the field of ancient and modern national, European, and extra-European literatures, relevant tools and methods, and ability to read literary texts in the original language of each tradition;
c) acquisition, in addition to full mastery of the Italian language (spoken and written) in its diachronic evolution, of satisfactory knowledge of one European Union second language, Latin language, and the Romance panorama;
d) acquisition of basic philological training, including knowledge of the history of philological sciences and their specific methods and tools, to be able to approach critical reading and analysis of literary texts in ancient and modern Italian and in classical languages;
e) acquisition of basic knowledge of historical and theoretical linguistics, with particular attention to synchronic language and language analysis models and to models explaining linguistic change.

Naturalist Technologist The career prospects for graduates in Natural Sciences can be placed in various fields:
- Public bodies responsible for territorial programming and control (Ministries, regional, provincial and municipal offices, forest authorities);
- Public environmental control structures (territorial technical services, ARPA);
- Bodies managing natural heritage (parks of all types, reserves, museums);
- Private professional studios engaged in research related to the analysis and evaluation of natural resources as project support for the realization of restoration and recovery works, impact and strategic assessment, and monitoring of natural and environmental resources (bioindicators of stress situations, pollution such as eutrophication);
- University institutes or other public and private institutions (Natural Sciences museums, bodies of the National Research Council, botanical gardens, aquariums) engaged in naturalistic research;
- Public and private structures responsible for teaching and disseminating scientific culture (schools, museums, NGOs etc.).
Graduates in Natural Sciences may access the state exam for the professional titles of Licensed Agrotechnician, Junior Biologist, Licensed Agricultural Engineer, Junior Landscape Planner to carry out professional activities.
Characteristics of final exam.
Degree examination with discussion of a thesis prepared based on the experience gained through an internship of at least 150 hours.
The objective of the final exam is to verify the maturity level achieved by the candidate who, without the aid of slides, must demonstrate to the examination committee for the Final Exam the ability to clearly and competently present and discuss a thesis related to the individual practical experience gained during the Internship period under the guidance of one or more supervisors.
The committee evaluates the candidate's ability for autonomous learning and their ability to retrieve bibliographic information and utilize available online databases.
Required knowledge for admission.
An initial preparation assessment test is required, which may entail additional educational obligations.
The required knowledge relates to adequate preparation in scientific subjects derived from attendance at secondary school;
in particular, for the initial preparation assessment, basic elements in mathematics are required.
Further details (such as verification methods, number and type of questions) are reported in the course's teaching regulations.
Degree awarded.

Communication skills.
The skills necessary for the exercise of the naturalist profession, with applications in broad contexts, will be developed during the training path within the study course. Graduates will be able to:
- effectively operate individually and as members of a group;
- use various methods to communicate effectively with the scientific community and generally with society on issues related to natural resources, the risks of their unsustainable use, and conservation and protection practices;
- effectively transmit information on the state of natural environments, the impact of naturalistic solutions in the social and environmental context of the reference territory,
- identify problems and propose solutions regarding the management of projects and practices for the use of natural resources, such as environmental risk management and change.

Acquisition methods and teaching tools: frontal courses and exercises will require continuous student participation and interaction with others. Examination assessments require written and/or oral presentation of a theoretical model, scientific paradigm, or concept with relevance, mastery, and linguistic proficiency.
Assessment: presentation and discussion of assignments, intermediate tests, and final exams.
Learning abilities.
Graduates will be provided with the necessary knowledge base to pursue a master's degree in natural and environmental sciences, as well as to undertake a level I master's course related to specific themes covered in the three-year program, such as environmental impact assessment, conservation and management of fauna and flora, and management of geosites of particular value.
Graduates will be prepared to profitably participate in courses aimed at training teachers for lower and upper secondary schools.
Additionally, the necessary foundations will be provided to maintain continuous updating on naturalist-environmental themes throughout the entire professional life. For this purpose, the following abilities will be developed:
- conduct advanced bibliographic research with reference to appropriate tools,
- identify university professors and high-level professionals in Italy on specific themes,
- identify European research institutes for continuous updating of specific knowledge.

Acquisition methods and teaching tools: the entire set of methods and teaching tools already described for other descriptors must enable the student to easily acquire the ability to learn all different themes and achieve the specified qualifying and specific training objectives.
Assessment: evaluation of assignments, intermediate tests, final exams, and final examination at the conclusion of the training path.

Independent Judgment.
Graduates will be autonomous in performing specific support roles in naturalistic projects coordinated by master's degree naturalists or other master's level professionals (engineers, architects, agronomists).
They will therefore develop the ability to make autonomous and responsible evaluations and judgments on issues concerning:
- territorial plans at various levels, in the characterization and quantification, also from an economic perspective, of natural resources and the impacts related to their exploitation;
- reintroduction and/or protection procedures for wild species,
- management of natural environments such as lakes, lagoons, habitats, forests, dunes, and in particular parks, marine protected areas, sites of community importance, special protection zones, and geosites.
They will have awareness of the social, health, and environmental implications of the adopted design solutions in different territorial contexts.
They will acquire awareness of the need for autonomous and continuous training and learning at any stage of their professional and personal life.
Acquisition methods and teaching tools: frontal courses and exercises will require the student to maintain continuous participation and interaction with others, even through the resolution of case studies.
Examination methods require the written and/or oral presentation of a theoretical model, a scientific paradigm, or a concept with relevance, mastery, and linguistic proficiency.
Assessment: presentation and discussion of reports, intermediate tests, and final exams.

the theoretical foundations of basic disciplines, particularly mathematical, physical, and chemical disciplines; the basic language related to these disciplines in Italian and English; the scientific method and its areas of application.
They also know the fundamentals of computer science and the main software useful for creating databases and processing data, and are able to quantify the value of natural resources.
Acquisition methods and teaching tools: knowledge and the ability to understand scientific and professional methods and content are acquired through frontal lessons with integrated teaching units including exercises and/or practical laboratory experiences.
Integrated laboratory activities are aimed at developing and achieving an adequate level of knowledge and understanding, and developing the ability to apply acquired knowledge in contexts limited to the phenomena under study, where applicable, through the guided use of appropriate scientific instrumentation.
Assessment: the verification of knowledge acquisition and understanding ability occurs through a final oral and/or written exam, and, where applicable, with intermediate knowledge tests. Active participation in exercises and practical experiences may also be evaluated.

in the combination of theory and practice to solve problems related to information acquisition;
in the evaluation of applicable techniques and methods and their limitations.
Acquisition methods and teaching tools: the ability to apply knowledge and understanding of scientific and professional methods and content is acquired through frontal lessons with integrated teaching units including exercises and/or practical field or laboratory experiences.
Integrated field or laboratory activities are aimed at developing and achieving an adequate level of knowledge and understanding, and the ability to apply acquired knowledge in contexts limited to the phenomena under study, even through the guided use of appropriate scientific instrumentation.
Assessment: the verification of the acquisition of knowledge and understanding ability occurs through a final oral and/or written exam, and, where applicable, with intermediate knowledge tests. Active participation in exercises and practical experiences may also be evaluated.
Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN
Competences Associated with the Function.
Naturalist Technologist For the performance of their functions, the Natural Sciences graduate relies on acquired competences that allow them to rigorously apply the scientific method, use standard monitoring methods, participate in multidisciplinary group work, disseminate information rigorously, continuously update their knowledge, and prepare reports in Italian and English.
Function in Work Context.
Naturalist Technologist The Natural Sciences graduate can find employment in public or private work contexts for performing various functions related to territorial management; monitoring the conservation status of habitats and animal and plant species and the effects of anthropogenic activities; controlling the health status of the environment; restoring compromised environmental resources; and scientific dissemination and environmental education.
Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The specific objectives of the degree course focus on structural and functional diversity at the biotic and abiotic levels within a systemic framework. In particular, diversity in all its systemic articulations, that is, at the level of individual, population, species, habitat, ecosystem, landscape, and biome, as well as at the level of geology, georesources, pedological and/or chemical, represent the educational objectives of this course.
Activities are aimed at providing basic knowledge in the indicated areas, as well as adequate preparation on general themes related to the territory and environment. These will be related to diversity and, in relation to specific objectives, integrated with mandatory laboratory, field, and internship activities.
The course will allow graduates, in accordance with the qualifying educational objectives of class L-32, to:
- acquire adequate knowledge of basic scientific and technical disciplines;
- effectively use, in written and oral form, in addition to Italian, the English language, within their specific area of competence and for the exchange of general information;
- develop appropriate tools for communication and information management, as well as for the continuous updating of environmental and natural knowledge;
- recognize the terrestrial and marine natural environmental system in its structural and functional specificity, also as a legal subject, thereby developing an appropriate awareness of the ethical dimension of their professionalism;
- approach the analysis of natural and environmental systems in a systematic manner, valuing and promoting their complexity and diversity within the non-negotiable scenario of environmental sustainability and permissibility, also from an economic value perspective and their related management policies;
- acquire the fundamental and essential methodologies of scientific investigation and be able to collaborate in experimental activities, as well as be capable of identifying problems;
- actively participate in problem-solving to maintain and promote terrestrial and/or aquatic environmental diversity and complexity;
- perform technical, managerial, and support tasks in environmental control and monitoring activities, in museums, laboratories, and services of public and private institutions.
The educational path is structured to develop specific competences in the various fields of Natural Sciences starting from solid basic knowledge. In particular, in the first year, basic disciplines are covered and biological and earth sciences disciplines are introduced; in the second year, ample space is given to characteristic disciplines, particularly biological, ecological, and earth sciences. English language skills are also introduced. In the third year, to complete the educational path, related and integrative disciplines are also included.
Student elective exams allow for personalization of the educational path.

Characteristics of the final exam.
The final exam, taking into account the characteristics of the training path, consists of the presentation and discussion of a written report or multimedia products with originality, capable of documenting the graduate's ability to analyze a chosen topic and communicate it effectively, with a thorough and updated review of the scientific content on the subject.
Required knowledge for access.

Function in work context.
Level I Communication Professional From a functional perspective, the graduate fits the profile of a Level I Communication Professional (defined according to UNI 11483/2013 standard, in line with the European Qualifications Framework EQF): a person who manages communication content and tools for work to achieve specific and clearly defined goals, on behalf of public, private, and non-profit institutions, and individuals.
Functional areas in professional contexts:
a) external communication functions (commercial correspondence, institutional correspondence, house organs, instructional texts for product use, public presentation texts, sponsorship texts, advertising and sales promotion texts, etc.);
b) public relations functions (public relations with other companies, competitors, citizens, mass media, public bodies, etc.);
c) internal communication functions (labor union communications, technical documentation in paper and digital form, service orders, communications between employees, between employees and managers, and between managers, etc.);
d) digital content implementation functions for web and social media (Internet, intranet, websites, social network sites, promotional CD-ROMs, etc.);
e) textual and audiovisual production functions (ideation, coordination, and management of messages for mass audiences, mastering traditional media and new media such as print, radio, television, and the entire multimedia systems associated with them, including web development).
Specific training objectives description.
The Study Course aims to train a Level I professional communicator, thus providing the necessary complex set of basic knowledge, skills, and competencies for managing communication content and tools, on which graduates can build subsequent professional specialization pathways of Level II, through formal, informal, or non-formal education activities.
In today's society, given the evolving dynamics of the labor market, interdisciplinarity becomes fundamental, and training must cover a broad thematic spectrum, taking into account the different sectors of communication: from journalism and information to various fields of the cultural industry, up to public, institutional, political communication, and organizational and corporate communication. Particular attention is also given to the development of new communication technologies, both from a theoretical reflection perspective and from the application perspective in specific multimedia environments aimed at enhancing human-machine interaction principles and new communication forms enabled by digital environments.
The two curricula (Political and Institutional Communication, Multimedia Communication and Journalism) are designed to emphasize, especially in the first year, the contribution of a qualified set of disciplines, such as linguistics and language theory, public law or information law, sociology of cultural processes, social research methodology, English language. The acquisition of interdisciplinary conceptual tools is completed in the second and third years through training activities related to economic and socio-political disciplines.
Starting from the second year, the teaching path focuses on activities more oriented towards the professional profiles defined by the class, through technological courses and communication sociology directed, also with laboratory activities, towards acquiring knowledge and competencies related to the cultural industry and media production.
The third year is finally reserved for building a path aimed at developing the specific vocations, interests, and talents of each student, including various courses in the communication area, ranging from public communication, journalism, radio-television languages, to corporate communication.
Alongside general critical reflection and the development of transversal competencies, a more technical training is provided, which can concretize in training internships at public and private companies, also to facilitate adequate employment outcomes. The Study Course therefore provides for and values the realization of internships and traineeships at public bodies, publishing companies, communication and advertising agencies, private companies, associations, and non-profit organizations, both in Italy and abroad. Teaching is structured into lectures, exercises, laboratories, case study analysis and development, and training internships. Active learning methods are emphasized, which through interaction and collaboration among students with teachers and other students, aim to foster the development of individual competencies and the ability to work in groups. Students are encouraged to build and deepen their knowledge through the study and discussion of emerging topics, both through seminar-style training proposals and through concrete involvement in specific projects of planning, research, and role-playing.
The Study Course, in line with the Department's guidelines in promoting and valuing international student mobility for study and internship purposes, actively participates in mobility programs provided by European education policies and considers the performance of study and internship activities abroad an integral part of its educational offer. For this reason, it adheres to various European and extra-European programs that, within the framework of inter-university cooperation agreements, facilitate, according to a principle of reciprocity, international student mobility.
The academic activity calendar, structured into two semesters, provides a balanced distribution of teaching loads with reference to students' learning abilities and CFU acquisition. Teaching, oriented to stimulate interaction and collaboration between teacher and student, takes place through lectures and seminars, also with the participation of professionals and external teachers (visiting professors), exercises, laboratory activities, project works, and self-assessment tests. Intermediate tests are also provided for profit exams.
Traditional learning verification activities are complemented by systematic use of the Department's e-Learning platform (Moodle), which allows both the use of a wide variety of evaluation tools and the monitoring of proposed study activities through specific reporting. Working in synergy with the University's orientation services, a team of teachers is responsible for tutoring activities, particularly for first-year students, with the aim of assessing student career progression, any emerging difficulties, and the actions to be taken to overcome them.

The bachelor's degree provides access to all second-cycle degree programs, including University Master's Programs of the first level Professional status conferred by the degree.
Chemistry graduates position themselves within a competence framework that ideally lies between the high-executive type competences typical of Technical Institute Diplomas (e.g., chemical engineer from Industrial Technical Institute) and the ideative-planning competences typical of Master's Degree Holders (or specialist graduates, or doctoral graduates in Chemistry) in Chemical Sciences. In essence, the Chemistry graduate has a sufficiently broad overview of chemical disciplines coupled with good practical skills and autonomy in laboratory and experimental activities. They correctly interpret data obtained from instruments/apparatus entrusted to them and can propose simple variations in procedures and methods in relation to the type of chemical problem addressed. The good mastery of the scientific method enables them to interact constructively within multidisciplinary contexts Self-employment, industrial employment, research and analysis laboratories, institutions dealing with environmental protection, conservation of cultural heritage, health, energy, and materials science.

Final exam characteristics.
The final exam consists of presenting and discussing in front of a designated committee a written report related to the experimental activity carried out by the student during the final internship. The internship can be completed at a university structure or an external institution recognized and accepted according to the Regulation. To be admitted to the final exam, all exams must be passed and all credits acquired in the training activities specified in the study plan Required knowledge for admission.
Enrollment in the Chemistry degree requires possession of a high school diploma or equivalent qualification. For optimal integration into the training activities specified in the Chemistry degree study plan, students are required to have:
- Mathematics knowledge and skills corresponding to the programs offered in secondary technical-scientific schools
- Adequate logical, reading, and comprehension abilities
- Mastery of the Italian language in both oral and written form, including basic scientific terminology The Chemistry degree program website will make available a syllabus of the mathematics and logic knowledge considered necessary for those intending to enroll in the degree program.
To verify the required knowledge for admission, all enrolled students or those intending to enroll must take a test consisting of multiple-choice questions. Students who fail the test will be assigned additional mandatory training requirements to be fulfilled in the first year of the course. Students who have not taken and passed the initial preparation verification test or the mathematics exam by this deadline cannot enroll in the second year but must choose between repeating the first year or switching to part-time status.
To guide student preparation for the basic knowledge verification test and ensure an adequate initial preparation level for all enrolled students, the Chemistry degree program may organize pre-courses in Mathematics, typically held before the start of lectures.

Communication Skills.
The graduate possesses the ability to organize in a concise yet comprehensive and scientifically accurate manner the results of their activities both in written and oral form. For this, they know how to use appropriate computer-based tools for communicating technical-scientific information and demonstrate an adequate level of English knowledge for understanding and critically reading scientific articles on topics related to experimental disciplines, in particular of a chemical nature. This skill is enhanced through experience gained during assessments connected to courses requiring the presentation of a summary report or the critical reading of scientific articles. A decisive moment for verifying communication skills is represented by the final examination.
Learning Ability.
The student develops the ability for autonomous learning and study, becoming independent and self-sufficient in addressing new topics, setting study methods, and using laboratory and analysis techniques not specifically covered in the study program. They acquire mastery and ability in retrieving bibliographic information by utilizing available online databases. A decisive moment for verifying the level of learning is the Internship, during which the student combines theory and practice in analyzing problems of relevance and current scientific importance, works in a group, and experiences autonomous learning, thereby consolidating awareness of their inclinations and aptitudes. Upon completion of all examinations required by the study program and the final examination, it is considered that graduates possess the learning abilities that enable them to successfully continue studies in a master's degree or a first-level master's program, even internationally, or to enter the workforce with good prospects of achieving appropriate professional levels.

Critical Judgment.
The study of disciplines based on theoretical and methodological criteria facilitates the development of a critical attitude aimed at selecting the most appropriate approach to address and solve specific problems. Achieving these goals stems from laboratory experience, autonomy in interpreting results, and commitment to presenting them in written and oral form. Graduates must be able to collect data from a variety of sources, compare directly obtained experimental results with those in the scientific literature, critically evaluate the reliability of different techniques and methodologies, and draft appropriate concluding reports to be presented orally. An important moment for developing critical sense and appreciating the graduate's ability to translate it into personal reflections on study topics occurs during their integration into the research group and/or applied experimentation group under the guidance of a scientific supervisor during the Internship period.
Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area: SYNTHESIS Expected knowledge and understanding: fundamental constituents of matter and chemical structure of simple systems at the atomic level; methods for measuring properties and expressing results; relationships between properties and composition; chemical transformations and involved energy exchanges; synthesis reactions of chemical substances and materials; main application fields of polymers and macromolecular systems; interactions of substances and materials with the environment, life cycle of substances and materials, recovery and recycling; fundamental chemical and physical properties and their determination; theoretical aspects of methodologies for property determination. For the correct learning process, participation in frontal lectures, theoretical-practical exercises, and laboratory experimental activities is essential. For knowledge and understanding, the Internship—a training activity conducted under the guidance of a scientific supervisor at the University's departmental structures or external companies and bodies—plays a significant role. The Internship and various forms of assisted teaching activities serve as tools through which students develop the ability to demonstrate understanding by presenting brief written reports on exercise topics and laboratory experiences. In this context, the mutual interaction between students and teachers during frontal lectures and, particularly, during laboratory activities plays a decisive role. The verification of the learning process is defined by each instructor and may consist of passing oral exams, in-course assessments in the form of closed or open-ended tests, or brief reports on practical work conducted during laboratory experiment design and execution. This is supplemented by the evaluation of the final exam report presented orally during the graduation session.
Basic Disciplines Basic Disciplines (Mathematics, Physics, and Basic Chemistry)
Students acquire an integrated knowledge framework through basic disciplines, enabling the application of fundamental concepts to understand the content of characterizing courses.
Chemistry graduates must have acquired:
basic mathematical knowledge:
- elementary algebra, calculations with complex numbers, linear algebra, methods for solving linear systems, function analysis, differential and integral calculus, statistical treatment of experimental data.
basic physical knowledge:
- mechanics, classical thermodynamics, optics, electromagnetism.
basic chemical knowledge:
- chemical terminology and nomenclature;
- use of measurement units;
- physical states and properties of matter;
- properties of elements and their compounds;
- relationships between groups and trends in the Periodic Table;
- chemical bonding;
- classes of chemical reactions and stoichiometry.
Characterizing Disciplines Chemistry graduates must have acquired knowledge and understanding in the following areas:
- fundamental constituents of matter and chemical structure of simple systems at the atomic level;
- methods for measuring properties and expressing results;
- relationships between properties and composition, and properties and structure;
- chemical transformations and involved energy exchanges;
- synthesis reactions of chemical substances and materials;
- main structural investigation techniques;
- main application fields of polymers and macromolecular systems;
- interactions of substances and materials with the environment, recovery and recycling;
- fundamental chemical and physical properties and their determination;
- theoretical aspects of methodologies for property determination;
- nomenclature, three-dimensional structure, chemical and physical properties of organic compounds;
- nomenclature, three-dimensional structure, chemical and physical properties of inorganic compounds;
- main types of chemical reactions and their characteristics;
- principles and procedures used in chemical analysis and characterization of chemical compounds;
- main instrumental investigation techniques and their applications in analytical chemistry;
- error analysis;
- principles of thermodynamics and their applications;
- principles of quantum mechanics and their applications;
- principles of chemical kinetics and mechanistic interpretation of chemical reactions;
- nature and behavior of functional groups in organic molecules;
- reactions and synthesis mechanisms in organic chemistry;
- principles and methods of analytical chemistry;
- chemical equilibria and simultaneous equilibria;
- meaning and correct expression of analytical data;
- structure and reactivity of important classes of biomolecules and chemistry of important biological processes;
- main aspects of structure-property relationships in organic, organometallic, and polymeric compounds.
For the correct learning process, participation in frontal lectures, theoretical-practical exercises, and laboratory experimental activities is essential. For knowledge and understanding, the Internship—a training activity conducted under the guidance of a scientific supervisor at the University's departmental structures or external companies and bodies—plays a significant role. The Internship and various forms of assisted teaching activities serve as tools through which students develop the ability to demonstrate understanding by presenting brief written reports on exercise topics and laboratory experiences. In this context, the mutual interaction between students and teachers during frontal lectures and, particularly, during laboratory activities plays a decisive role. The verification of the learning process is defined by each instructor and may consist of passing oral exams, in-course assessments in the form of closed or open-ended tests, or brief reports on practical work conducted during laboratory experiment design and execution. This is supplemented by the evaluation of the final exam report presented orally during the graduation session.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area: SYNTHESIS The course organization is structured to provide graduates with the tools to address and solve problems in various fields of chemistry through the selection of appropriate techniques and methodologies, respecting bioethical and environmental issues. Expected outcomes in terms of knowledge and skills: know how to describe in simple terms the atomic and molecular structure of substances; know how to perform simple syntheses of chemical substances and materials; know how to measure fundamental chemical and physical properties; know how to describe the effects of chemical transformations of matter; know how to measure energy transfers; know how to determine relationships between properties and composition; know how to use bibliographic and computer tools; know how to handle substances safely; know how to classify waste substances, exhausted solvents, processing residues, and dispose of them correctly; ability to work in a group and operate with a sense of responsibility; know how to identify relationships between measured chemical and physical properties and chemical composition; know how to correctly calculate fundamental properties in relation to the composition of a pure substance or mixture; know how to apply methodologies for the experimental determination of properties; ability to work on projects to solve simple real problems. Verification is carried out through oral or written exams, both aimed at verifying not only the level of learning but also maturity and critical ability in addressing study topics.
Basic Disciplines Basic Disciplines (Mathematics, Physics, and Basic Chemistry)
Chemistry graduates must be able to apply mathematical methods to analyze and solve problems in the chemical field. Graduates must also be able to use the laws governing physical phenomena in interpreting physical and chemical phenomena.
In the chemical field, graduates must be able to:
- perform stoichiometric calculations;
- conduct practical operations related to solution preparation;
- safely use and manage the correct disposal of chemical substances;
- collect and process experimental data in relation to general chemistry principles;
- perform standard preparations and purifications;
- apply basic chemistry knowledge across various chemistry sectors.
Laboratory activities complement theoretical activities to enable students to:
- know and practice safety rules in chemical laboratories;
- know and use common laboratory glassware and equipment;
- know and use common chemical reagents.
For the correct learning process, participation in frontal lectures, theoretical-practical exercises, and laboratory experimental activities is essential. The verification of the learning process is defined by each instructor and may consist of passing oral and/or written exams, in-course assessments in the form of closed or open-ended tests, or brief reports on practical work conducted during laboratory experiment design and execution.
Characterizing Disciplines The course organization is structured to provide graduates with the tools to address and solve problems in various fields of chemistry through the selection of appropriate techniques and methodologies, respecting bioethical and environmental issues.
Expected outcomes:
- know how to describe in simple terms the atomic and molecular structure of substances;
- know how to perform simple syntheses of chemical substances and materials;
- know how to measure fundamental chemical and physical properties;
- know how to describe the effects of chemical transformations of matter;
- know how to interpret results from common structural investigations;
- know how to measure energy transfers;
- know how to determine relationships between properties and composition;
- know how to perform simple analytical determinations with due rigor using completely developed and described methodologies;
- be able to choose, among known possibilities, the most suitable analytical method for solving a simple analytical problem;
- be able to correctly express the results of an analytical determination;
- know how to use bibliographic and computer tools;
- know how to handle substances safely;
- know how to classify waste substances, exhausted solvents, processing residues, and dispose of them correctly;
- possess the ability to work in a group and operate with a sense of responsibility;
- know how to identify relationships between measured chemical and physical properties and chemical composition;
- know how to correctly calculate fundamental properties in relation to the composition of a pure substance or mixture;
- know how to apply methodologies for the experimental determination of properties;
- possess project-work ability to solve simple real problems;
- be able to solve problems in various fields of chemistry by selecting appropriate techniques and methodologies, also respecting environmental issues;
- know and use programs for calculating molecular energy and structure.
Verification is carried out through oral or written exams, both aimed at verifying not only the level of learning but also maturity and critical ability in addressing study topics.
Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN Competencies Associated with the Role.
Chemistry graduates position themselves within a competency framework that ideally lies between high-executive competencies typical of Technical Institute Diplomas (e.g., chemical engineer from Industrial Technical Institute) and ideative-planning competencies typical of Master's Degree holders (or specialized graduates, or doctoral graduates in Chemistry) in Chemical Sciences. In essence, the Chemistry graduate has a sufficiently broad understanding of chemical disciplines coupled with good practice and autonomy in laboratory and experimental activities. They correctly interpret data obtained from instruments/apparatus assigned to them and are able to propose simple variations in procedures and methods in relation to the type of chemical problem addressed. The good level of mastery of the scientific investigation method enables them to interact constructively within multidisciplinary contexts. Adequate understanding of chemical aspects associated with industrial fields, research and analysis laboratories, environmental protection, cultural heritage conservation, health, energy, and materials science.
Good ability to use chemical instrumentation, even non-routine, and interpret data derived from it.
Ability to propose modifications to aspects of chemical procedures and analysis methods in relation to the specific nature of the problem at hand.
Sufficient level of interaction in multidisciplinary contexts.
Good degree of autonomy in their work, potential ability to coordinate a small group of subordinates.
Potentially able to perform freelance activities as a Category B Chemist.
Role in the Workplace Context.
Chemistry graduates position themselves within a competency framework that ideally lies between high-executive competencies typical of Technical Institute Diplomas (e.g., chemical engineer from Industrial Technical Institute) and ideative-planning competencies typical of Master's Degree holders (or specialized graduates, or doctoral graduates in Chemistry) in Chemical Sciences. In essence, the Chemistry graduate has a sufficiently broad understanding of chemical disciplines coupled with good practice and autonomy in laboratory and experimental activities. They correctly interpret data obtained from instruments/apparatus assigned to them and are able to propose simple variations in procedures and methods in relation to the type of chemical problem addressed. The good level of mastery of the scientific investigation method enables them to interact constructively within multidisciplinary contexts. Chemistry graduates find employment in industrial settings, research and analysis laboratories, environmental protection, cultural heritage conservation, health, energy, and materials science sectors, as well as in freelance activities as a Category B Chemist. They are able to conveniently apply the experimental method, use scientific instrumentation with a good degree of autonomy (or quickly learn the principles and usage modes of complex instruments), correctly interpret results from analytical measurements of even non-routine nature, plan their activities and those of a small group under their supervision with a certain degree of autonomy, and interact constructively with multidisciplinary scientific contexts.
Description of Specific Educational Objectives.
The Chemistry degree from the University of Sassari provides theoretical, methodological, experimental, and applied competencies in the fundamental areas of Chemistry. The fundamental objective of the course is to create a figure capable of accessing the widest possible range of opportunities in scientific and technological fields, offered by the diverse current job market. Graduates will be able to apply acquired competencies in industrial, research and analysis laboratory, environmental protection, cultural heritage conservation, health, and energy sectors.
Graduates will be able to use complex scientific equipment and apply the scientific investigation method, even in relation to practical problems, in all sectors involving chemical methodologies, technologies, and processes. Graduates must also have developed the necessary learning abilities to pursue future studies with a sufficient degree of autonomy.
Regarding the Chemistry sector, graduates must acquire the following disciplinary competencies and practical skills:
- knowledge and understanding of essential facts, concepts, and principles, as well as theories related to the identified disciplinary area.
- the ability to apply such knowledge and understanding to solve common qualitative and quantitative problems.
- the ability to evaluate, interpret, and synthesize chemical information and data.
- the ability to recognize and implement, through theoretical and experimental knowledge, good laboratory practice.
- ability to present scientific materials and arguments in oral and written form to a competent audience, even in English.
- computer and data-processing skills related to chemical information and data.
- ability to handle chemical materials safely, considering their physical and chemical properties, including specific risks associated with their use.
- ability to conduct standard laboratory processes, including the use of instrumentation for synthesis and analysis activities, in relation to both organic and inorganic systems.
- ability to monitor, through observation and measurement of chemical and physical properties, events or transformations of real systems, through systematic and reliable recording and documentation of process variables.
- ability to interpret data derived from laboratory observation and measurement, and relate them to appropriate theories.
- ability to use computer tools and automatic calculation tools in the collection, management, processing, and transfer of scientific data.
Organization of the Educational Path.
The new educational path is structured as a study plan with a single track lasting three years and totaling 180 credit points. Training activities will be organized on a semester basis and, depending on the specific characteristics of each course, may be conducted differently (frontal lectures, practical and seminar activities, experimental exercises, internships, etc.). The weekly workload for each CFU is defined in the Academic Regulations.
In accordance with the Chemistry Eurobachelor (CE) model, the educational path is based on a predominant core of CFUs (at least 127) in the areas of Mathematics, Physics, Analytical Chemistry, Physical Chemistry, Inorganic Chemistry, Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry, Industrial Chemistry. Credits are distributed between theoretical courses and practical exercises and laboratory courses (at least 30 CFUs). Affine and integrative activities extend to at least 18 CFUs, and student-choice activities to 12 CFUs. For this second area, while maintaining the freedom of choice and proposal by individuals, consistency with the course's educational project is required. Four (4) CFUs are reserved for linguistic skills, understood as knowledge of the English language, an indispensable tool for communication in the scientific field. Fourteen (14) CFUs are allocated to training internships and the final exam, consisting of the presentation and discussion of a written report related to the internship activity performed. These are acquired upon passing the final exam. The maximum number of credits recognizable for professional activities or other skills and competencies acquired in advanced extracurricular training activities in accordance with Article 5 of DM 270/2004 is set at 30 CFUs.

Medical Radiology Technician The TSRM works as an employee or self-employed professional in hospitals, clinics, outpatient clinics, medical and dental offices, and generally in public or private facilities.
Final exam characteristics.
To be admitted to the final exam, all credits in the training activities provided for in the study plan must be earned, including having completed the required training internships.
The final exam, which has the value of a State Exam enabling the profession of Medical Radiology Technician, Imaging and Radiotherapy, consists of:
a) Practical test, in which the student must demonstrate to have acquired the theoretical-practical and technical-operative knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile.
b) Thesis dissertation. The thesis will address a topic related to one of the basic, characterizing, related or complementary scientific-disciplinary fields, or otherwise consistent with the training objectives of the degree course; in the work, the student reports the acquired knowledge on the topic, demonstrating the ability to critically process information derived from research on bibliographic data consulted.
Students who fail the practical test cannot be admitted to the thesis dissertation.
For the thesis work, the student will be supervised by a lecturer of the degree course, called the supervisor, and by any co-supervisors, also external to the degree course.
The final grade (expressed in hundredths, with possible honors) is determined by the following parameters:
- weighted average of the marks obtained in the exams converted to hundredths;
- points assigned by the Graduation Committee for the final exam based on the following parameters: practical test, thesis work, graduation in progress, honors obtained in the exams, participation in international exchange programs (Internships or Erasmus programs).
The Final Exam Committee, appointed by the Dean of the Faculty, consists of a minimum of seven to a maximum of eleven members, to be chosen among Professors and Researchers or lecturers of teaching (one of whom is the Course Coordinator or his substitute, who serves as Committee Chair), the General Internship Coordinator or his substitute and at least 2 representatives proposed by the Professional College. The majority of the Committee members must be permanent lecturers. To these names are added in excess 2 representatives, respectively designated by the Ministry of University and Research and the Ministry of Health. In case of failure to designate by the Ministries, the Rector exercises the substitutive power.
The final exam is organized in two sessions in periods defined at national level by a decree of the Ministry of University in agreement with the Competent Ministry. The first, normally, in the period October-November and the second in March-April. The dates are set by the Class Council Coordinator.
Required knowledge for access.
To be admitted to the degree course, one must possess a high school diploma or another foreign degree recognized as suitable; additionally, one must possess or acquire adequate initial preparation, obtained through previous studies, in mathematics, physics, chemistry and biology, general culture and logical reasoning.
The course is nationally programmed, in accordance with Article 1 of Law 264/1999; the provisions on national programming annually issued by the Ministry of University and Research and published in the competition notices apply.
The admission test has a selective function and is also intended to verify the possession of adequate initial preparation.
Students admitted to the degree course who obtained a score below the annual threshold set by the Course Council in the admission test are assigned additional mandatory training obligations in the disciplines of Chemistry, Biology and Physics. The Course Council defines the recovery activities for the training debt to be carried out obligatorily during the first year of the course; personalized recovery plans will be activated under the responsibility of the lecturers of the disciplines or of specially selected teaching tutors. The training debts are considered fulfilled with a written verification of the integrated part at the same time as the regular exam of the relevant courses.
Expected employment and professional opportunities for graduates.
Medical Radiology Technician The TSRM works as an employee or self-employed professional in hospitals, clinics, outpatient clinics, medical and dental offices, and generally in public or private facilities.

Judgment Autonomy.
Considering the level of responsibility assumed by graduates during the performance of their professional role, the educational standard is such as to allow professional autonomy within a multidisciplinary approach to patient management. In this context, autonomy refers to taking responsibility for one's professional role in the accurate planning, delivery, and control of the diagnostic technical process (acquisition, processing, printing, archiving, and remote transmission) or therapeutic process (e.g., a radiation treatment during work in therapy units).

Knowledge and Understanding.
1) Foundational Sciences Graduates must have demonstrated knowledge and understanding in each of the following fields:
- Detailed topographic anatomy of the musculoskeletal system and central nervous system, general anatomy of all human systems, in preparation for radiological imaging;
- General principles of biology, histology, medical chemistry, and biochemistry necessary for understanding physiological and pathological processes;
- Fundamental physics necessary for understanding electric and magnetic fields, wave phenomena, emission and absorption of electromagnetic and corpuscular radiation, and more generally physiological and pathological processes of interest;
- General principles of physiology and pathology of interest;
- Fundamentals of radiobiology and radiation protection;
- Physical foundations of equipment and imaging in conventional radiology, computed tomography, nuclear magnetic resonance, mammography, interventional radiology, angiography, neuroradiology, nuclear medicine diagnostics and therapy, radiotherapy, all to facilitate achieving higher quality through a deeper understanding of the involved processes.

Graduates must have demonstrated knowledge of written and spoken English up to the intermediate level (B1) in order to study topics within their field in English texts, to be able to ask questions to English-speaking patients and understand their responses.

Teaching Methods and Activities, Didactic Tools to Develop Expected Outcomes:
• Frontal lectures and seminar activities;
• Videos, image demonstrations, diagrams and materials, graphs;
• Case discussions.

Evaluation Tools to Verify Achievement of Expected Outcomes:
• Written and oral interim assessments, written and oral exams, staged case tests, project work, reports;
• Evaluation feedback during internship;
• Structured objective station examination;
• Debriefing sessions to reflect and reprocess professional practice experiences;
• Didactic Laboratories.

Clinical and Radiological Sciences Graduates must have demonstrated knowledge and understanding in each of the following fields:
- Formation of anatomical images in conventional radiology, computed tomography, nuclear magnetic resonance, mammography, interventional radiology, angiography, neuroradiology, nuclear medicine, and their main indications; analysis of image characteristics and quality; principles of radiometabolic therapy and radiotherapy and their indications;
- Equipment and techniques of conventional radiology, computed tomography, nuclear magnetic resonance, mammography, interventional radiology, angiography, neuroradiology, nuclear medicine, and radiotherapy; use and preparation of radiopharmaceuticals;
- Principles of psychology to facilitate establishing correct relationships with the patient, their relatives, specialist doctors, technical colleagues, and support staff;
- Foundations of life support, internal medicine; nursing sciences, similarities and differences in tasks between nursing and medical radiology graduates;
- Elements of medical-surgical sciences and interdisciplinary clinical sciences chosen from the fields of particular interest.

Teaching Methods and Activities, Didactic Tools to Develop Expected Outcomes:
• Frontal lectures and seminar activities
• Videos, image demonstrations, diagrams and materials, graphs
• Case discussions

Evaluation Tools to Verify Achievement of Expected Outcomes:
• Written and oral interim assessments, written and oral exams, staged case tests, project work, reports.
• Evaluation feedback during internship
• Structured objective station examination
• Debriefing sessions to reflect and reprocess professional practice experiences
• Didactic Laboratories

Prevention and Management Graduates must have demonstrated knowledge and understanding in each of the following fields:
- Radiation protection and quality control of equipment, with particular attention to operational aspects of interest, both in diagnostic and therapeutic settings;
- Fundamental computer science necessary for managing equipment in use and ensuring quality in therapeutic interventions and in the production, processing, transmission, and archiving of images; fundamental statistics for information processing; fundamental organizational health sciences and information systems; e-learning;
- Principles of prevention sciences and health services, with regard to personal and workplace hygiene, occupational medicine, and legal medicine, to be aware of risks and responsibilities in performing interventions within their competence; principles of professional ethics;
